question: (a) Define abortion and classify it. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and management of threatened, inevitable, incomplete, complete and missed abortion. (8 marks) (c) Describe septic abortion – its causes, clinical features, complications, management and nursing care. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Clinical types of spontaneous abortion
labels: Five uterus sketches side by side – threatened (slight bleeding
sac intact with live embryo); inevitable (os open
membranes bulging or ruptured); incomplete (part of the products in the cervical canal
uterus smaller than dates); complete (uterus empty and contracted

answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks)

Definition

  • Abortion (miscarriage) is the expulsion or extraction of an embryo or fetus from the uterus before it is viable – that is, before 20 completed weeks of pregnancy, or when the fetus weighs less than 500 g (WHO).
  • In everyday speech, a spontaneous loss is called a "miscarriage" and a deliberate termination an "abortion"; medically, both are abortions.
  • About 10–20% of clinically recognised pregnancies end in spontaneous abortion, and about 80% of these happen in the first trimester.

Classification

Group Types
Spontaneous (occurs on its own) Threatened, inevitable, incomplete, complete, missed and septic abortion; recurrent miscarriage (traditionally three or more consecutive losses; many guidelines now use two)
Induced (deliberately ended) Legal (safe) – medical termination of pregnancy by a registered medical practitioner at an approved place under the MTP Act 1971 (amended 2021); Illegal (unsafe) – by untrained persons or in unhygienic conditions, the commonest cause of septic abortion

Common causes of spontaneous abortion

  • Chromosomal abnormalities of the embryo – about half of first-trimester losses (trisomies, monosomy X, triploidy).
  • Maternal factors – uncontrolled diabetes or thyroid disease, uterine anomalies (septate uterus), submucous fibroids, cervical insufficiency (second-trimester loss), antiphospholipid syndrome, severe infections (malaria, high fever, TORCH), trauma, smoking, alcohol and some drugs.
  • In many women no cause is found.

(b) Clinical features and management of the types of spontaneous abortion (8 marks)

Type Bleeding and pain Cervical os Uterine size Ultrasound
Threatened Slight bleeding; little or no pain Closed Equal to dates Live embryo with cardiac activity
Inevitable Heavy bleeding with colicky pain Open; membranes felt or ruptured Equal to or less than dates Sac low in the uterus or in the cervix
Incomplete Bleeding continues; cramps; part of the products passed Open; tissue felt at the os Smaller than dates Retained products
Complete Bleeding and pain settle Closed Small and firm Empty uterus, thin endometrium
Missed Brownish discharge or none; pregnancy symptoms regress Closed Smaller than dates No cardiac activity (CRL ≥7 mm) or empty sac (mean diameter ≥25 mm)

1. Threatened abortion

  • The pregnancy is threatened but may continue: slight vaginal bleeding, mild or no lower abdominal pain, closed os, uterine size matching the dates.
  • Management
    • Confirm with transvaginal ultrasound (live intrauterine pregnancy, size, subchorionic haematoma); check haemoglobin, blood group and Rh type.
    • Reassure – most pregnancies continue normally once fetal heart activity is seen.
    • Advise relative rest and avoidance of heavy work and intercourse until the bleeding stops; strict bed rest has not been shown to help.
    • Vaginal micronised progesterone may be prescribed when there is bleeding and a history of previous miscarriage.
    • Anti-D immunoglobulin for an Rh-negative woman when bleeding is heavy or after 12 weeks.
    • Teach her to report heavy bleeding, increasing pain, passage of tissue or fever; repeat the scan in 1–2 weeks.

2. Inevitable abortion

  • The process has gone too far to be stopped – increasing bleeding, painful uterine contractions, an open os, with or without rupture of membranes.
  • Management
    • Admit; record pulse, BP and blood loss; start an IV line with Ringer lactate or normal saline; send blood for grouping and cross-matching; treat shock.
    • Before 12 weeks – evacuate the uterus by manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) or electric suction, or give misoprostol.
    • After 12 weeks – hasten expulsion with oxytocin infusion or misoprostol, then check that the products are complete and remove any retained tissue.
    • Oxytocics to control bleeding; anti-D for Rh-negative women.

3. Incomplete abortion

  • Part of the products (usually the fetus) is expelled; the placenta or membranes are retained. Bleeding continues and may be heavy enough to cause shock; the os is open and tissue may be felt in the canal.
  • Management
    • Resuscitate – two IV lines, fluids, oxygen and blood transfusion if needed.
    • Remove the products lying in the cervical canal with sponge-holding forceps; this relieves "cervical shock" (vasovagal collapse) and reduces bleeding at once.
    • Evacuate the retained products – MVA under paracervical block is the preferred method up to 12–14 weeks; routine sharp curettage is no longer recommended.
    • Medical option for a stable woman with a uterus of less than 13 weeks' size: misoprostol 600 µg orally or 400 µg sublingually, as a single dose.
    • Oxytocics, antibiotics, anti-D where needed, and iron to correct anaemia.

4. Complete abortion

  • All products have been expelled; bleeding and pain subside, the os closes and the uterus is small and firm.
  • Management – confirm by ultrasound; no evacuation is needed; observe for bleeding; anti-D if Rh negative; iron supplements; counselling on the loss and on contraception.

5. Missed abortion (missed miscarriage)

  • The embryo or fetus has died but is retained in the uterus. Symptoms of pregnancy disappear (nausea stops, breast changes regress), there may be a brownish discharge, and the uterus is smaller than dates. The urine pregnancy test may stay positive for some weeks.
  • Danger – when a dead second-trimester fetus is retained for more than about 4 weeks, release of thromboplastin can cause hypofibrinogenaemia and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
  • Management
    • Make sure of the diagnosis – repeat the scan if there is any doubt; never evacuate on an uncertain single scan.
    • Check haemoglobin, blood group, and the coagulation profile (platelets, fibrinogen, PT/aPTT).
    • Options – expectant management; medical management with mifepristone 200 mg orally followed 1–2 days later by misoprostol 800 µg (vaginal or sublingual); or surgical evacuation (MVA or suction) in the first trimester; induction with misoprostol in the second trimester.
    • Give anti-D if Rh negative and provide emotional support – the woman has lost a wanted pregnancy without any warning.

(c) Septic abortion (4 marks)

Meaning and causes

  • Septic abortion is an abortion complicated by infection of the uterus and its contents, which may spread to the pelvis and bloodstream.
  • Most cases follow unsafe induced abortion (instruments, sticks, pastes and unclean hands); some follow incomplete spontaneous abortion.
  • Organisms – E. coli and other gram-negative bacilli, anaerobes (Bacteroides, anaerobic streptococci), Clostridium perfringens, staphylococci and group A streptococci.

Clinical features and grading

  • Fever with chills and rigors, a rapid pulse, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, lower abdominal pain and tenderness; a tender, boggy uterus with an open os; injuries on the cervix or vagina suggest instrumentation.
  • Grade I – infection limited to the uterus.
  • Grade II – spread to the pelvis (parametritis, salpingitis, pelvic peritonitis).
  • Grade III – generalised peritonitis, septicaemia, endotoxic (septic) shock, jaundice or renal failure.

Complications – septic shock, DIC, acute kidney injury, ARDS, uterine perforation with bowel injury, pelvic abscess, tetanus, gas gangrene and death; later, chronic pelvic pain, tubal block, infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

Management

  • Admit to a hospital with a blood bank and ICU; take the history of interference tactfully and in confidence.
  • Investigations – cervical swab and blood culture, CBC, coagulation profile, renal and liver function, electrolytes, blood group, ultrasound (retained products, collections) and X-ray abdomen (gas under the diaphragm, foreign body).
  • Resuscitation – IV fluids, oxygen, an indwelling catheter for hourly urine output, blood transfusion and vasopressors for shock in the ICU.
  • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics at once – for example ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole, or ceftriaxone + metronidazole – modified by culture reports.
  • Evacuate the uterus (MVA or suction) within a few hours of starting antibiotics, because the infected tissue must be removed.
  • Laparotomy for perforation, bowel injury, pelvic abscess, gas gangrene or failure to respond; hysterectomy may be life-saving.
  • Tetanus prophylaxis; anti-D for Rh-negative women.

Nursing care

  • Record temperature, pulse, BP, respiration and SpO₂ every 15–30 minutes in the acute phase; watch for early signs of shock – rising pulse, falling BP, cold extremities, restlessness and urine output below 30 ml/hour – and for oozing from puncture sites (DIC).
  • Keep a fluid balance chart; give catheter and perineal care with sterile pads; handle soiled linen with standard precautions.
  • Give antibiotics on time; tepid sponging and antipyretics for fever; maintain nutrition and hydration.
  • Offer non-judgemental, confidential support; the woman may fear legal action or her family's reaction.
  • Before discharge, counsel on post-abortion contraception (fertility returns within about two weeks), iron intake, danger signs, follow-up and where to obtain safe, legal abortion services in future.

Nursing importance

  • The nurse at the PHC or first referral unit is often the first to see a bleeding woman; correct recognition of the type of abortion decides whether the pregnancy is protected or the uterus is emptied urgently.
  • Abortion-related deaths in India are largely due to unsafe abortion – promoting safe, legal services and post-abortion family planning saves lives.
  • Rh-negative women, women with recurrent losses and grieving couples need specific follow-up.

Conclusion Quick diagnosis of the type of abortion, timely MVA or misoprostol, aggressive early treatment of septic abortion and compassionate nursing care prevent most deaths and long-term complications of abortion.

question: (a) Define ectopic pregnancy and list its sites and risk factors. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnosis of tubal pregnancy, including ruptured tubal pregnancy. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a woman with a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Sites of ectopic pregnancy with approximate frequency
labels: tubes and ovaries in front view with labelled implantation sites – ampulla (about 70–80%)
caesarean scar and abdominal cavity; small inset of a ruptured isthmic pregnancy with blood in the pouch of Douglas

answer_html:
(a) Definition, sites and risk factors (4 marks)

Definition

  • An ectopic pregnancy is one in which the fertilised ovum implants and develops outside the normal uterine cavity.
  • It occurs in about 1–2% of pregnancies and is the commonest cause of maternal death in the first trimester, mainly from intraperitoneal haemorrhage.

Sites

Site Approximate share Remarks
Fallopian tube About 95% Ampulla (commonest, 70–80%) → tubal abortion or late rupture; isthmus (about 12%) → early rupture at 6–8 weeks; fimbrial end; interstitial (cornual) (2–3%) → rupture late (12–16 weeks) with torrential bleeding
Ovary 0.5–3%
Cervix <1% Severe bleeding on attempted evacuation
Abdominal cavity About 1% Usually secondary to tubal abortion or rupture
Caesarean scar Increasing Rising with the caesarean rate; risk of rupture and accreta
Heterotopic Rare Intrauterine and ectopic pregnancy together; more common after IVF

Risk factors (anything that damages the tube or delays the passage of the ovum)

  • Previous ectopic pregnancy (recurrence about 10–15%).
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease, especially chlamydial salpingitis, and previous septic abortion.
  • Tubal surgery – tubal reconstruction and failed sterilisation.
  • Pregnancy occurring with an IUCD in place or on progestogen-only pills.
  • Assisted reproduction (IVF) and infertility itself.
  • Endometriosis, smoking, increasing maternal age and multiple sexual partners.

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis of tubal pregnancy (5 marks)

Natural course – the tube cannot hold the growing pregnancy. It may end in tubal abortion (through the fimbrial end, typical of ampullary pregnancy), tubal rupture, spontaneous resolution, or a chronic ectopic with a pelvic haematocele.

1. Unruptured (or slowly leaking) tubal pregnancy

  • Amenorrhoea of 6–8 weeks (sometimes absent – the bleeding is mistaken for a period).
  • Lower abdominal pain on one side – dull or colicky.
  • Slight dark vaginal bleeding from shedding decidua; rarely a decidual cast is passed.
  • On examination – tenderness in one iliac fossa; on vaginal examination, a tender adnexal mass and cervical motion (excitation) tenderness; the uterus is slightly enlarged and soft.

2. Ruptured tubal pregnancy (acute presentation)

  • Sudden, severe lower abdominal pain, fainting or collapse.
  • Shoulder-tip pain from blood irritating the diaphragm; urge to defaecate from blood in the pouch of Douglas.
  • Signs of hypovolaemic shock – pallor, cold clammy skin, rapid thready pulse, low BP, air hunger; the degree of shock is out of proportion to the visible vaginal bleeding.
  • Abdomen distended and tender with guarding, rigidity and shifting dullness; rarely, bluish discolouration around the umbilicus (Cullen's sign).
  • Vaginal examination (only where theatre is ready) – marked cervical excitation tenderness and fullness of the posterior fornix.

3. Investigations

  • Urine pregnancy test – positive.
  • Serum β-hCG – in a normal intrauterine pregnancy it rises by at least about 35–50% in 48 hours (roughly doubling); a slow rise or plateau suggests an ectopic or failing pregnancy.
  • Transvaginal ultrasound – empty uterus with an adnexal mass (a "ring of fire" on colour Doppler), sometimes a live embryo outside the uterus, and free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. A pseudo-gestational sac (fluid in the cavity) can mislead.
  • Discriminatory zone – an intrauterine sac should be visible on transvaginal scan once β-hCG reaches about 1,500–2,000 IU/L (some units use up to 3,500); an empty uterus above this level strongly suggests ectopic pregnancy.
  • Haemoglobin, blood group and cross-match.
  • Laparoscopy – the gold standard for diagnosis and treatment in doubtful cases.
  • Differential diagnosis – threatened or incomplete abortion, ruptured corpus luteum cyst, twisted ovarian cyst, acute salpingitis and appendicitis.

(c) Management and nursing care of ruptured ectopic pregnancy (6 marks)

1. Emergency resuscitation – start at once and do not delay surgery

  • Call for help; lay the woman flat with legs raised; give oxygen by mask.
  • Insert two large-bore cannulae (16–18 G); draw blood for haemoglobin, grouping and cross-matching of at least 2–4 units.
  • Infuse warm crystalloids rapidly and transfuse blood as soon as it is available.
  • Insert a Foley catheter and measure hourly urine output.
  • Resuscitation and surgery go together – in a woman bleeding inside the abdomen, operating stops the bleeding; waiting for her to "stabilise" can be fatal.

2. Surgery

  • Immediate laparotomy (or laparoscopy in a stable woman where expertise is available).
  • Salpingectomy (removal of the affected tube) is the usual operation for a ruptured tube.
  • Salpingostomy (opening the tube and removing the pregnancy) may be chosen for an unruptured pregnancy when the other tube is damaged and future fertility is wanted; β-hCG is then followed to exclude persistent trophoblast.
  • Blood clots are removed and the abdomen washed out.
  • Anti-D immunoglobulin for an Rh-negative woman.

3. Treatment options for unruptured ectopic pregnancy (for completeness)

  • Medical – methotrexate 50 mg/m² intramuscularly (single dose) for a stable woman with an unruptured mass of less than about 3.5 cm, no fetal heart activity, low β-hCG and the ability to attend follow-up. β-hCG is checked on days 4 and 7 (a fall of 15% or more is expected), then weekly until negative. Pregnancy is avoided for 3 months.
  • Expectant – for small ectopics with low, falling β-hCG.

4. Nursing care

Pre-operative

  • Continuous monitoring of pulse, BP, respiration, SpO₂, colour and consciousness every 5–15 minutes; record and report a falling BP or rising pulse.
  • Rapid preparation – informed consent, nil by mouth, removal of jewellery and dentures, skin preparation, catheterisation, blood arranged, and safe transfer to theatre with the team.
  • Calm, simple explanations to the woman and her family; she is frightened and in pain.

Post-operative

  • Vital signs every 15 minutes until stable, then hourly; watch the wound and drain for bleeding; maintain IV fluids and transfusion; keep an intake–output chart.
  • Pain relief as prescribed; early ambulation and deep-breathing exercises; prevention of thromboembolism.
  • Correct anaemia with iron and a protein-rich diet.
  • Emotional care – she has lost a pregnancy and may fear for her fertility; allow her to grieve and answer questions honestly.

Health education at discharge

  • Chance of a future normal pregnancy is good, but the risk of another ectopic is higher; she should have an early ultrasound at 6–7 weeks in every future pregnancy.
  • Report pain or bleeding in early pregnancy without delay.
  • Use of contraception until she is ready; prompt treatment of genital infections; follow-up β-hCG after conservative surgery or methotrexate.

Nursing importance

  • Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, fainting or shock should be asked about her last menstrual period – the nurse's suspicion can save a life.
  • Quick, organised preparation for theatre and continuous monitoring determine survival in a ruptured ectopic.

Conclusion Ectopic pregnancy is an emergency that must be suspected early. Early diagnosis by β-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound allows conservative treatment, while a ruptured ectopic needs simultaneous resuscitation and surgery with skilled nursing care.

question: (a) Define antepartum haemorrhage and list its causes. (3 marks) (b) Differentiate between placenta praevia and abruptio placentae. (6 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a woman with placenta praevia. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Degrees (types) of placenta praevia
labels: Four sagittal diagrams of the lower uterus and cervix – Type I (lateral
low-lying: placenta in the lower segment

edge not reaching the os); Type II (marginal: edge reaches the internal os); Type III (incomplete central: covers the closed os partly); Type IV (complete central: covers the os completely); note beneath – current ultrasound terms: "placenta praevia" (covers the internal os) and "low-lying placenta" (edge within 20 mm of the os)

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (3 marks)

Definition

  • Antepartum haemorrhage (APH) is bleeding from or into the genital tract after the 28th week of pregnancy (the age of viability used in India; 20–24 weeks in some other countries) and before the birth of the baby.
  • It complicates about 3–5% of pregnancies and is a major cause of maternal and perinatal death.

Causes

Group Causes
Placental Placenta praevia (about one-third); abruptio placentae (about one-third)
Unexplained (indeterminate) Bleeding from the placental margin (marginal sinus) where no cause is found
Local lesions of the genital tract Cervical polyp, cervical erosion or cervicitis, carcinoma of the cervix, vaginal varicosities, trauma
Fetal Vasa praevia – rupture of unprotected fetal vessels running over the os (the bleeding is fetal blood)

(b) Differences between placenta praevia and abruptio placentae (6 marks)

Placenta praevia – the placenta is implanted partly or completely in the lower uterine segment, over or near the internal os. As the lower segment forms and the cervix effaces, the placenta separates and the maternal sinuses bleed.

Abruptio placentae (accidental haemorrhage) – premature separation of a normally situated placenta. Bleeding may come out through the cervix (revealed), collect behind the placenta (concealed) or both (mixed).

Feature Placenta praevia Abruptio placentae
Nature of bleeding Painless, causeless and recurrent; first bleed often slight ("warning haemorrhage") Painful; often with pre-eclampsia, trauma, sudden decompression of the uterus, smoking or cocaine use
Colour of blood Bright red Dark red, may be clotted; may be absent (concealed)
General condition Shock proportionate to visible blood loss Shock out of proportion to the visible loss
Uterus Soft, relaxed, non-tender Tense, tender, rigid ("woody hard"); may be larger than dates in concealed bleeding
Fetal parts Easily felt Difficult to feel
Presenting part High, floating; malpresentation (breech, transverse lie) common Usually normal and may be engaged
Fetal heart Usually present Often fetal distress or fetal death
Signs of pre-eclampsia Not related Often present (hypertension, proteinuria)
Ultrasound Placenta in the lower segment Normally sited placenta; retroplacental clot may be seen (a normal scan does not exclude abruption)
Main complications PPH from the lower segment, placenta accreta spectrum (especially with a previous caesarean scar), preterm birth DIC, acute kidney injury, Couvelaire uterus, PPH, fetal death

(c) Management and nursing care of placenta praevia (6 marks)

Golden rule – no vaginal examination in any woman with APH until placenta praevia has been excluded by ultrasound; a finger in the cervix can provoke torrential bleeding.

1. First contact (sub-centre, PHC or CHC)

  • Assess pulse, BP, pallor, amount of bleeding (pads), fetal heart.
  • Start an IV line with Ringer lactate or normal saline, take blood for grouping and cross-matching, and keep her in the left lateral position.
  • Refer at once to a first referral unit with blood bank and caesarean facility, accompanied by a health worker and blood donors; inform the receiving facility.

2. At the hospital – assessment

  • Rapid assessment of the mother (vital signs, haemoglobin, blood group, coagulation profile, urine) and the fetus (heart rate, CTG).
  • Ultrasound to locate the placenta and exclude accreta (colour Doppler; MRI if needed).
  • Blood cross-matched and kept ready (at least two units) throughout the stay.

3. Expectant management (Macafee–Johnson regime) Aim – to gain fetal maturity without endangering the mother. Suitable when the mother is haemodynamically stable, the bleeding has stopped or is slight, the pregnancy is less than 37 weeks, the fetus is alive and well, and the hospital has blood and theatre facilities round the clock.

  • Admission until delivery in most cases (some stable women with minor praevia are allowed home near the hospital).
  • Initial bed rest, then gradual mobility; avoid intercourse, enemas and heavy work.
  • Maintain haemoglobin with iron and transfusion when needed.
  • Antenatal corticosteroids (dexamethasone 6 mg IM 12-hourly × 4 doses) when delivery before 34 weeks is likely.
  • Anti-D for Rh-negative women after each bleed.
  • Serial ultrasound for fetal growth and placental position (a low placenta may "migrate" upward as the lower segment forms).
  • Planned delivery at about 36–37 weeks if no further major bleeding occurs.

4. Active management (termination of pregnancy) Indications – heavy or recurrent bleeding endangering the mother, pregnancy of 37 weeks or more, onset of labour, fetal death or a lethal anomaly.

  • Caesarean section by an experienced obstetrician – for all major praevia (placenta covering or reaching the os) and for most bleeding women; blood and anaesthetist ready; prepared for hysterectomy if placenta accreta is found.
  • Vaginal delivery may be allowed in a minor (low-lying, anterior) placenta when the head is engaged and bleeding is slight – artificial rupture of membranes and oxytocin, with any vaginal examination done in the operation theatre with everything ready for caesarean section ("double set-up").
  • Active management of the third stage; the lower segment contracts poorly, so watch for PPH and be ready with uterotonics, balloon tamponade and blood.

5. Nursing care

  • Monitor pulse, BP and respiration every 15–30 minutes during bleeding and 4-hourly when stable; count and weigh pads; maintain an intake–output chart.
  • Fetal monitoring – fetal heart rate, fetal movement count, CTG as ordered.
  • Keep an IV line patent, blood available and the theatre informed; prepare for emergency caesarean section at any time.
  • Positioning (left lateral), comfortable bed rest, prevention of constipation and pressure sores, leg exercises to prevent thrombosis.
  • Iron-rich diet; correct anaemia.
  • Psychological support – long hospital stays cause anxiety and boredom; involve the family, explain each step.
  • After delivery – watch for PPH and infection; care for a possibly preterm baby (warmth, early breastfeeding, KMC).

6. Complications of placenta praevia and how care prevents them

Complication Nursing and medical prevention
Haemorrhagic shock and anaemia from repeated bleeds No vaginal examination, early referral, blood always cross-matched, iron and transfusion to keep Hb up
Malpresentation, unstable lie, cord prolapse after rupture of membranes Admission near term, check the lie daily, planned caesarean section
Preterm labour and premature rupture of membranes Rest, antenatal corticosteroids, delivery in a centre with a newborn unit
PPH from the poorly contracting lower segment Active management of the third stage, oxytocin infusion, balloon tamponade and surgical measures ready
Placenta accreta spectrum over a caesarean scar Antenatal Doppler/MRI, senior team, consent for hysterectomy
Puerperal infection (placental site near the vagina, anaemia, operative delivery) Strict asepsis, perineal care, antibiotics as prescribed
Fetal – prematurity, low birth weight, asphyxia, fetal blood loss if the placenta is cut at caesarean section Corticosteroids, paediatrician at birth, neonatal resuscitation ready

Nursing importance

  • A painless bright-red bleed in the third trimester is placenta praevia until proved otherwise – the nurse's refusal to allow a vaginal examination and her prompt referral can prevent a catastrophe.
  • With the rising caesarean rate, placenta praevia over a previous scar (with a risk of accreta) is increasing; such women must deliver in a centre with blood bank and senior surgeons.

Conclusion APH is an obstetric emergency. Careful differentiation of placenta praevia from abruption, no vaginal examination, prompt referral, expectant management where safe and timely caesarean delivery with blood ready save both mother and baby.

question: (a) Classify the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and define pre-eclampsia. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features, investigations and management of pre-eclampsia with severe features. (6 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a woman with eclampsia. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Pathophysiology of pre-eclampsia
labels: Flowchart – failure of trophoblast invasion of the spiral arteries → poor placental perfusion → release of anti-angiogenic factors into the maternal blood → widespread endothelial dysfunction → three arms: vasospasm (raised BP)

answer_html:
(a) Classification and definition (3 marks)

Classification of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

Disorder Meaning
Chronic (pre-existing) hypertension BP ≥140/90 mm Hg before pregnancy or before 20 weeks, or persisting beyond 12 weeks after delivery
Gestational hypertension New hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or organ involvement; settles after delivery
Pre-eclampsia Gestational hypertension with proteinuria or maternal organ dysfunction or fetal growth restriction
Pre-eclampsia superimposed on chronic hypertension A woman with chronic hypertension who develops proteinuria or organ dysfunction
Eclampsia Generalised tonic-clonic convulsions in a woman with pre-eclampsia, not due to any other cause
HELLP syndrome Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelets – a severe variant

Definition of pre-eclampsia

  • New-onset hypertension (BP ≥140/90 mm Hg on two occasions at least 4 hours apart) after 20 weeks of pregnancy together with
  • Proteinuria – ≥300 mg in 24 hours, protein–creatinine ratio ≥0.3, or dipstick 1+ or more (2+ is more reliable); or, in the absence of proteinuria, any of: platelets below 1 lakh/µl, raised creatinine, liver transaminases twice normal, pulmonary oedema, new headache or visual disturbance, or fetal growth restriction.
  • Hypertensive disorders complicate about 5–10% of pregnancies and cause roughly one in seven maternal deaths worldwide.

(b) Pre-eclampsia with severe features (6 marks)

1. Risk factors – first pregnancy, previous pre-eclampsia, family history, age below 18 or above 35, multiple pregnancy, molar pregnancy, chronic hypertension, diabetes, renal disease, obesity, antiphospholipid syndrome, and pregnancy after IVF.

2. Clinical features

  • Severe features – systolic BP ≥160 or diastolic ≥110 mm Hg, platelets <1 lakh/µl, liver enzymes twice normal or severe right upper quadrant/epigastric pain, serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dl or doubling, pulmonary oedema, and new cerebral or visual disturbances.
  • Symptoms of impending eclampsia – severe frontal headache, blurred vision or flashes of light, epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting, oliguria, brisk reflexes.
  • Oedema of the face and hands and rapid weight gain are common but are no longer part of the definition.
  • Fetal effects – growth restriction, oligohydramnios, abruption and fetal distress.

3. Investigations

  • Urine – protein by dipstick, protein–creatinine ratio or 24-hour collection.
  • Blood – haemoglobin, platelet count, peripheral smear (haemolysis), liver function (AST, ALT, LDH), renal function (creatinine, uric acid), coagulation profile, blood group.
  • Fundoscopy for retinal oedema or haemorrhage.
  • Fetal – ultrasound for growth and liquor, umbilical artery Doppler, NST/CTG and daily fetal movement count.

4. Management

  • Admit to a first referral unit or tertiary centre; quiet room; BP every 15–30 minutes until stable.
  • Control severe hypertension promptly (within 30–60 minutes) to prevent stroke:
    • Labetalol 20 mg IV slowly, then 40, 80 and 80 mg every 10 minutes as needed (maximum about 300 mg), or
    • Nifedipine 10 mg orally (immediate-release), repeated every 20–30 minutes, or
    • Hydralazine 5 mg IV, repeated as needed.
    • Aim for about 140–150/90–100 mm Hg – a sudden fall can reduce placental blood flow.
  • Prevent convulsions with magnesium sulphate (regimen as in part c).
  • Restrict IV fluids to about 80 ml/hour to avoid pulmonary oedema; record intake and hourly urine output.
  • Antenatal corticosteroids (dexamethasone 6 mg IM 12-hourly × 4) if delivery before 34 weeks is likely.
  • Delivery is the definitive cure:
    • 34 weeks or more – deliver after the mother is stabilised.
    • Below 34 weeks – expectant care in a tertiary centre only if BP is controlled and mother and fetus are stable; deliver at once for uncontrolled BP, eclampsia, HELLP, pulmonary oedema, abruption, renal failure or fetal compromise.
    • Mode – vaginal delivery by induction if conditions are favourable; caesarean section for obstetric indications.
  • Third stage – oxytocin; avoid ergometrine, which raises BP.
  • Postpartum – continue BP checks; most eclampsia after delivery occurs within 48 hours, but it can occur up to 6 weeks.

5. Prevention in high-risk women – low-dose aspirin (75–150 mg at night) started between 12 and 16 weeks and continued till about 36 weeks, and calcium supplementation (1 g/day after the first trimester, as in the national programme), along with regular BP and urine checks at every antenatal visit.

(c) Management and nursing care of eclampsia (6 marks)

Stages of an eclamptic fit – premonitory (about 30 seconds: twitching, eyes roll up), tonic (about 30 seconds: body rigid, breathing stops, cyanosis), clonic (1–2 minutes: violent jerking, frothing, tongue bite) and coma of variable length. Fits may occur before (about half), during or after labour.

1. Immediate care during a fit

  • Call for help; never leave the woman alone.
  • Place her on her left side, protect her from injury (padded side rails, bed lowered); do not restrain her limbs.
  • Airway – after the tonic phase, clear secretions by suction and insert an oral airway; do not force anything between clenched teeth.
  • Oxygen 4–6 L/minute by mask; check pulse and SpO₂.
  • Note the time, duration and type of the fit.

2. Magnesium sulphate – the anticonvulsant of choice

  • Pritchard (IM) regimen – loading dose 4 g of 20% solution IV slowly over 5–10 minutes, plus 10 g of 50% solution deep IM (5 g in each buttock); maintenance 5 g of 50% solution IM every 4 hours in alternate buttocks.
  • Zuspan (IV) regimen – 4 g IV loading dose, then 1 g/hour by infusion pump.
  • At a sub-centre or PHC, give the loading dose and refer with an attendant.
  • Before each dose, check – patellar reflex present, respiratory rate ≥16/minute, urine output ≥30 ml/hour (≥100 ml in 4 hours); withhold and inform the doctor if any is abnormal.
  • Keep calcium gluconate 10%, 10 ml ready (given IV over 10 minutes) as the antidote for magnesium toxicity.
  • For a recurrent fit – a further 2 g IV over 5 minutes.
  • Continue for 24 hours after delivery or after the last fit, whichever is later.

3. Further medical care

  • Control BP with labetalol, nifedipine or hydralazine as in part (b).
  • Two IV lines; investigations as for severe pre-eclampsia; blood cross-matched.
  • Indwelling (Foley) catheter with hourly urine measurement; fluid restriction.
  • Deliver within about 6–12 hours of stabilisation, whatever the gestation – vaginally if labour progresses, otherwise by caesarean section.
  • Watch for complications – pulmonary oedema, HELLP, DIC, acute kidney injury, cerebral haemorrhage, aspiration pneumonia, abruption and PRES – and shift to ICU when needed.

4. Nursing care

  • Nurse in a quiet, dimly lit room with minimal disturbance; group nursing procedures together.
  • Eclampsia tray at the bedside – mouth gag, airway, suction, oxygen, MgSO₄, calcium gluconate, syringes, antihypertensives, catheter.
  • One-to-one nursing with a chart for BP, pulse, respiration, SpO₂, temperature, reflexes, level of consciousness, fits, fluid intake and urine output, and fetal heart rate.
  • Turn every 2 hours; oral and eye care in the unconscious woman; keep the bladder empty; nil by mouth till she is fully conscious.
  • Watch for labour – an eclamptic woman may labour silently; check the perineum and fetal heart regularly.
  • Postpartum – continue monitoring for 48 hours; care of the newborn (often preterm or growth-restricted); encourage breastfeeding when the mother is able.
  • Support the family, who are usually terrified; explain her condition in simple words.

5. Health education before discharge

  • BP checks weekly till normal, follow-up at 6 weeks; continue antihypertensives as advised.
  • Risk of pre-eclampsia in the next pregnancy – book early, and take aspirin and calcium as advised.
  • Women who had pre-eclampsia have a higher lifelong risk of hypertension, heart disease and stroke, so they need yearly BP and lifestyle checks.

Nursing importance

  • Measuring BP and urine protein correctly at every visit and recognising imminent signs allows treatment before fits begin.
  • The nurse gives and monitors magnesium sulphate – correct dosing, toxicity checks and readiness with calcium gluconate are her direct responsibility.

Conclusion Pre-eclampsia is a multisystem disorder cured only by delivery. Early detection, timely BP control, magnesium sulphate, well-timed delivery and vigilant nursing prevent eclampsia and its deadly complications.

question: (a) Define gestational diabetes mellitus and explain its testing and diagnosis as per Government of India guidelines. (4 marks) (b) Explain the effects of diabetes on pregnancy and on the fetus. (5 marks) (c) Describe the antenatal, intranatal and postnatal management and nursing care of a woman with gestational diabetes. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: GDM testing and management pathway (Government of India, 2018)
labels: Flowchart – first antenatal contact: 75 g glucose in about 300 ml water

irrespective of the last meal → plasma glucose at 2 hours → ≥140 mg/dl = GDM → medical nutrition therapy and exercise for 2 weeks → 2-hour post-meal glucose below 120 mg/dl: continue MNT; 120 or above: start insulin → plan delivery → 75 g OGTT 6 weeks after delivery; branch for <140 mg/dl: repeat test at 24–28 weeks (at least 4 weeks after the first)

answer_html:
(a) Definition, testing and diagnosis (4 marks)

Definition

  • Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is carbohydrate intolerance of varying severity with onset or first recognition during pregnancy.
  • It differs from pregestational diabetes (type 1 or type 2 diabetes present before pregnancy) and from overt diabetes detected in pregnancy (fasting glucose ≥126 or HbA1c ≥6.5%).
  • Why it occurs – placental hormones (human placental lactogen, progesterone, cortisol, prolactin) cause insulin resistance, especially after 24 weeks; women whose pancreas cannot increase insulin output develop high blood sugar.
  • India has a high prevalence of GDM (often quoted as 10–14% in different studies), so universal testing is recommended.

Risk factors – obesity, age above 25–30 years, family history of diabetes, previous GDM, previous big baby (>4 kg), unexplained stillbirth or congenital anomaly, polyhydramnios, PCOS, and South Asian ethnicity itself.

Testing as per the Government of India (MoHFW 2018) guidelines

  • Universal testing of all pregnant women – the first test at the first antenatal contact, and a second test at 24–28 weeks if the first is negative (at least 4 weeks apart). A woman seen first after 28 weeks gets one test at that contact.
  • Single-step method (DIPSI) – 75 g oral glucose dissolved in about 300 ml of water, given irrespective of the time of the last meal; plasma glucose is measured 2 hours later, using a plasma-calibrated glucometer or laboratory.
  • Diagnosis – a 2-hour plasma glucose of ≥140 mg/dl is GDM.
  • If she vomits within 30 minutes of the drink, the test is repeated the next day.
  • The test is simple and cheap and can be done at any level – sub-centre, PHC or Ayushman Arogya Mandir.

(b) Effects of diabetes on pregnancy and the fetus (5 marks)

1. Effects on the mother

  • Abortion (with poorly controlled pregestational diabetes).
  • Pre-eclampsia – two to four times more common.
  • Polyhydramnios (fetal polyuria) with risk of preterm labour and malpresentation.
  • Infections – urinary tract infection, vulvovaginal candidiasis, wound and puerperal infection.
  • Preterm labour, prolonged labour, shoulder dystocia, perineal tears, operative delivery and caesarean section.
  • PPH from an over-distended uterus.
  • Diabetic ketoacidosis (mainly type 1), hypoglycaemia on insulin, worsening retinopathy and nephropathy.
  • Future type 2 diabetes – up to about half of women with GDM develop it within 5–10 years; GDM also recurs in later pregnancies.

2. Effects on the fetus

  • Congenital malformations – with high sugar at conception (pregestational diabetes): heart defects, neural tube defects, caudal regression syndrome, renal anomalies.
  • Macrosomia (birth weight >4 kg) – maternal glucose crosses the placenta, fetal insulin rises and acts as a growth hormone (Pedersen hypothesis); the baby has excess fat over the shoulders and trunk.
  • Birth injuries from shoulder dystocia – Erb's palsy, fractured clavicle, asphyxia.
  • Unexplained late stillbirth (fetal hypoxia and acidosis).
  • Fetal growth restriction when the mother has vascular disease.
  • Delayed lung maturity, so a respiratory distress syndrome risk even near term.
  • After birth, the baby faces hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, polycythaemia and jaundice (the infant of a diabetic mother), and in later life a higher risk of obesity and diabetes.

(c) Management and nursing care (6 marks)

1. Antenatal management

  • Medical nutrition therapy (MNT) – a balanced diet with controlled carbohydrate, three meals and two or three small snacks, complex carbohydrates and fibre (whole grains, millets, pulses, vegetables), avoidance of sugar, sweets and sweet drinks; adequate protein; calories matched to her pre-pregnancy weight.
  • Physical activity – about 30 minutes of brisk walking daily (or walking for 15 minutes after each meal) unless contraindicated.
  • Glucose monitoring – recheck after 2 weeks of MNT; targets of about 90–95 mg/dl fasting and 120 mg/dl 2 hours after meals.
  • Drug treatment – if the 2-hour post-meal glucose stays ≥120 mg/dl despite MNT, insulin is started (the drug of choice; it does not cross the placenta); metformin may be used by the specialist in selected women. Referral to a medical officer or specialist is needed for insulin.
  • Fetal surveillance – growth scans for macrosomia and polyhydramnios, daily fetal movement count, and NST/CTG in the third trimester (more often for women on insulin).
  • More frequent antenatal visits; screen for pre-eclampsia and urinary infection; teach the signs and treatment of hypoglycaemia to women on insulin.

2. Timing and mode of delivery

  • Well controlled on diet alone – await spontaneous labour; usually not beyond 40 weeks.
  • On insulin or poorly controlled – delivery is planned at about 38–39 weeks, earlier if complications arise.
  • Vaginal delivery is preferred; caesarean section for obstetric indications or a suspected very large baby.
  • Delivery in a facility with a newborn care unit; paediatrician informed.

3. Intranatal care

  • Check capillary blood glucose every 1–2 hours in labour; keep it roughly between 70 and 110–126 mg/dl with dextrose and insulin infusions as per protocol.
  • Continuous fetal heart monitoring; watch the progress of labour – avoid prolonged labour.
  • Be prepared for shoulder dystocia (McRoberts position, suprapubic pressure, extra staff) and for PPH (active management of the third stage).

4. Postnatal care

  • Insulin for GDM is stopped after delivery; check blood glucose for the first 1–2 days.
  • Breastfeed within half an hour of birth and frequently thereafter – this protects the baby against hypoglycaemia and lowers the mother's future diabetes risk.
  • Monitor the baby's blood glucose in the first hours and days of life; watch for jaundice and breathing difficulty.
  • 75 g OGTT at about 6 weeks after delivery, and regular screening (every 1–3 years) thereafter.
  • Family planning counselling – plan the next pregnancy with good glucose control; lifestyle advice on weight, diet and exercise.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Perform the GDM test correctly (75 g anhydrous glucose, timing, calibrated glucometer) and record it on the MCP card.
  • Counsel on diet using local foods and portion sizes; teach self-monitoring and insulin injection technique, storage and site rotation.
  • Recognise hypoglycaemia (sweating, tremor, confusion) and treat with 15 g of glucose; recognise ketoacidosis.
  • Monitor fetal movements and arrange scans; educate on danger signs.
  • Support the woman emotionally – frequent pricks and diet restrictions can be stressful.

6. A sample day's meal plan for a woman with GDM (medical nutrition therapy)

  • Early morning – tea or milk without sugar with a few roasted chana or two plain biscuits.
  • Breakfast – two vegetable-stuffed rotis, moong dal chilla or vegetable poha/upma with sprouts, and a bowl of curd.
  • Mid-morning – one fruit such as guava, apple, orange or papaya (not juice).
  • Lunch – two rotis (wheat, jowar or bajra) or one small bowl of rice, a bowl of dal, a green vegetable, salad and buttermilk.
  • Evening – roasted makhana, sprouts chaat or a handful of peanuts with unsweetened tea.
  • Dinner – two rotis, vegetable, and dal, paneer, egg or fish.
  • Bedtime – a glass of milk without sugar, which prevents hunger and ketosis overnight.
  • The "plate method" is easy to teach – half the plate vegetables, a quarter cereal and a quarter protein; avoid sweets, fried snacks, sugary drinks and fruit juices, and keep meal timings regular.

Nursing importance

  • Simple universal testing at the first visit and at 24–28 weeks, done by the nurse or ANM, detects most GDM in time to prevent big babies, stillbirth and birth injury.
  • Every GDM mother is a future diabetic unless lifestyle changes – the nurse's follow-up after delivery is primary prevention of type 2 diabetes.

Conclusion GDM is common in India and can be detected cheaply with the single-step 75 g test. Diet, exercise, insulin when needed, planned delivery and postnatal screening protect both mother and baby.

question: (a) Explain the effects of pregnancy on heart disease and state the NYHA functional classification. (4 marks) (b) Explain the antenatal management of a pregnant woman with heart disease. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care during labour and the puerperium. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Cardiac output in pregnancy, labour and the puerperium, with critical periods for a woman with heart disease
labels: Line graph – cardiac output rising from early pregnancy to about 40–50% above the non-pregnant level by 28–32 weeks; further rises with each contraction in labour and a sharp peak immediately after delivery (autotransfusion from the contracted uterus and relief of caval compression); gradual return towards normal by 6–12 weeks; shaded critical periods: 28–32 weeks
immediately after delivery and the first days of the puerperium

answer_html:
(a) Effects of pregnancy on heart disease and NYHA classification (4 marks)

Introduction

  • Heart disease complicates about 1% of pregnancies and is an important indirect cause of maternal death.
  • In India rheumatic heart disease is still the commonest type, and mitral stenosis is the commonest lesion; congenital heart disease, peripartum cardiomyopathy and hypertensive heart disease are increasing.

Effects of pregnancy on the diseased heart

  • Blood volume rises by 40–50% and cardiac output by 30–50%, with a faster heart rate – an extra load that a damaged heart may not bear.
  • Anaemia, infections and the hypercoagulable state add to the strain.
  • Critical periods when heart failure is most likely:
    • 28–32 weeks, when the haemodynamic load nears its peak.
    • During labour, especially the second stage – each contraction pushes 300–500 ml of blood into the circulation and bearing down strains the heart.
    • Immediately after delivery – the contracted uterus returns blood to the circulation (autotransfusion) and pressure on the vena cava is relieved; this sudden overload can cause acute pulmonary oedema.
    • The first few days of the puerperium.
  • Complications – heart failure, pulmonary oedema, atrial fibrillation, thromboembolism, infective endocarditis and maternal death.
  • Effects on the fetus – preterm birth, fetal growth restriction, fetal hypoxia, and a higher risk of congenital heart disease when the mother herself has congenital disease.

NYHA functional classification

Class Functional capacity
I No limitation; ordinary physical activity causes no symptoms
II Slight limitation; comfortable at rest, but ordinary activity causes fatigue, palpitation or breathlessness
III Marked limitation; comfortable at rest, but less than ordinary activity causes symptoms
IV Unable to do any physical activity without discomfort; symptoms present even at rest
  • Most women in class I–II go through pregnancy safely with good care; class III–IV carry a high maternal risk.
  • The modified WHO (mWHO) classification is also used to predict risk; in mWHO class IV – for example severe pulmonary hypertension, severe left ventricular dysfunction or severe symptomatic mitral stenosis – pregnancy is advised against.

(b) Antenatal management (5 marks)

1. Team care and assessment

  • Booking as early as possible at a tertiary centre, with joint care by the obstetrician, cardiologist and anaesthetist.
  • History, NYHA class, ECG, echocardiography, haemoglobin and thyroid function; review of all drugs (stop ACE inhibitors; change warfarin as advised).
  • Visits every 2 weeks till 28–30 weeks and weekly thereafter.

2. Reducing the load on the heart

  • Adequate rest – about 10 hours at night and 2 hours in the afternoon; avoid heavy household work and strenuous activity; class III–IV may need hospital rest.
  • Diet – nutritious, with moderate salt restriction; avoid excess weight gain.
  • Prevent and treat anaemia (IFA, IV iron if needed) and infections – urinary, respiratory and dental.
  • Control hypertension, arrhythmias and thyroid disease.

3. Drugs

  • Continue benzathine penicillin prophylaxis in rheumatic heart disease.
  • Digoxin, diuretics (furosemide) and beta-blockers (for mitral stenosis and arrhythmias) as prescribed.
  • Anticoagulation for mechanical valves or atrial fibrillation – heparin (low molecular weight or unfractionated) in the first trimester and from about 36 weeks, warfarin in between or as the cardiologist decides; switch to heparin before delivery.

4. Special measures

  • Balloon mitral valvotomy in the second trimester for severe mitral stenosis not responding to drugs.
  • Termination of pregnancy in early pregnancy may be advised for mWHO class IV disease or class IV heart failure.
  • Fetal monitoring – growth scans and fetal echocardiography when the mother has congenital heart disease.
  • Elective admission at about 36–37 weeks (earlier for class III–IV) so that labour begins in hospital.
  • Teach her the warning signs of heart failure – increasing breathlessness, cough, inability to lie flat, palpitations, swelling, chest pain.

(c) Management and nursing care during labour and the puerperium (6 marks)

1. First stage of labour

  • Spontaneous onset of labour is preferred; induction only for obstetric reasons. Vaginal delivery is the aim; caesarean section is done mainly for obstetric indications.
  • Position – propped up or left lateral; never flat on the back.
  • Oxygen by mask as needed.
  • Pain relief – epidural analgesia reduces pain-induced rises in heart rate and BP (used with care in some lesions such as severe aortic stenosis).
  • Restrict IV fluids (about 75 ml/hour); keep an accurate intake–output chart.
  • Monitor pulse, respiration, BP and SpO₂ every 15 minutes, with ECG monitoring; listen for basal crackles.
  • Warning signs of failure – pulse above 110/minute, respiratory rate above 24–28/minute, breathlessness, cough, crackles at the lung bases – report at once.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis for high-risk lesions, as per the unit's policy.
  • Continuous fetal heart monitoring.

2. Second stage

  • Cut the second stage short – avoid prolonged bearing down; assisted delivery with outlet forceps or vacuum when the head is low.
  • If the lithotomy position is used, lift both legs together and do not keep them raised for long (venous return rises suddenly).

3. Third stage

  • Active management with oxytocin 10 IU IM or a slow diluted infusion; avoid ergometrine (it causes vasoconstriction and can precipitate pulmonary oedema) and avoid rapid IV bolus of oxytocin.
  • In women at high risk of overload, furosemide 40 mg IV may be given soon after delivery as ordered.
  • Watch blood loss carefully and replace it cautiously.

4. Puerperium

  • Close monitoring for 24–48 hours (the post-delivery overload period), in an ICU or high-dependency unit for class III–IV.
  • Propped-up position, oxygen if needed, early but gradual mobilisation, compression stockings and leg exercises to prevent thrombosis.
  • Restart anticoagulants and cardiac drugs as advised.
  • Breastfeeding is encouraged for most women (not for those in severe failure).
  • Prevent infection – perineal and breast care, aseptic technique.
  • Hospital stay is usually longer (about a week or more); discharge after the cardiologist's review.

5. Contraception and future pregnancy

  • Barrier methods, progestogen-only methods, and IUCDs in most women; avoid combined oral pills where there is a risk of thrombosis.
  • Permanent sterilisation (or the husband's vasectomy) once the family is complete, done when her cardiac condition is stable.
  • Future pregnancies should be planned after cardiac evaluation and, where needed, valve surgery.

6. Recognition and emergency care of heart failure (acute pulmonary oedema)

  • Warning features – increasing breathlessness, cough (especially at night), inability to lie flat (orthopnoea), waking up breathless, pink frothy sputum, pulse above 110/minute, respiratory rate above 24/minute, crackles at the lung bases, raised jugular venous pressure and spreading oedema.
  • Immediate nursing action
    • Make her sit upright with legs hanging down to reduce venous return; give high-flow oxygen; call the doctor at once.
    • Keep IV access; give IV furosemide and other drugs as ordered; stop or restrict IV fluids.
    • Monitor SpO₂, pulse, BP, respiration and urine output continuously; insert a urinary catheter.
    • Continue fetal heart monitoring; prepare for transfer to the ICU and for delivery if the obstetrician decides.
    • Stay with her and calm her – fear increases the heart rate.

Nursing importance

  • The nurse is the one who sees early breathlessness, a rising pulse or a cough at night – prompt reporting prevents pulmonary oedema and death.
  • Correct positioning, careful fluid control, avoiding ergometrine and close monitoring after delivery are simple nursing actions that protect a cardiac mother.

Conclusion With team care, rest, prevention of anaemia and infection, careful labour management with a shortened second stage, avoidance of ergometrine and close watch after delivery, most women with heart disease have a safe pregnancy and childbirth.

question: Explain hyperemesis gravidarum – its causes, complications, management and nursing care.
answer_html:
Introduction Nausea and vomiting are common in early pregnancy and usually settle by 12–16 weeks. Hyperemesis gravidarum is persistent, severe vomiting in pregnancy causing dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, ketosis and loss of more than 5% of the pre-pregnancy weight. It affects about 0.3–3% of pregnant women and starts in the first trimester.

1. Causes and risk factors

  • High hCG levels – first pregnancy, multiple pregnancy, molar pregnancy.
  • Hormonal – oestrogen; transient hCG-induced hyperthyroidism (gestational thyrotoxicosis).
  • Previous hyperemesis or family history; psychological stress may worsen it.
  • Always exclude other causes – urinary infection, gastroenteritis, hepatitis, appendicitis, thyrotoxicosis.

2. Clinical features and assessment

  • Vomiting many times a day, inability to keep food or fluid down, weakness, weight loss.
  • Dehydration – dry tongue, sunken eyes, rapid pulse, low BP, scanty concentrated urine.
  • Ketonuria, low potassium and sodium, raised urea; in severe cases jaundice and confusion.
  • Severity can be scored with the PUQE score (Pregnancy-Unique Quantification of Emesis).
  • Investigations – urine ketones and culture, electrolytes, renal and liver function, thyroid function, haemoglobin, and ultrasound to exclude twins or a molar pregnancy.

3. Complications

  • Maternal – severe dehydration, hypokalaemia, metabolic disturbance, Mallory–Weiss tear, Wernicke's encephalopathy (vitamin B1 deficiency – confusion, ataxia, abnormal eye movements), thromboembolism, malnutrition, depression.
  • Fetal – low birth weight in prolonged cases.

4. Management

  • Admit when she cannot retain fluids, has ketonuria or significant weight loss.
  • IV fluids – normal saline or Ringer lactate with potassium chloride as guided by electrolytes; dextrose is avoided until thiamine has been given, because it can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy.
  • Thiamine (100 mg IV/orally) to all women with prolonged vomiting.
  • Antiemetics – doxylamine–pyridoxine, promethazine, metoclopramide or ondansetron as prescribed; antacids or H₂ blockers for heartburn.
  • Thromboprophylaxis (low molecular weight heparin) for admitted women, as advised.
  • Refractory cases – corticosteroids, or enteral/parenteral nutrition.
  • Oral fluids and food are started gradually once vomiting settles.

5. Nursing care

  • Record intake–output, vomiting episodes and daily weight; test urine for ketones.
  • Give small, frequent, dry, bland meals (dry toast, biscuits, rice), cold drinks between meals, ginger; avoid fatty, spicy food and strong smells.
  • Oral hygiene after each episode; keep the room fresh and calm.
  • Reassure her and the family that the condition is temporary and treatable; ask about stress and support at home.

Conclusion Hyperemesis gravidarum needs early rehydration, electrolyte and thiamine replacement, antiemetics and gentle nursing; it usually settles by mid-pregnancy without harm to the baby.

question: Explain the clinical features, diagnosis, management and follow-up of a woman with a hydatidiform (molar) pregnancy.
answer_html:
Introduction A hydatidiform mole is an abnormal pregnancy in which the chorionic villi become swollen fluid-filled vesicles and the trophoblast proliferates. A complete mole has no fetus; a partial mole has an abnormal fetus or fetal tissue. Its importance lies in bleeding and in the risk of persistent trophoblastic disease (choriocarcinoma), so careful follow-up is essential.

1. Clinical features

  • Amenorrhoea followed by vaginal bleeding in the first half of pregnancy, sometimes with passage of grape-like vesicles.
  • Uterus larger than the period of amenorrhoea (in about half), soft and doughy; fetal parts and fetal heart absent (complete mole).
  • Excessive vomiting, pre-eclampsia before 20 weeks, features of hyperthyroidism (high hCG stimulates the thyroid).
  • Anaemia, enlarged ovaries with theca-lutein cysts.
  • Rarely, breathlessness from trophoblastic embolism.

2. Diagnosis

  • Serum β-hCG – very much higher than expected for the gestation.
  • Ultrasound – a "snowstorm" or "cluster of grapes" appearance with no fetus (complete mole); a partial mole may show an abnormal fetus with a cystic placenta.
  • Baseline chest X-ray, haemoglobin, blood group, thyroid, liver and renal function.
  • Histopathology of the evacuated tissue confirms the type.

3. Management

  • Correct anaemia; cross-match blood.
  • Suction evacuation is the method of choice, done by an experienced doctor with blood available. Oxytocin infusion is started after evacuation has begun to reduce bleeding (not before, to avoid pushing trophoblast into the circulation).
  • All tissue is sent for histology; anti-D to Rh-negative women with a partial mole.
  • Hysterectomy with the mole in situ may be chosen for an older woman who has completed her family – but follow-up is still needed.

4. Follow-up – the most important part

  • Serum β-hCG every 1–2 weeks until it becomes normal, then monthly for about 6 months (shorter for partial mole, as per the unit's protocol).
  • A plateau or rise in hCG means persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia – she is referred for chemotherapy (methotrexate), which cures almost all cases.
  • Reliable contraception during follow-up – combined pills or barrier methods; avoid an IUCD until hCG is normal (risk of perforation and confusion with bleeding).
  • In any future pregnancy – early ultrasound, and hCG check 6–8 weeks after delivery.

5. Nursing care

  • Prepare for evacuation (consent, IV line, blood, oxytocin); after the procedure monitor bleeding, vital signs and breathing.
  • Explain clearly why follow-up matters even when she feels well, and keep a follow-up card with dates of hCG tests.
  • Give emotional support – she has lost a pregnancy and fears cancer; reassure her that the outlook with follow-up is excellent.

Conclusion A molar pregnancy is managed by suction evacuation and – most importantly – regular β-hCG follow-up with contraception, which detects and cures persistent disease early.
