question: Explain multiple (twin) pregnancy – its types, diagnosis, complications and management.

diagram.caption: Types of twin pregnancy by chorionicity and the ultrasound signs
labels: Panels – dichorionic diamniotic (two placentas or fused placenta
entangled cords); with a timeline of monozygotic splitting: before day 3 → DCDA

answer_html:
Introduction Multiple pregnancy means more than one fetus in the uterus at the same time. Twins are the commonest – about 1 in 80 pregnancies in India – and their number is rising with assisted reproduction. By Hellin's law, triplets occur in about 1 in 80², quadruplets 1 in 80³.

1. Types

  • Dizygotic (binovular, fraternal) – about two-thirds – two ova fertilised by two sperms; always dichorionic diamniotic; may be of different sex. Favoured by heredity, increasing age and parity, and ovulation induction/IVF.
  • Monozygotic (uniovular, identical) – about one-third – one fertilised ovum splits; same sex. Chorionicity depends on the time of splitting: before day 3 → DCDA; days 4–8 → MCDA (commonest); days 8–12 → MCMA; after day 13 → conjoined twins.
  • Chorionicity matters more than zygosity: monochorionic twins share one placenta and face more complications.

2. Diagnosis

  • History of ART or twins in the family; excessive vomiting.
  • Uterus larger than dates, many fetal parts, two fetal heads; two fetal hearts heard at different spots with a rate difference of 10 beats/minute or more.
  • Ultrasound confirms – and chorionicity is determined at 11–14 weeks (lambda sign = dichorionic; T sign = monochorionic).

3. Complications

  • Maternal – hyperemesis, anaemia, pre-eclampsia, GDM, polyhydramnios, APH, preterm labour, malpresentations, operative delivery and PPH from an over-stretched uterus.
  • Fetal – prematurity (the main cause of perinatal death), growth restriction and discordant growth, congenital anomalies, twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (monochorionic), cord entanglement (monoamniotic), death of one twin, locked twins (rare).

4. Antenatal management

  • Early booking; more frequent visits; extra calories, double IFA, calcium and protein; adequate rest.
  • Screening for anaemia, pre-eclampsia and GDM.
  • Serial ultrasound – every 4 weeks for dichorionic twins and every 2 weeks from 16 weeks for monochorionic twins (to detect TTTS).
  • Corticosteroids when preterm delivery is expected.
  • Timing of delivery (commonly followed) – uncomplicated DCDA at about 37 weeks, MCDA at about 36 weeks, MCMA at about 32–34 weeks by caesarean section.

5. Management of labour

  • Delivery in a hospital with a newborn care unit, two resuscitation sets, IV line and blood ready; continuous monitoring of both fetal hearts.
  • Vaginal delivery is usually planned when the first twin is cephalic; caesarean section if the first twin is non-cephalic, for monoamniotic or conjoined twins, or for other indications.
  • After the first twin is born – clamp the cord; check the lie and heart of the second twin; correct the lie to longitudinal; rupture membranes and deliver the second twin with continuous monitoring (oxytocin infusion if contractions become weak); an internal podalic version or breech extraction may be needed.
  • Give the oxytocic only after the second twin is delivered, then continue an oxytocin infusion for an hour to prevent PPH.
  • Label babies "Twin 1" and "Twin 2"; examine the placenta(s) and membranes.

6. Nursing role

  • Educate on danger signs and preterm labour; help with breastfeeding two babies (rugby/football hold, alternating breasts); KMC for small babies; family support.

Conclusion Early diagnosis with chorionicity, close surveillance, planned delivery in a well-equipped hospital and expert care of the second twin and the third stage reduce the high risks of twin pregnancy.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: Explain polyhydramnios and oligohydramnios – causes, complications and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Amniotic fluid (liquor amnii) protects the fetus, allows movement and lung development, and keeps the cord free. At term it measures about 800–1,000 ml. Its volume is assessed by ultrasound using the amniotic fluid index (AFI) (the sum of the deepest pockets in four quadrants) or the single deepest pocket (SDP).

A. Polyhydramnios (hydramnios)

  • Definition – excess of amniotic fluid: AFI ≥24–25 cm or SDP ≥8 cm (more than about 2 litres).
  • Causes
    • Fetal – anencephaly, open spina bifida, oesophageal or duodenal atresia (fetus cannot swallow), neuromuscular disorders, fetal hydrops, chromosomal anomalies.
    • Maternal – diabetes (fetal polyuria).
    • Placental and twin – chorioangioma, monochorionic twins with TTTS.
    • Idiopathic in about half.
  • Types – chronic (gradual, commoner, third trimester) and acute (rapid accumulation in a few days, usually at 20–24 weeks in monochorionic twins).
  • Features – breathlessness, abdominal discomfort, oedema of legs; uterus larger than dates, tense and shiny, fluid thrill present, fetal parts and heart sounds difficult to make out; unstable lie.
  • Complications – preterm labour, PROM, cord prolapse and abruption when membranes rupture suddenly, malpresentation, uterine inertia and PPH.
  • Management
    • Ultrasound for anomalies; GDM test; TORCH tests if indicated.
    • Mild cases – observation, rest, regular review.
    • Severe symptomatic cases – amnioreduction (slow removal of fluid) or, before 32 weeks, a short course of indomethacin as prescribed.
    • In labour – controlled amniotomy (slow release of fluid with the head guarded), watch for cord prolapse; oxytocin for inertia; prevent PPH.

B. Oligohydramnios

  • Definition – deficiency of amniotic fluid: AFI ≤5 cm or SDP <2 cm (less than about 200 ml at term).
  • Causes
    • Fetal – renal agenesis (Potter syndrome), obstructive uropathy, chromosomal anomalies.
    • Rupture of membranes (PPROM).
    • Placental insufficiency – pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction, post-term pregnancy.
    • Drugs – NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors; idiopathic.
  • Features – uterus smaller than dates, fetal parts easily felt, reduced fetal movements.
  • Complications – early onset: pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities (club foot), Potter facies; late: cord compression, fetal distress, meconium-stained liquor, increased caesarean rate.
  • Management
    • Find and treat the cause; maternal hydration (extra oral fluids of about 2 litres a day, or IV fluids).
    • Close fetal surveillance – NST/CTG, Doppler, growth scans.
    • Delivery at term or earlier if the fetus is compromised; amnioinfusion in labour in selected cases.

Nursing role

  • Measure fundal height and girth regularly; teach fetal movement counting; prepare for ultrasound.
  • In polyhydramnios – position her propped up for breathlessness; be alert for cord prolapse after rupture of membranes.
  • In oligohydramnios – encourage fluids; monitor the fetal heart closely in labour.

Conclusion Both excess and deficiency of liquor are warning signs of fetal or maternal disease; ultrasound diagnosis, search for the cause and close surveillance guide safe management.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: Explain intrauterine fetal death – causes, diagnosis, complications, management and bereavement care.
answer_html:
Introduction Intrauterine fetal death (IUFD) is the death of the fetus in the uterus after 20 weeks (in India, a fetal death after 28 weeks is registered as a stillbirth). It is a devastating event for the family, and many cases are preventable with good antenatal and intrapartum care. The India Newborn Action Plan aims for a single-digit stillbirth rate by 2030.

1. Causes

  • Maternal – hypertensive disorders and abruption, diabetes, severe anaemia, infections (malaria, syphilis, listeria), intrahepatic cholestasis, antiphospholipid syndrome, Rh isoimmunisation, post-term pregnancy, trauma.
  • Fetal – congenital and chromosomal anomalies, growth restriction, fetal infection, twin complications.
  • Placental and cord – abruption, placental insufficiency or infarction, cord accidents (true knot, prolapse, tight entanglement).
  • Unexplained in a considerable proportion.

2. Diagnosis

  • Symptoms – absence of fetal movements, regression of breast changes, weight loss, sometimes brownish discharge.
  • Signs – uterus smaller than dates, fetal heart not heard, fetal parts less distinct.
  • Ultrasound confirms – no cardiac activity (confirmed by a second person where possible).
  • Old X-ray signs – Spalding sign (overlapping skull bones, about 7 days after death) and Robert's sign (gas in the great vessels).

3. Complications

  • Coagulation failure (hypofibrinogenaemia, DIC) when the dead fetus is retained for more than about 4 weeks, or with abruption.
  • Infection, especially after rupture of membranes; PPH.
  • Psychological trauma – grief, guilt, depression.

4. Management

  • Investigations – haemoglobin, platelets, fibrinogen and coagulation profile, blood group and antibody screen, blood sugar/HbA1c, thyroid function, syphilis and other infection tests, Kleihauer test, antiphospholipid antibodies; after birth – examination of baby and placenta, autopsy and karyotype (with consent).
  • Delivery – most women go into labour within about 2 weeks, but most prefer early delivery. Induction with mifepristone 200 mg, followed 24–48 hours later by misoprostol (dose reduced at later gestation and in a scarred uterus), or oxytocin; caesarean section only for obstetric reasons.
  • Adequate pain relief in labour; active management of the third stage.
  • After delivery – suppression of lactation (cabergoline 1 mg single dose, breast support), anti-D if Rh negative, contraception counselling.

5. Bereavement (respectful) care – the nurse's special role

  • Break the news gently, in private, with the family present; use simple honest words.
  • Offer parents the chance to see and hold the baby, name it, and keep mementoes (handprints, footprints, a photograph, a lock of hair), respecting cultural and religious wishes.
  • Provide a private room away from crying babies; continuity of the same nurse where possible.
  • Allow and acknowledge grief; avoid blaming remarks; involve the husband and family.
  • Help with formalities (stillbirth registration, release of the body).
  • Follow-up visit to discuss results, emotional recovery and planning of the next pregnancy (early booking, preconception care, closer surveillance).

Conclusion IUFD needs confirmation by ultrasound, a search for the cause, safe induction with watch for DIC and, above all, compassionate bereavement care and careful planning of the next pregnancy.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: Explain the management of a pregnant woman with severe anaemia during the antenatal period, labour and the puerperium.
answer_html:
Introduction Anaemia remains common in Indian pregnant women (52.2% in NFHS-5). Under the Anaemia Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan Operational Guidelines (MoHFW, June 2026), anaemia in pregnancy is graded as follows:

Trimester Mild Moderate Severe
First and third 10.0–10.9 g/dl 7.0–9.9 g/dl <7.0 g/dl
Second (WHO 2024 cut-offs) 9.5–10.4 g/dl 7.0–9.4 g/dl <7.0 g/dl

A woman with severe anaemia is at risk of heart failure, PPH, shock, infection and death, and her baby of preterm birth, low birth weight and stillbirth. She must be referred to an FRU or district hospital.

1. Antenatal management

  • Find the cause – complete blood count with red cell indices, peripheral smear, serum ferritin, stool for ova and occult blood, urine, malaria test, sickling test (in endemic areas such as Vidarbha) and Hb electrophoresis for thalassaemia; vitamin B₁₂ and folate where megaloblastic anaemia is suspected.
  • Treat the cause – deworming (albendazole 400 mg after the first trimester), treatment of malaria, bleeding piles or other blood loss.
  • Iron replacement
    • IV iron – iron sucrose (5 doses) or ferric carboxymaltose (2 doses) as advised by the treating physician, after the first trimester (13 weeks), when oral iron is not tolerated or a quick rise is needed.
    • Oral IFA (two tablets daily) where appropriate.
  • Blood transfusion – for very severe anaemia (Hb <5 g/dl), severe anaemia close to term or in labour, anaemic heart failure or acute blood loss; packed red cells given slowly, with a diuretic if heart failure threatens.
  • Diet rich in iron, protein and vitamin C; rest; treat infections.
  • Recheck Hb after one month; plan delivery at a facility with a blood bank.

2. Management during labour

  • Admit early; propped-up position, oxygen if breathless; IV line with restricted fluids (avoid overload); blood cross-matched and kept ready.
  • Monitor pulse, respiration, BP and SpO₂ closely; watch for signs of heart failure (rising pulse and respiratory rate, crackles).
  • Adequate pain relief; avoid prolonged labour; cut short the second stage with forceps or vacuum if she is tiring.
  • Active management of the third stage with oxytocin; minimise blood loss – even a normal loss may cause shock; avoid ergometrine in heart failure.
  • Strict asepsis – resistance to infection is low.

3. Management in the puerperium

  • Watch for PPH, shock, heart failure, infection, thromboembolism and subinvolution.
  • Continue iron – one IFA tablet daily for 180 days after delivery (prophylaxis), or treatment doses/IV iron if still anaemic, with Hb retesting.
  • Encourage breastfeeding with good nutrition; early ambulation.
  • Family planning counselling to space the next pregnancy by at least 2–3 years.

4. Nursing role

  • Screen Hb at every ANC contact (digital haemoglobinometer), track defaulters and ensure compliance – the T4 approach: Test, Treat, Talk and Track.
  • Counsel on taking IFA after meals, with water or lemon juice, not with tea or milk; manage side effects.
  • Observe for reactions during IV iron and blood transfusion.

Conclusion Severe anaemia is a referral emergency in pregnancy. Correcting it with IV iron or transfusion before labour, careful conduct of labour with minimal blood loss and continued iron after delivery save the lives of many Indian mothers.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: Explain urinary tract infection and malaria in pregnancy – their effects and management.
answer_html:
A. Urinary tract infection (UTI) in pregnancy

1. Why pregnancy predisposes

  • Progesterone relaxes the ureters (hydroureter, more on the right), the enlarged uterus presses on them, and urine stagnates; glycosuria encourages bacterial growth.
  • Common organisms – E. coli (most), Klebsiella, Proteus, group B streptococcus.

2. Types and effects

  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria – ≥10⁵ colony-forming units/ml of a single organism in a clean-catch midstream urine without symptoms (in about 2–10% of pregnant women). Untreated, about a quarter develop acute pyelonephritis, and it is linked with preterm labour and low birth weight.
  • Acute cystitis – frequency, burning micturition, urgency, suprapubic pain.
  • Acute pyelonephritis – fever with chills, loin pain (often right), vomiting, renal angle tenderness; can lead to septic shock, respiratory distress and preterm labour.

3. Management

  • Screen all women at the first visit by urine culture (or dipstick where culture is unavailable).
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria and cystitis – oral antibiotics safe in pregnancy as per culture (for example cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, nitrofurantoin – avoided near term); repeat culture after treatment.
  • Pyelonephritis – admission, IV fluids, IV antibiotics (such as ceftriaxone), antipyretics, monitoring of urine output and contractions; then oral antibiotics to complete about 14 days.
  • Nursing advice – 2–3 litres of fluid a day, frequent voiding, wiping front to back, cotton undergarments, completing the full course of antibiotics.

B. Malaria in pregnancy

1. Why it is dangerous

  • Pregnancy lowers immunity and P. falciparum-infected red cells collect (sequester) in the placenta, so pregnant women get more frequent and more severe malaria.

2. Effects

  • Mother – severe anaemia, hypoglycaemia, high fever, cerebral malaria, pulmonary oedema, renal failure, death.
  • Fetus – abortion, preterm labour, fetal growth restriction and low birth weight, stillbirth, congenital malaria.

3. Diagnosis – every pregnant woman with fever in an endemic area is tested by RDT or blood smear on the same day.

4. Treatment (follow the current national drug policy of NCVBDC)

  • P. vivax – chloroquine for 3 days; primaquine is contraindicated in pregnancy.
  • Uncomplicated P. falciparum – first trimester: quinine under the national policy (WHO has recommended artemether–lumefantrine in the first trimester since 2022); second and third trimesters: ACT (artesunate + sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine; artemether–lumefantrine in north-eastern states).
  • Severe malaria – urgent referral; parenteral artesunate (preferred in all trimesters by WHO) or quinine; monitor blood glucose; manage complications.
  • Treat fever with paracetamol and tepid sponging; correct anaemia; monitor fetal heart and contractions.

5. Prevention – long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLIN), indoor residual spraying, removal of breeding sites, early testing of every fever.

Conclusion Routine urine screening and prompt treatment prevent pyelonephritis and preterm labour, while early testing and correct trimester-wise treatment of malaria, with bed nets, protect mother and fetus in endemic areas.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: Explain thyroid disorders in pregnancy – hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism – and their management.
answer_html:
Introduction Thyroid hormones are essential for a healthy pregnancy and for the brain development of the fetus, which depends entirely on maternal thyroxine until its own thyroid works from about 10–12 weeks. In pregnancy, hCG stimulates the thyroid (TSH falls slightly in the first trimester), thyroxine-binding globulin rises, and iodine needs increase to about 250 µg/day.

A. Hypothyroidism

  • Types – overt (high TSH, low free T4) and subclinical (high TSH, normal free T4); common causes are autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis and iodine deficiency.
  • Effects – infertility, abortion, anaemia, pre-eclampsia, abruption, PPH, preterm birth, low birth weight, stillbirth and impaired intellectual development of the child.
  • Screening (MoHFW National Guidelines, 2014) – TSH at the first antenatal visit, interpreted with trimester-specific limits: up to 2.5 mIU/L in the first trimester and 3.0 mIU/L in the second and third trimesters.
  • Management
    • Levothyroxine daily, on an empty stomach 30–60 minutes before breakfast, 4 hours apart from iron and calcium tablets.
    • Women already on levothyroxine increase the dose by about 25–30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.
    • TSH every 4–6 weeks in the first half of pregnancy, then at least once each trimester.
    • After delivery, return to the pre-pregnancy dose; ensure newborn TSH screening.

B. Hyperthyroidism

  • Causes – Graves' disease (commonest), gestational transient thyrotoxicosis (high hCG, often with hyperemesis; self-limiting), toxic nodule, molar pregnancy.
  • Features – palpitations, tachycardia, heat intolerance, tremor, weight loss despite good appetite, goitre, eye signs.
  • Effects – abortion, pre-eclampsia, preterm labour, fetal growth restriction, stillbirth, maternal heart failure, thyroid storm (with labour, infection or surgery), and fetal/neonatal thyrotoxicosis (stimulating antibodies cross the placenta).
  • Management
    • Propylthiouracil (PTU) in the first trimester (less teratogenic), then carbimazole/methimazole from the second trimester (PTU can damage the liver); lowest dose that keeps free T4 at the upper normal limit.
    • Propranolol for a short time to control symptoms.
    • Radioactive iodine is contraindicated; surgery (second trimester) only for failure of drugs.
    • Thyroid storm – an emergency in ICU: antithyroid drugs, iodine, propranolol, steroids, cooling, fluids.
    • Paediatrician to examine the newborn for thyroid dysfunction.

Nursing role

  • Ensure TSH testing at booking and follow-up tests; teach correct timing of levothyroxine.
  • Promote iodised salt; monitor pulse, weight, BP and fetal growth.
  • Teach warning signs – fever with fast pulse and agitation (storm) – and the importance of not stopping drugs.

Conclusion Early TSH screening, careful dose adjustment and trimester-appropriate antithyroid drugs prevent the maternal and fetal complications of thyroid disease and protect the baby's brain.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: Explain post-abortion care – its elements and the role of the nurse.
tags: treatment of incomplete and unsafe abortion
answer_html:
Introduction Post-abortion care (PAC) is a package of services for women who have had a spontaneous or induced abortion, especially an incomplete or unsafe one. Its aim is to save the woman's life, treat complications, and prevent repeat unwanted pregnancy and unsafe abortion. In India, it forms part of Comprehensive Abortion Care (CAC) under the national guidelines, alongside safe legal abortion under the MTP Act (amended 2021).

1. Elements of post-abortion care

  • Community and service-provider partnership – awareness of the danger of unsafe abortion, of where safe services are available, and quick referral and transport.
  • Counselling – about her condition, the procedure, her emotional needs and future fertility, given privately and without judgement.
  • Treatment of incomplete and unsafe abortion and its complications – resuscitation, uterine evacuation, antibiotics, management of haemorrhage, sepsis and injuries.
  • Contraceptive and family planning services – before she leaves the facility.
  • Reproductive and other health services – STI/HIV testing, anaemia treatment, cervical screening, gender-based violence screening, referral as needed.

2. Uterine evacuation by manual vacuum aspiration (MVA)

  • Preparation – history, vital signs, uterine size by bimanual examination; consent; empty bladder; pain control (oral analgesic plus paracervical block with 1% lignocaine); prophylactic antibiotic (such as doxycycline) as per protocol.
  • Procedure – aseptic cleaning, speculum, tenaculum on the cervix, gentle dilatation if needed; a cannula of size matching the weeks of gestation is inserted and attached to the charged aspirator; the valves are released and the contents are evacuated with gentle rotating, in-and-out movements.
  • Signs of completion – red or pink foam in the cannula, a gritty feeling, the uterus contracting around the cannula.
  • Tissue inspection – the aspirate is floated in water to identify villi.
  • Medical alternative – misoprostol for incomplete abortion in a stable woman with a small uterus.
  • Post-procedure – monitor pulse, BP and bleeding for at least 30–60 minutes; analgesics; iron.

3. Post-abortion contraception

  • Fertility returns within about 2 weeks – contraception should start immediately.
  • Almost all methods are suitable after an uncomplicated first-trimester abortion – IUCD insertion at the time of evacuation, injectable (Antara), oral pills (Mala-N, Chhaya), implant, condoms, and sterilisation (if not infected and the decision is informed and voluntary).

4. Role of the nurse

  • Early identification and stabilisation of bleeding or septic women; arranging referral and transport.
  • Assisting MVA, maintaining the MVA kit (cleaning, high-level disinfection) and asepsis.
  • Respectful, confidential, non-judgemental care, privacy and emotional support.
  • Counselling and providing the chosen contraceptive; teaching danger signs (heavy bleeding, fever, foul discharge, severe pain).
  • Follow-up visit at 1–2 weeks; linking the woman to safe abortion and family planning services.

Conclusion Post-abortion care – emergency treatment with MVA, counselling, immediate contraception and links to other services – is a simple, nurse-supported package that greatly reduces abortion-related deaths and repeat abortions.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: Explain TORCH infections in pregnancy and their effects on the fetus, with preventive measures.
tags: caesarean section for active genital herpes
answer_html:
Introduction TORCH is a group of infections that can cross the placenta (or infect the baby at birth) and cause abortion, stillbirth, growth restriction, congenital malformations and neonatal disease. The letters stand for Toxoplasmosis, Others (syphilis, varicella-zoster, parvovirus B19, hepatitis B, HIV, Zika), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus and Herpes simplex. The mother may have only mild illness or none.

1. Toxoplasmosis

  • Caused by Toxoplasma gondii, acquired from cat faeces, contaminated soil and undercooked meat.
  • The risk of transmission rises with gestation, but early infection causes more severe disease.
  • Fetal effects – chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcification (classic triad), convulsions, microcephaly.
  • Treatment – spiramycin; pyrimethamine–sulfadiazine when fetal infection is confirmed, as prescribed.

2. Rubella (German measles)

  • Most dangerous in the first 12 weeks, when the risk of fetal damage is very high.
  • Congenital rubella syndrome – cataract, sensorineural deafness and heart defects (PDA, pulmonary stenosis) (Gregg's triad), microcephaly, intellectual disability, hepatosplenomegaly, low birth weight.
  • Prevention – MR (measles–rubella) vaccination of girls and women before pregnancy; the vaccine is not given in pregnancy and pregnancy is avoided for one month after it.

3. Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

  • The commonest congenital viral infection; spread through saliva, urine and genital secretions of young children and partners.
  • Fetal effects – sensorineural hearing loss (most frequent long-term problem), microcephaly, periventricular calcification, chorioretinitis, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, low platelets.
  • No vaccine – prevention is by hygiene.

4. Herpes simplex virus

  • Usually transmitted during birth through an infected genital tract, especially with a primary infection near term.
  • Neonatal herpes – skin, eye and mouth lesions, encephalitis or disseminated infection with high mortality.
  • Caesarean section if active genital lesions are present at the onset of labour; aciclovir from 36 weeks for women with recurrences, as prescribed.

5. Others (briefly)

  • Varicella – congenital varicella syndrome (limb hypoplasia, skin scarring); VZIG after exposure for non-immune women.
  • Parvovirus B19 – fetal anaemia and hydrops fetalis.
  • Hepatitis B – infection of the baby at birth; prevented by birth-dose hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG within 12–24 hours.
  • Syphilis and HIV – screened at the first visit and managed under the national elimination of vertical transmission programme.

6. Diagnosis

  • Serology (IgM, IgG, IgG avidity) when there is a suggestive illness, exposure or abnormal ultrasound; routine TORCH panels in healthy women are not recommended.
  • Ultrasound for fetal anomalies; amniocentesis (PCR) for confirmation in selected cases.

7. Prevention and nursing role

  • Rubella immunity before pregnancy (preconception care).
  • Hand washing after handling children's diapers and saliva, after gardening and before eating; avoid sharing cups and utensils with young children.
  • Food safety – eat well-cooked meat, wash fruit and vegetables, drink safe water; avoid cleaning cat litter.
  • Safe sex; screening for syphilis, HIV and hepatitis B at booking.
  • Counsel women with confirmed infection sensitively; arrange newborn hearing, eye and developmental follow-up.

Conclusion TORCH infections can damage the fetus silently. Preconception rubella vaccination, simple hygiene and food safety, targeted testing and newborn follow-up are the key nursing measures.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: What is cervical insufficiency? Explain cervical cerclage.
answer_html:
• Cervical insufficiency (incompetence) is the inability of the cervix to retain a pregnancy – it dilates painlessly in the second trimester, causing recurrent mid-trimester abortion or preterm birth. Causes include congenital weakness and injury (forceful dilatation, conisation, deep tears).
  • Cervical cerclage is a purse-string suture of non-absorbable tape placed around the cervix near the internal os to keep it closed – McDonald (simple purse-string) or Shirodkar (placed higher, under the mucosa).
  • It is done as history-indicated (about 12–14 weeks), ultrasound-indicated (short cervix below 25 mm) or rescue (cervix already dilating).
  • The stitch is removed at about 36–37 weeks, or at once if labour starts or membranes rupture. It is not done with bleeding, infection, ruptured membranes or labour.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: What is Couvelaire uterus?
answer_html:
• Couvelaire uterus (uteroplacental apoplexy) occurs in severe concealed abruptio placentae: blood from the retroplacental clot extravasates into the myometrium and may reach the serosa, broad ligaments and tubes.
  • The uterus looks purplish, bluish or coppery and mottled, like a bruise.
  • It is seen only at caesarean section or laparotomy.
  • It is often associated with DIC and PPH.
  • The uterus usually still contracts with oxytocics, so it is not by itself an indication for hysterectomy; hysterectomy is done only for uncontrolled bleeding.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: What is HELLP syndrome?
answer_html:
• HELLP syndrome is a severe form of pre-eclampsia with Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelets.
  • Laboratory features – haemolysis on the smear with LDH ≥600 IU/L, AST/ALT about twice normal or more (≥70 IU/L), platelets below 1 lakh/µl.
  • Symptoms – epigastric or right upper abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, malaise; BP may be only mildly raised.
  • Complications – DIC, abruption, acute kidney injury, pulmonary oedema, liver haematoma or rupture, maternal death.
  • Management – stabilise in a tertiary centre, magnesium sulphate, BP control, platelet transfusion if very low before surgery, steroids for fetal lungs when appropriate, and prompt delivery.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: Who is an elderly primigravida? List the risks.
answer_html:
• An elderly primigravida is a woman pregnant for the first time at the age of 35 years or more. The pregnancy is often precious ("premium pregnancy"), sometimes after years of infertility treatment.
  • Risks
    • Abortion and chromosomal anomalies such as Down syndrome.
    • Multiple pregnancy (after ART), pre-eclampsia, GDM, fibroids, placenta praevia.
    • Malpresentation, prolonged labour, operative and caesarean delivery, PPH, stillbirth.
  • Care – preconception counselling, early booking, aneuploidy screening, regular BP and GDM checks, fetal surveillance, and delivery in a well-equipped hospital (often planned around 39–40 weeks).

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: What is placenta accreta spectrum?
answer_html:
• Placenta accreta spectrum is abnormally firm attachment of the placenta to the uterine wall because the decidua basalis (Nitabuch's layer) is deficient, so the placenta cannot separate after birth.
  • Grades – accreta (villi attached to the myometrium), increta (villi invade the myometrium) and percreta (villi pass through the serosa, often into the bladder).
  • Major risk factor – previous caesarean section, especially with placenta praevia over the scar; also previous curettage, myomectomy and IVF.
  • Diagnosis – antenatal ultrasound with colour Doppler; MRI.
  • Management – planned delivery at about 34–36 weeks in a tertiary centre with blood products; usually caesarean hysterectomy with the placenta left in place; the main danger is massive PPH.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: What is twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome?
answer_html:
• Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) is a serious complication of monochorionic twins (in about 10–15% of MCDA twins), caused by unbalanced blood flow through vascular connections in the shared placenta.
  • Donor twin – loses blood: becomes anaemic and small, passes little urine, develops oligohydramnios ("stuck twin").
  • Recipient twin – receives excess blood: polycythaemia, polyuria, polyhydramnios, heart failure and hydrops.
  • Diagnosis – ultrasound (deepest pocket <2 cm in one sac and >8 cm in the other); staged by Quintero staging (I–V). Monochorionic twins are scanned every 2 weeks from 16 weeks.
  • Treatment – fetoscopic laser ablation of the connecting vessels (best results), amnioreduction, or early delivery.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: What is recurrent miscarriage? List its causes.
answer_html:
• Recurrent miscarriage is the loss of two or more (traditionally three or more) consecutive pregnancies before viability.
  • Causes
    • Parental chromosomal abnormality (such as a balanced translocation).
    • Antiphospholipid syndrome – the most important treatable cause (treated with low-dose aspirin and heparin).
    • Uterine anomalies (septate uterus), submucous fibroids, Asherman's syndrome, cervical insufficiency (mid-trimester losses).
    • Endocrine – uncontrolled diabetes, thyroid disease, PCOS.
    • Thrombophilias, smoking, obesity, advanced maternal age.
    • About half remain unexplained – yet most such couples later have a live birth with supportive care.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Problems during Pregnancy
question: What is intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy?
answer_html:
• Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is a liver disorder of the late second and third trimester in which bile flow is impaired.
  • Main symptom – itching without a rash, worst on the palms and soles and at night; occasionally mild jaundice.
  • Diagnosis – raised serum bile acids (above about 10 µmol/L) and liver enzymes, after excluding other liver diseases.
  • Risks to the fetus – preterm labour, meconium-stained liquor, fetal distress and sudden stillbirth (higher when bile acids are very high).
  • Management – ursodeoxycholic acid and antihistamines for itch, calamine lotion, fetal monitoring, and planned delivery (earlier when bile acids are very high). It clears after delivery but may recur.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)

question: (a) Define preterm labour and list its causes and risk factors. (4 marks) (b) Explain the diagnosis, prediction and prevention of preterm labour. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a woman in preterm labour. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Management pathway for a woman in preterm labour
labels: fetal compromise) → transfer in utero to a facility with SNCU → 24–34 weeks: tocolysis for up to 48 hours + antenatal corticosteroids; below 32 weeks: add magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection → GBS prophylaxis as per policy → delivery with continuous monitoring

answer_html:
(a) Definition, causes and risk factors (4 marks)

Definition

  • Preterm labour is the onset of regular, painful uterine contractions leading to progressive effacement and dilatation of the cervix after the age of viability (28 weeks in India) and before 37 completed weeks of pregnancy.
  • Threatened preterm labour – contractions without cervical change.
  • WHO sub-groups of preterm birth – extremely preterm (<28 weeks), very preterm (28 to <32 weeks), moderate to late preterm (32 to <37 weeks).
  • India has the largest number of preterm births in the world – about 3 million a year (WHO estimates for 2020) – and prematurity is the leading cause of newborn and under-five deaths.

Causes and risk factors

Group Examples
Previous history Previous preterm birth (the strongest predictor), previous mid-trimester loss
Infection Chorioamnionitis, asymptomatic bacteriuria and pyelonephritis, bacterial vaginosis, malaria, periodontal disease
Over-distension of the uterus Multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios
Cervical and uterine factors Cervical insufficiency, short cervix, uterine anomalies, fibroids
Placental Abruption, placenta praevia
Membranes Preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM)
Maternal disease Pre-eclampsia, diabetes, severe anaemia, thyroid disease
Social and lifestyle Teenage or elderly pregnancy, short interpregnancy interval, low BMI, heavy physical work, smoking and tobacco chewing, stress, poverty
Iatrogenic (indicated) Planned early delivery for pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction, APH

(b) Diagnosis, prediction and prevention (4 marks)

Diagnosis

  • Regular painful contractions (about 4 in 20 minutes or 8 in an hour), low backache, pelvic pressure, increased mucoid or blood-stained discharge.
  • Cervical change on examination – dilatation of 2 cm or more, or progressive effacement.
  • Sterile speculum examination first, to look for rupture of membranes and avoid repeated digital examinations.
  • Supporting tests – transvaginal cervical length (less than 15–25 mm suggests a high risk), fetal fibronectin (a negative test makes delivery within 7–14 days unlikely), ultrasound for gestational age, presentation, weight and liquor, urine culture, vaginal swab and blood count.

Prediction and prevention

  • Take a careful history of previous preterm birth; screen cervical length at 18–24 weeks in high-risk women.
  • Vaginal progesterone daily for women with a short cervix or previous spontaneous preterm birth, as prescribed.
  • Cervical cerclage for cervical insufficiency.
  • Screen and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria, vaginal infections and malaria; dental care.
  • Correct anaemia and undernutrition; birth spacing of at least 2–3 years; avoid tobacco; reduce heavy work; manage pre-eclampsia and diabetes well.

(c) Management and nursing care (7 marks)

1. Initial assessment

  • Confirm the gestational age (early scan, LMP) and the diagnosis; record contractions, fetal heart, maternal vitals.
  • Look for conditions in which labour should not be stopped – chorioamnionitis, abruption, severe pre-eclampsia, fetal distress, fetal death or lethal anomaly, advanced labour.

2. In-utero transfer

  • If the facility has no newborn intensive or special care unit, transfer the mother before delivery – "the uterus is the best transport incubator". Send referral notes, ensure an IV line and a trained escort.

3. Tocolysis (to delay delivery for about 48 hours)

  • Purpose – to gain time for corticosteroids to act and for transfer; it does not prolong pregnancy much longer.
  • Used between 24 and 34 weeks when there is no contraindication.
  • Nifedipine (oral) is the usual first choice; atosiban is an alternative; indomethacin may be used before 32 weeks for a short period.
  • Nursing watch – BP, pulse and headache with nifedipine; contractions and fetal heart throughout.

4. Antenatal corticosteroids – the most important single measure

  • WHO (2022) recommends them for women at 24–34 weeks when preterm birth is expected within 7 days, provided the gestational age is accurate, there is no maternal infection, and adequate childbirth and preterm newborn care are available.
  • Dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses (or betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses).
  • They reduce newborn death, respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotising enterocolitis.
  • Watch blood sugar in diabetic women.

5. Magnesium sulphate for fetal neuroprotection

  • For women likely to deliver before 32 weeks – it reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in the baby.
  • Usually 4 g IV over 20–30 minutes, then 1 g/hour until birth (maximum about 24 hours), with the same toxicity checks as in eclampsia.

6. Antibiotics

  • Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis against group B streptococcus in established preterm labour, as per policy.
  • Antibiotics are not given routinely when membranes are intact and there is no infection; specific treatment for urinary or other infections.

7. Conduct of preterm delivery

  • Deliver in a unit with a neonatal team present and resuscitation equipment checked (small masks, warmer, plastic wrap for very small babies).
  • Continuous fetal heart monitoring; vaginal delivery for cephalic presentation; caesarean section only for obstetric indications.
  • Gentle delivery of the head; vacuum is avoided before 34 weeks.
  • Delayed cord clamping (at least 1 minute) when the baby does not need immediate resuscitation.
  • Prevent hypothermia – warm room, dry and wrap, cap; immediate kangaroo mother care for stable small babies; early breastfeeding or expressed breast milk.

8. Nursing care

  • Left lateral position; hydration; record contractions, cervical progress, fetal heart, temperature and pulse regularly.
  • Give drugs on time and monitor side effects (tachycardia, hypotension, flushing, headache; magnesium toxicity signs).
  • Keep the woman and her family informed – fear and guilt are common; arrange a visit to the newborn unit if time allows.
  • Explain the plan for the baby (SNCU care, KMC, breast milk).
  • Health education for the future – early booking, cervical length check, progesterone or cerclage if advised, treatment of infections, and reporting tightenings, backache or leaking early.

9. Problems of the preterm baby and the nurse's preventive actions

Problem Why it occurs Preventive nursing action
Respiratory distress syndrome, apnoea Surfactant deficiency, immature breathing centre Antenatal corticosteroids; gentle resuscitation; CPAP in SNCU; apnoea monitoring
Hypothermia Thin skin, little brown fat, large surface area Warm chain – warm room, drying, cap, KMC, plastic wrap below 32 weeks
Hypoglycaemia Low glycogen stores Early and frequent breastfeeding or expressed milk; blood glucose checks
Infection (sepsis) Immature immunity Hand hygiene, clean cord care, exclusive breast milk, minimal handling
Feeding difficulty Weak suck and swallow Expressed breast milk by paladai, cup or tube; support the mother to express
Jaundice Immature liver Early feeding, regular checks, phototherapy when needed
Intraventricular haemorrhage, retinopathy of prematurity, necrotising enterocolitis Fragile vessels, immature organs Magnesium sulphate before 32 weeks, careful oxygen use, ROP screening, breast milk

Long-term follow-up for growth, development, vision and hearing is needed for all very preterm babies.

Nursing importance

  • Most preterm deaths can be prevented by simple, low-cost care – corticosteroids, warmth, breastfeeding, KMC and infection prevention – which nurses deliver.
  • Recognising early signs and arranging timely in-utero transfer gives the baby the best chance.

Conclusion Preterm labour is a leading cause of newborn death in India. Early diagnosis, short-term tocolysis, antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulphate before 32 weeks, delivery in the right place and good newborn care greatly improve survival.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)

question: (a) Define premature rupture of membranes (PROM) and preterm PROM, and list the causes. (3 marks) (b) Explain the diagnosis of rupture of membranes and of chorioamnionitis. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management of PROM at term and of preterm PROM, with nursing care. (7 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definitions and causes (3 marks)

Definitions

  • Premature (prelabour) rupture of membranes (PROM) – rupture of the fetal membranes before the onset of labour, at any gestation; when it happens at or after 37 weeks it is called term PROM (about 8–10% of term pregnancies).
  • Preterm PROM (PPROM) – rupture of membranes before 37 completed weeks and before labour begins (about 2–3% of pregnancies; responsible for about one-third of preterm births).
  • Latent period – the interval between rupture and the start of labour; prolonged rupture – more than 18–24 hours.

Causes and risk factors

  • Ascending infection of the lower genital tract (bacterial vaginosis, chlamydia, gonorrhoea, GBS) – the commonest cause, especially of PPROM.
  • Over-distension – multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios.
  • Cervical insufficiency, previous cerclage or cervical surgery.
  • Malpresentation and a high head (unequal pressure on the membranes).
  • APH, previous PPROM, smoking, poor nutrition (vitamin C, copper deficiency), low socio-economic status, invasive procedures (amniocentesis).

(b) Diagnosis of rupture of membranes and chorioamnionitis (5 marks)

1. History – a sudden gush or continuous trickle of watery fluid from the vagina; ask about time of leaking, colour (clear, meconium, blood) and smell.

2. Sterile speculum examination (the key examination)

  • Pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix, or fluid seen leaking from the os when she coughs.
  • Look for cord prolapse, assess cervical dilatation visually, and take swabs.
  • Avoid digital vaginal examination in PPROM (and at term until labour) because it introduces infection and shortens the latent period.

3. Bedside tests on the fluid

  • Nitrazine test – amniotic fluid is alkaline (pH 7.0–7.5) and turns nitrazine paper blue; false positives with blood, semen and bacterial vaginosis.
  • Fern test – dried fluid on a glass slide shows a fern-like (arborisation) pattern under the microscope.
  • Newer immunoassays – placental alpha-microglobulin-1 (PAMG-1) or insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 (IGFBP-1) dipsticks; more accurate when available.

4. Ultrasound – reduced liquor supports the diagnosis; also gives gestational age, presentation, fetal weight and well-being.

5. Diagnosis of chorioamnionitis (intra-amniotic infection)

  • Maternal fever ≥38°C with one or more of: maternal tachycardia (>100/minute), fetal tachycardia (>160/minute), uterine tenderness, foul-smelling or purulent liquor.
  • Laboratory – raised white cell count (>15,000/mm³) and C-reactive protein; culture of vaginal swab and blood.
  • It is an indication for antibiotics and delivery, whatever the gestation.

(c) Management and nursing care (7 marks)

1. General measures for all women

  • Admit; confirm the diagnosis and gestational age; check presentation and fetal heart (exclude cord prolapse); record temperature and pulse.
  • Look for signs of infection, labour, abruption and fetal compromise.
  • Sterile vulval pads; no enemas; no unnecessary vaginal examinations.

2. PROM at term (≥37 weeks)

  • Induction of labour with oxytocin is recommended (WHO) – it reduces maternal and newborn infection compared with waiting; some women may choose to wait up to 24 hours if all is well.
  • Prostaglandins may be used if the cervix is very unfavourable, as per protocol.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis when membranes have been ruptured for more than 18 hours or the woman is a known GBS carrier.
  • Continuous fetal monitoring in labour; delivery; the newborn is observed for 12–24 hours for signs of sepsis.

3. Preterm PROM (PPROM)

  • Before viability (below 24 weeks) – counsel the couple honestly; outlook is poor (infection, pulmonary hypoplasia); termination is an option.
  • 24–34 weeks – expectant management in a hospital with a newborn unit, if there is no infection, labour or fetal compromise:
    • Antibiotics – erythromycin 250 mg orally 6-hourly for 10 days (or until labour); co-amoxiclav is avoided because it increases the risk of necrotising enterocolitis in the baby.
    • Antenatal corticosteroids (dexamethasone 6 mg IM 12-hourly × 4).
    • Magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection if delivery before 32 weeks is imminent.
    • Tocolysis is generally not advised (it may be used briefly to complete steroids or transfer).
    • Monitoring – temperature and pulse 4-hourly, fetal heart and CTG, colour and smell of liquor on pads, blood count and CRP once or twice a week, and ultrasound for liquor and growth.
    • Timing of delivery – usually planned between 34 and 37 weeks, as per the unit's policy.
  • Deliver at once at any gestation for chorioamnionitis, abruption, fetal distress, cord prolapse or established labour.

4. Management of chorioamnionitis

  • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (for example ampicillin + gentamicin, with metronidazole or clindamycin if a caesarean section is done), paracetamol, fluids.
  • Expedite delivery – vaginally if possible; caesarean only for obstetric reasons.
  • Inform the paediatrician; the baby needs a sepsis evaluation.

5. Complications to watch

  • Maternal – chorioamnionitis, endometritis, sepsis, abruption, operative delivery.
  • Fetal and neonatal – cord prolapse and cord compression, prematurity and RDS, neonatal sepsis, pulmonary hypoplasia and limb deformities (early, prolonged oligohydramnios), death.

6. Nursing care

  • Strict asepsis – sterile pads changed often, perineal hygiene, handwashing before any examination.
  • Temperature and pulse every 4 hours; fetal heart regularly; report fever, fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness or foul smell at once.
  • Observe the liquor for meconium or blood; note contractions.
  • Encourage oral fluids and a nutritious diet; allow gentle mobility as advised; prevent thrombosis.
  • Give antibiotics and steroids on time and record them.
  • Provide emotional support during a long, anxious stay; explain the plan and prepare her for a preterm baby.
  • At discharge after delivery – teach signs of puerperal and neonatal infection; counsel about the risk of recurrence and early booking next time.

7. Differential diagnosis of watery vaginal discharge

  • Urinary incontinence (common in late pregnancy) – smells of urine, occurs with coughing; nitrazine and fern tests negative.
  • Physiological discharge or infection (leucorrhoea, candidiasis, bacterial vaginosis) – thicker, may itch or smell.
  • Show (cervical mucus) at the onset of labour and semen after intercourse.

8. Care of the newborn after PROM or PPROM

  • Risk factors for early-onset sepsis – rupture of membranes more than 18 hours, maternal fever or chorioamnionitis, foul-smelling liquor, prematurity.
  • Observe closely for 24–48 hours – temperature instability, lethargy, poor feeding, fast breathing or grunting, apnoea, jaundice, abdominal distension.
  • A sepsis screen and antibiotics as ordered when risk factors or signs are present.
  • Early and exclusive breastfeeding, KMC, hand hygiene and clean cord care.

9. Prevention of PPROM in women at risk

  • Early booking; screening and treatment of urinary and genital infections (including bacterial vaginosis in women with a previous preterm birth).
  • Stopping smoking and tobacco chewing; good nutrition with adequate vitamin C and protein; correction of anaemia.
  • Progesterone or cervical cerclage where indicated for a short cervix or cervical insufficiency.
  • Avoiding unnecessary vaginal examinations and intercourse in women with a previous PPROM, as advised.

Nursing importance

  • Correct diagnosis without digital examination, early detection of infection, and timely antibiotics and steroids, carried out by the nurse, decide the outcome for many preterm babies.

Conclusion PROM at term is best managed by induction, while PPROM is managed expectantly with erythromycin, corticosteroids and close watch for infection until about 34–37 weeks, with immediate delivery if chorioamnionitis develops.

question: (a) Define breech presentation; list its types and causes. (4 marks) (b) Explain its diagnosis and antenatal management, including external cephalic version. (4 marks) (c) Describe the conduct of an assisted vaginal breech delivery, its complications and the nurse's role. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Types of breech presentation
labels: Four sketches – complete (flexed) breech: hips and knees flexed
feet beside the buttocks; frank (extended) breech: hips flexed
feet near the face; footling breech: one or both feet below the buttocks; knee presentation: knees lowest; label the sacrum as denominator and the common left sacro-anterior position

answer_html:
(a) Definition, types and causes (4 marks)

Definition

  • Breech presentation is a longitudinal lie in which the buttocks and/or the feet of the fetus present at the pelvic brim and the head occupies the fundus. The denominator is the sacrum; the commonest position is left sacro-anterior.
  • About 20–25% of fetuses are breech at 28 weeks, but most turn spontaneously; about 3–4% remain breech at term.

Types

Type Attitude of the fetal legs Remarks
Complete (flexed) breech Thighs flexed at hips, legs flexed at knees; feet beside the buttocks Commoner in multiparae
Frank (extended) breech Thighs flexed, legs extended at the knees (feet near the face) Commonest, especially in primigravidae; the splinted legs prevent turning
Footling breech One or both feet lie below the buttocks High risk of cord prolapse
Knee presentation Knees lowest Rare

Causes

  • Prematurity (the commonest).
  • Fetal – multiple pregnancy, hydrocephalus or anencephaly, fetal death, extended legs, short cord.
  • Uterine – bicornuate or septate uterus, fibroids, a lax uterus in grand multiparae, cornual placenta.
  • Placenta praevia, polyhydramnios or oligohydramnios, contracted pelvis.

(b) Diagnosis and antenatal management (4 marks)

Diagnosis

  • Abdominal palpation – a hard, round, ballotable head in the fundus (often felt under the ribs, causing discomfort), a broad, soft, irregular mass over the pelvic brim; the fetal heart is heard above the umbilicus.
  • Vaginal examination (in labour) – soft irregular buttocks, the anal opening, the sacrum and ischial tuberosities; fresh meconium on the glove; a foot is told from a hand by the heel and the toes in a straight line.
  • Ultrasound confirms the type, flexion of the head, estimated weight, liquor, placental site and anomalies.

External cephalic version (ECV)

  • Turning the fetus to cephalic presentation through the abdominal wall, offered at about 36 weeks in nulliparae and 37 weeks in multiparae; it succeeds in about half of women and reduces caesarean births.
  • Requirements – singleton pregnancy, reactive CTG, adequate liquor, consent, facilities for emergency caesarean section.
  • Contraindications – APH or placenta praevia, ruptured membranes, abnormal CTG, multiple pregnancy, major uterine anomaly; a previous caesarean scar is a relative contraindication.
  • Procedure – empty bladder, ultrasound check, tocolysis (terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously), the breech is lifted out of the pelvis and the fetus turned with a "forward roll"; CTG for 30 minutes afterwards; anti-D for Rh-negative women.
  • Complications – transient fetal bradycardia, abruption, cord entanglement, rupture of membranes, labour.

Choosing the mode of delivery

  • After the Term Breech Trial (2000), planned caesarean section became common because it reduced perinatal death and serious injury.
  • Vaginal breech delivery remains acceptable for well-selected women after counselling – frank or complete breech, estimated weight about 2.5–3.5 kg, flexed head, adequate pelvis, no other complications, and a skilled attendant. It is also needed when a woman arrives in advanced labour.
  • Caesarean section is preferred for footling breech, hyperextended head, a big or very small baby, contracted pelvis or other obstetric indications.

(c) Conduct of assisted vaginal breech delivery, complications and nurse's role (7 marks)

1. First stage

  • Deliver in a hospital with an obstetrician, a paediatrician and an anaesthetist available; IV line; blood grouped.
  • Avoid early artificial rupture of membranes; when membranes rupture, examine at once to exclude cord prolapse.
  • Continuous fetal heart monitoring; adequate pain relief (epidural if available).
  • Confirm full dilatation before she bears down – pushing through an incompletely dilated cervix risks head entrapment.

2. Second stage – "hands off the breech"

  • Lithotomy position at the edge of the bed with the bladder empty; a second skilled person and resuscitation equipment ready.
  • Episiotomy when the anterior buttock distends the perineum (as indicated).
  • Do not pull – allow the breech to deliver spontaneously up to the umbilicus with maternal effort; traction causes extension of the arms and head.
  • Legs – deliver spontaneously; extended legs are delivered by Pinard's manoeuvre (pressure in the popliteal fossa flexes the knee).
  • Loop of cord – pull down gently to avoid tension.
  • Hold the baby only by the bony pelvis (thumbs over the sacrum, fingers over the iliac crests), never by the abdomen, and keep the back anterior.
  • Arms – usually deliver spontaneously; extended arms are delivered by the Løvset manoeuvre – the body is rotated 180° so that the posterior shoulder comes anterior under the pubic arch and the arm is delivered, then rotated back 180° to deliver the other arm.
  • After-coming head – must be delivered slowly and in a controlled way:
    • Burns–Marshall method – the baby is allowed to hang until the nape of the neck is seen, then lifted by the feet in an arc over the mother's abdomen while the head is guarded.
    • Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit (MSV) manoeuvre – the baby lies along the operator's forearm, fingers on the malar bones flex the head, the other hand on the shoulders and occiput assists, and an assistant gives suprapubic pressure.
    • Piper forceps to the after-coming head.
  • Clear the airway as the mouth appears; note the time of delivery of the umbilicus to the head (it should be within a few minutes).

3. Third stage – active management; inspect for tears; watch for PPH.

4. Complications

  • Fetal – cord prolapse and compression, birth asphyxia, entrapment of the after-coming head, intracranial haemorrhage from rapid delivery of the head, fractures (humerus, clavicle, femur), Erb's palsy, spinal cord injury (hyperextended head), injury to liver, spleen or adrenals from grasping the abdomen, sternomastoid haematoma.
  • Maternal – perineal and cervical tears, PPH, infection, operative delivery.

5. Role of the nurse

  • Identify breech early in the antenatal period and refer for ECV and planning; counsel the couple about options.
  • Prepare the delivery room – warm, with neonatal resuscitation equipment, Piper forceps, episiotomy set and oxytocin.
  • Monitor the fetal heart closely and report membrane rupture at once.
  • Assist the doctor or midwife – suprapubic pressure, timing, warm towels; do not apply fundal pressure.
  • After birth – full examination of the baby for injuries; hip examination for developmental dysplasia (breech babies need hip ultrasound at about 6 weeks); support breastfeeding.

6. Management of an entrapped after-coming head (an emergency)

  • Call senior help and the paediatrician; keep the baby's back anterior and flex the head with fingers on the malar bones while an assistant gives suprapubic pressure.
  • McRoberts position (sharp flexion of the mother's thighs) and Piper forceps help a head held at the inlet or in the cavity.
  • If the head is trapped by an incompletely dilated cervix (typically in a preterm footling breech), the experienced obstetrician may make cervical (Dührssen's) incisions at about 2 and 10 o'clock.
  • Never pull hard on the trunk – this causes spinal and brachial plexus injury; record the time from delivery of the umbilicus to delivery of the head.

Nursing importance

  • Many breech babies are still born vaginally in India because mothers arrive late in labour; a nurse-midwife skilled in "hands off" breech delivery and the Løvset and MSV manoeuvres saves lives.

Conclusion Breech presentation is managed by early diagnosis, ECV at 36–37 weeks, careful selection of the mode of delivery and, when vaginal delivery occurs, patient "hands off" conduct with skilled delivery of the arms and after-coming head.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)

question: (a) Define obstructed labour and list its causes. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and complications of obstructed labour. (6 marks) (c) Describe its management, nursing care and prevention. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Abdominal and vaginal signs of obstructed labour
labels: Sagittal diagram of the labouring uterus – thick retracted upper segment
oblique Bandl's ring rising towards the umbilicus
fetal head jammed at the brim with a large caput and overlapping skull bones; side panel listing signs: exhausted
dehydrated mother with fast pulse; tender lower segment; hot
dry vagina; oedematous cervix and vulva; absent or abnormal fetal heart

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (3 marks)

Definition

  • Obstructed labour is labour in which, in spite of good uterine contractions, the progressive descent of the presenting part is arrested because of a mechanical obstruction, so the baby cannot be born vaginally without assistance.
  • It is a neglected, largely preventable condition and a major cause of ruptured uterus, obstetric fistula, sepsis and maternal and perinatal death in low-resource settings.

Causes

Fault in Causes
Passage – bony pelvis Contracted pelvis / cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD) – short stature (below 145 cm), rickets, osteomalacia, pelvic fractures, deformities
Passage – soft tissues Pelvic tumours (fibroid in the lower segment or cervix, impacted ovarian tumour), rigid or scarred cervix, vaginal septum or stenosis
Passenger – size Big baby (macrosomia), hydrocephalus, fetal ascites or tumours, conjoined twins
Passenger – presentation and position Brow presentation, mentoposterior face, neglected shoulder (transverse lie), persistent occipito-posterior with deep transverse arrest, compound presentation, locked twins

(b) Clinical features and complications (6 marks)

1. General condition

  • The woman is exhausted, anxious and restless, often after a long labour, sometimes after untrained interference at home.
  • Dehydration and ketoacidosis – dry coated tongue, sunken eyes, acetone smell of breath, ketones in urine.
  • Rapid pulse (above 100/minute), fever, falling urine output, sometimes shock.

2. Abdominal examination

  • Uterus tonically contracted, hard and tender, with little relaxation between contractions.
  • Bandl's ring (pathological retraction ring) – an oblique groove between the thick upper segment and the thinned, tender lower segment, rising towards the umbilicus; a sign of impending rupture.
  • Distended bladder, pulled up above the pubis.
  • Fetal parts difficult to feel; fetal heart irregular, slow or absent.

3. Vaginal examination

  • Hot, dry vagina; oedematous vulva and cervix (anterior lip swollen); foul-smelling discharge when infected.
  • Presenting part high and jammed in the pelvis, with a large caput succedaneum and severe moulding (overlapping skull bones) – the caput may reach the perineum while the head itself is high, misleading the examiner.
  • Cause may be felt – brow, shoulder with a prolapsed arm, contracted pelvis.

4. Complications

Maternal Fetal
Rupture of the uterus, shock and death Asphyxia and acidosis
Sepsis – chorioamnionitis, peritonitis, septicaemia Intracranial haemorrhage from excessive moulding
Obstetric fistula – vesico-vaginal or recto-vaginal, from pressure necrosis, appearing 3–10 days after delivery Infection, neonatal sepsis
PPH (exhausted uterus, trauma) Stillbirth
Foot drop (pressure on the lumbosacral nerves), vaginal scarring, secondary infertility, Sheehan's syndrome Neurological damage in survivors

(c) Management, nursing care and prevention (6 marks)

1. Immediate measures

  • Do not give oxytocin, do not apply fundal pressure and do not attempt forceps on a high head – these can rupture the uterus.
  • Resuscitate – IV line with Ringer lactate to correct dehydration and ketosis; send blood for haemoglobin, grouping and cross-matching; treat shock.
  • Catheterise the bladder (often difficult; use gentle technique) and measure urine output; note haematuria.
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics (for example ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole).
  • Oxygen; pain relief; reassurance.
  • At a PHC or CHC – resuscitate and refer at once to a facility with caesarean section facilities and blood.

2. Delivery

  • Caesarean section is the usual method, whether the fetus is alive or not, unless delivery is easier vaginally.
  • For a dead fetus, a destructive operation (craniotomy) may be done only by an experienced obstetrician when it is safer than caesarean section; it is rarely used now.
  • If the uterus has ruptured – laparotomy with repair or hysterectomy.
  • Active management of the third stage; watch for PPH.

3. Post-delivery care

  • Continuous bladder drainage for 10–14 days after prolonged obstruction to prevent or allow healing of a fistula; encourage plenty of fluids.
  • Continue antibiotics; correct anaemia; monitor for sepsis and paralytic ileus.
  • Physiotherapy for foot drop.
  • Emotional support – especially if the baby has died.
  • Future pregnancy – institutional delivery; planned caesarean section where the cause persists (contracted pelvis).

4. Nursing care

  • Record pulse, BP, temperature and respiration every 15–30 minutes; intake–output chart and urine colour.
  • Prepare her quickly for theatre; maintain IV fluids and antibiotics.
  • After surgery – catheter care with closed drainage, perineal hygiene, wound care, early mobility, nutrition.
  • Watch for leakage of urine or faeces through the vagina (fistula) and report it; reassure that fistulas can be repaired.

5. Prevention

  • Antenatal identification of risk – short stature, previous difficult labour or caesarean section, malpresentation, big baby, pelvic tumours – and planning the place of delivery.
  • Birth preparedness and institutional delivery by skilled birth attendants.
  • Use of the partograph / WHO Labour Care Guide to detect slow progress early and act on alerts.
  • Timely referral with transport (102/108) – no waiting at home or in a facility without surgical capability.
  • Trial of labour in borderline CPD only in a hospital with close monitoring and caesarean facilities.
  • No unskilled interference (fundal pressure, oxytocin injections by quacks).

6. Assessment of cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD) and trial of labour

  • CPD means a mismatch between the size of the fetal head and the maternal pelvis, so that the head cannot pass safely. It is the commonest cause of obstructed labour in India.
  • Clinical suspicion – maternal height below 145 cm, history of difficult labour or rickets, head not engaged in a primigravida after 37 weeks, pendulous abdomen, malpresentation.
  • Clinical pelvimetry – diagonal conjugate of about 11.5 cm or more (sacral promontory not reached), non-prominent ischial spines, subpubic angle of 90° or more, intertuberous diameter that admits four knuckles (about 10 cm); smaller measurements suggest a contracted pelvis.
  • Munro Kerr–Müller method – the head is pushed down into the pelvis by abdominal pressure while a vaginal finger and the thumb on the pubis judge whether it enters and whether it overrides the symphysis; overriding suggests significant disproportion.
  • Degrees – minor (vaginal delivery likely), moderate (borderline) and major (caesarean section needed).
  • Trial of labour – spontaneous labour in a woman with borderline CPD and a vertex presentation, allowed in a hospital with caesarean facilities under close observation; progress is plotted on the Labour Care Guide, with attention to contractions, descent, moulding, caput and the fetal heart; the trial is successful if she delivers vaginally (spontaneously or with outlet forceps), and terminated by caesarean section if there is no progress, fetal distress or signs of obstruction.
  • Trial of labour is not done in major CPD, malpresentation, elderly primigravida with other risks, or medical complications.

7. Warning signs of impending obstruction on the Labour Care Guide

  • Cervical dilatation that stops progressing or triggers repeated alerts despite good contractions.
  • No descent of the head (remains 3/5 or more above the brim) with increasing moulding (+3) and caput.
  • Rising maternal pulse, fever, ketonuria, haematuria and a distended bladder.
  • Abnormal fetal heart pattern. These findings call for immediate review by the doctor and, at a peripheral facility, referral.

Nursing importance

  • The nurse-midwife who plots labour correctly and refers on time prevents obstruction; one who recognises Bandl's ring, a hot dry vagina and maternal ketosis can save a mother from rupture and fistula.

Conclusion Obstructed labour is preventable. Early recognition, resuscitation, catheterisation, antibiotics and prompt caesarean delivery – never oxytocin – save the mother and often the baby, while good labour monitoring and timely referral prevent it altogether.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)

question: (a) Classify abnormal uterine action. (3 marks) (b) Explain hypotonic uterine inertia and incoordinate uterine action – causes, features and management. (7 marks) (c) Define prolonged labour; explain its effects and the nurse's role in preventing it. (5 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Classification of abnormal uterine action (3 marks)

Normal uterine contractions show fundal dominance, coordination between the two halves of the uterus, good relaxation between contractions and a regular rhythm. Abnormal uterine action is classified as follows:

Group Types
Inefficient uterine action (dystocia) Hypotonic uterine dysfunction (uterine inertia) – primary or secondary
Incoordinate (hypertonic) uterine action – colicky uterus (asymmetric action), hyperactive lower segment (reversed polarity), constriction ring, cervical dystocia, generalised tonic contraction
Over-efficient uterine action Precipitate labour, tachysystole (hyperstimulation)

(b) Hypotonic uterine inertia and incoordinate uterine action (7 marks)

A. Hypotonic uterine inertia

Features

  • Contractions are weak, infrequent (fewer than 3 in 10 minutes) and short (less than 40 seconds); the uterus can be easily indented at the height of a contraction.
  • The woman has little pain; progress of cervical dilatation and descent is slow.
  • Mother and fetus usually remain in good condition at first.

Types and causes

  • Primary inertia – weak contractions from the onset: elderly primigravida, over-distension (twins, polyhydramnios, big baby), grand multiparity, uterine anomaly or fibroids, anaemia, fear and anxiety, early heavy sedation, a full bladder or rectum.
  • Secondary inertia – contractions were good but become weak, usually because of exhaustion or obstruction (CPD, malposition) – so obstruction must always be excluded first.

Management

  • Exclude CPD and malpresentation (abdominal and vaginal examination, pelvic assessment).
  • General measures – reassurance, birth companion, oral fluids and light food or IV fluids, empty bladder, walking and upright positions, adequate pain relief.
  • Artificial rupture of membranes (amniotomy) when the head is engaged – it often improves contractions.
  • Oxytocin augmentation under close monitoring (in a hospital, preferably by infusion pump):
    • A commonly used WHO regimen – 2.5 IU oxytocin in 500 ml of normal saline or Ringer lactate, starting at 10 drops/minute, increased by 10 drops every 30 minutes until there are 3–4 contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting more than 40 seconds (maximum about 60 drops/minute; a stronger solution only under specialist orders).
    • Monitor contractions and fetal heart every 15–30 minutes; stop if contractions become more than 5 in 10 minutes or the fetal heart becomes abnormal.
    • Use with great caution in grand multiparae and women with a uterine scar; never in obstruction.
  • If no progress despite good contractions – caesarean section; in the second stage, assisted vaginal delivery if criteria are met.
  • Third stage – active management and oxytocin infusion continued, because atonic PPH is likely.

B. Incoordinate uterine action

Features

  • Contractions are frequent, irregular and very painful but ineffective; the uterus does not relax fully between contractions (raised resting tone); fundal dominance is lost or the lower segment contracts more strongly (reversed polarity).
  • Severe backache and pain out of proportion to progress; early exhaustion; cervix dilates slowly and may hang loosely; often with occipito-posterior position, CPD or early rupture of membranes; common in anxious primigravidae.
  • Fetal distress appears early because placental blood flow is reduced.

Special forms

  • Constriction ring – a localised spasm of circular muscle, often around the fetal neck or at the junction of the segments, which does not move (unlike Bandl's ring) and is felt only on vaginal examination; caused by intrauterine manipulation, early rupture of membranes or excess oxytocin. Relieved by tocolysis or deep anaesthesia; otherwise caesarean section.
  • Cervical dystocia – the cervix fails to dilate despite good contractions, because it is rigid (primary) or scarred by previous surgery or cauterisation (secondary); caesarean section is usually needed.

Management

  • Effective pain relief – epidural analgesia works very well and often makes contractions coordinated.
  • Rehydration, emotional support, change of position, bladder emptying.
  • Amniotomy and careful oxytocin may help once pain is controlled.
  • Caesarean section for fetal distress, constriction ring that does not relax, cervical dystocia or lack of progress.

(c) Prolonged labour – definition, effects and nurse's role (5 marks)

Definition

  • Labour is prolonged when it lasts longer than normal for that woman. Traditionally, labour lasting more than 18–24 hours was called prolonged.
  • WHO (2018) intrapartum care – the active first stage starts at 5 cm and usually does not exceed 12 hours in a first labour and 10 hours in later labours; the second stage usually does not exceed 3 hours in nulliparae and 2 hours in multiparae. A slower rate than 1 cm/hour by itself is not an indication for intervention if mother and baby are well.
  • The WHO Labour Care Guide gives time-based alerts at each centimetre of dilatation that prompt review.

Causes – the "3 Ps" – Powers (inefficient contractions), Passenger (big baby, malposition, malpresentation), Passage (contracted pelvis, soft-tissue obstruction) – plus Psyche (fear, anxiety) and injudicious sedation.

Effects

  • Maternal – exhaustion, dehydration and ketoacidosis, intrapartum infection, increased operative delivery and caesarean section, PPH, genital tract injuries, obstructed labour and fistula when neglected, and a traumatic birth experience.
  • Fetal – hypoxia and asphyxia, infection, birth injuries from operative delivery, and higher perinatal mortality.

Nurse's role in prevention

  • Correct diagnosis of labour – avoid admitting or intervening in the latent phase unnecessarily.
  • Plot progress on the Labour Care Guide; record contractions and fetal heart; recognise alerts and report delays promptly.
  • Supportive care – a birth companion, freedom of movement and upright positions, oral fluids and light food, emptying the bladder every 2 hours, comfort measures and pain relief.
  • Avoid routine early amniotomy, routine oxytocin and fundal pressure.
  • Timely referral from peripheral facilities when progress is slow or there are risk factors.
  • Monitor oxytocin infusions carefully and stop for tachysystole or fetal heart changes.

Nursing care plan for a woman with prolonged labour

Nursing diagnosis Key nursing interventions
Acute pain related to strong or incoordinate contractions Comfort measures, upright positions, massage, breathing techniques; analgesia/epidural as ordered
Risk of fluid deficit and ketosis related to prolonged labour and vomiting Oral fluids or IV Ringer lactate; urine ketones; intake–output chart
Fatigue related to long labour and lack of sleep Rest between contractions in a lateral position; light food; calm, dim room
Risk of fetal injury related to hypoxia Fetal heart every 15–30 minutes (5 minutes in second stage); left lateral position; stop oxytocin for abnormal findings; report early
Risk of infection related to prolonged rupture of membranes and repeated examinations Limit vaginal examinations, aseptic technique, temperature 4-hourly, perineal care
Anxiety related to slow progress Birth companion, explanation of progress, involvement in decisions
Risk of urinary retention and bladder injury Encourage voiding 2-hourly; catheterise if unable

Nursing importance

  • Abnormal uterine action is the commonest cause of slow labour; careful assessment by the nurse – exclusion of obstruction before oxytocin, good support and early alerts – prevents both unnecessary caesareans and dangerous neglect.

Conclusion Hypotonic inertia responds to support, amniotomy and carefully titrated oxytocin once obstruction is excluded, while incoordinate action needs good pain relief and early caesarean section for fetal distress. Good labour monitoring prevents prolonged labour and its complications.
