question: (a) Define postpartum haemorrhage as per the latest WHO criteria, classify it and list its causes and risk factors. (4 marks) (b) Explain the prevention of postpartum haemorrhage. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management of atonic PPH, including the first-response (MOTIVE) bundle and the role of the nurse. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Detection and first-response treatment of postpartum haemorrhage (WHO 2025)
labels: Flowchart – calibrated drape placed under the woman after birth → blood loss measured during the first 2 hours → trigger: ≥300 ml with any abnormal sign (pulse >100
diastolic BP <60) or ≥500 ml → MOTIVE bundle given together within about 15 minutes: Massage of uterus
Escalation → if bleeding continues: bimanual or aortic compression

answer_html:
(a) Definition, classification, causes and risk factors (4 marks)

Definition

  • PPH has traditionally been defined as blood loss of 500 ml or more within 24 hours after birth (1,000 ml or more after caesarean section).
  • The WHO, FIGO and ICM consolidated guidelines (5 October 2025) advise starting treatment when objectively measured blood loss reaches 300 ml with any abnormal haemodynamic sign – pulse above 100/minute, shock index above 1, systolic BP below 100 mm Hg or diastolic BP below 60 mm Hg – or 500 ml whichever comes first, with special vigilance in the first 2 hours after birth.
  • Any blood loss that causes deterioration of the woman's condition is PPH, whatever the volume. PPH is the leading cause of maternal death worldwide and in India.

Classification

  • Primary PPH – within 24 hours of birth (most cases).
  • Secondary (late) PPH – from 24 hours to 12 weeks after birth.
  • By severity – minor (500–1,000 ml) and major/severe (more than 1,000 ml or with shock).

Causes – the "four Ts"

T Cause Share
Tone Atonic uterus – the commonest About 70%
Trauma Tears of perineum, vagina, cervix; haematoma; rupture or inversion of the uterus About 20%
Tissue Retained placenta, cotyledon, membranes or clots; placenta accreta About 10%
Thrombin Coagulation defects – DIC (abruption, IUFD, sepsis, AFE), HELLP, anticoagulants About 1%

Risk factors

  • Antenatal – previous PPH, anaemia, grand multiparity, over-distended uterus (twins, polyhydramnios, big baby), fibroids, APH, pre-eclampsia, obesity, advanced age.
  • Intrapartum – prolonged or precipitate labour, induced or augmented labour, chorioamnionitis, operative vaginal delivery, caesarean section, retained placenta, general anaesthesia, magnesium sulphate.
  • Remember – many women who bleed have no risk factor, so every birth needs preventive care.

(b) Prevention of PPH (4 marks)

1. Antenatal

  • Correct anaemia (IFA, IV iron); identify high-risk women and plan delivery in an FRU with blood availability; birth preparedness.

2. During labour

  • Skilled birth attendance; monitoring with the Labour Care Guide to avoid prolonged labour; judicious use of oxytocin; no routine episiotomy and no fundal pressure.

3. Active management of the third stage of labour (AMTSL)

  • A uterotonic for every woman immediately after birth (within 1 minute) – oxytocin 10 IU IM (or IV) is the drug of choice; heat-stable carbetocin is an alternative where oxytocin quality cannot be assured; misoprostol 600 µg orally where injectable drugs are not available (for example at home births attended by trained health workers).
  • Controlled cord traction by a skilled provider, with counter-pressure on the uterus.
  • Assessment of uterine tone after delivery of the placenta (sustained massage is not needed when oxytocin has been given).

4. Fourth stage and objective measurement

  • Calibrated blood-collection drape to measure blood loss accurately (visual estimates underestimate loss).
  • Monitor uterine tone, bleeding, pulse and BP every 15 minutes for the first 2 hours; keep the bladder empty; examine the placenta for completeness and the genital tract for tears.

(c) Management of atonic PPH and the role of the nurse (7 marks)

1. Call for help and resuscitate (at once)

  • Shout for help – mobilise the team; one person leads and one records.
  • ABC – airway, oxygen by mask, lay her flat with legs raised, keep her warm.
  • Two large-bore IV cannulae (16–18 G); send blood for haemoglobin, grouping and cross-matching, coagulation tests and a bedside clotting test.

2. The first-response MOTIVE bundle – all elements are given together, as soon as PPH is diagnosed, ideally within 15 minutes, even if bleeding seems to settle:

  • M – Massage of the uterus until it is firm (rub up the fundus); expel clots.
  • O – Oxytocic drugs – oxytocin 10 IU slowly IV (or IM), followed by an infusion of 20 IU in 1,000 ml over 4 hours; misoprostol 800 µg sublingually if used; further uterotonics if needed – ergometrine (not in hypertension or heart disease) or carboprost (not in asthma).
  • T – Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes, given within 3 hours of birth; a second 1 g dose if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours.
  • IV – IV fluids – warmed crystalloids for resuscitation through the second line; blood transfusion as soon as available.
  • E – Examination – empty the bladder (catheterise), check the placenta for completeness, examine the vagina, cervix and perineum for tears, look for haematoma or inversion.
  • E – Escalation (the second "E") – if bleeding continues after the first response, or the cause cannot be identified or managed, call senior help and move to the next steps.
  • This approach (E-MOTIVE = early detection with a calibrated drape + MOTIVE) reduced the combined risk of severe bleeding, surgery for bleeding or death from bleeding by about 60% in a large WHO-supported trial (2023).

3. Measures for refractory bleeding (escalation)

  • Bimanual uterine compression (one fist in the anterior fornix, the other hand compressing the fundus through the abdomen) or external aortic compression as a temporary measure.
  • Intrauterine balloon tamponade – a balloon or condom catheter filled with 300–500 ml of saline, kept for 12–24 hours with oxytocin running.
  • Non-pneumatic anti-shock garment (NASG) to stabilise a woman for transfer.
  • Surgery – B-Lynch compression sutures, uterine or internal iliac artery ligation, uterine artery embolisation where available, and hysterectomy as a life-saving step.
  • Correct coagulopathy with blood products (fresh frozen plasma, platelets, cryoprecipitate).

4. After the bleeding is controlled

  • Monitor in a high-dependency area for 24 hours – pulse, BP, uterine tone, lochia, urine output (at least 30 ml/hour), SpO₂.
  • Continue oxytocin infusion and antibiotics if manipulations were done.
  • Correct anaemia (iron, IV iron or transfusion); encourage breastfeeding; watch for infection, thrombosis and Sheehan's syndrome (failure of lactation, amenorrhoea).
  • Explain what happened and plan care for the next pregnancy.

5. Role of the nurse

  • Prevention – identifying risk, giving the uterotonic within one minute of birth, close fourth-stage observation and measuring blood loss with the drape.
  • Early recognition – noticing a soft uterus, a trickle that does not stop, rising pulse or falling BP, restlessness and pallor.
  • First response under standing orders – massage, IV access, oxytocin infusion, tranexamic acid as per protocol, catheterisation, oxygen, keeping warm.
  • Teamwork – calling for help, preparing the PPH tray/kit (drugs, condom catheter, catheters, blood sample tubes), arranging blood and theatre, and escorting during referral.
  • Accurate documentation – time of birth, blood loss, vital signs, drugs with time and dose, fluids and urine output.
  • Taking part in regular PPH emergency drills so that every team member knows her role.

Nursing importance

  • PPH can kill within two hours. The nurse is at the bedside in those two hours – her vigilance, objective measurement and rapid first response are the most important life-saving actions.

Conclusion Every birth needs PPH prevention through AMTSL and close watch in the first 2 hours. With the new WHO criteria, early objective detection and immediate use of the MOTIVE bundle, followed by timely escalation, most deaths from PPH can be prevented.

question: (a) Define caesarean section; list its types and indications. (5 marks) (b) Describe the pre-operative preparation and the role of the nurse in the operation theatre. (4 marks) (c) Explain the post-operative care and complications of caesarean section, with reference to caesarean rates in India. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Uterine incisions for caesarean section
labels: Front view of the pregnant uterus and abdominal wall – Pfannenstiel (transverse suprapubic) skin incision and lower midline skin incision; uterine incisions: transverse lower segment (LSCS
and classical vertical upper-segment incision; note that the upper-segment scar has a higher risk of rupture in later pregnancy

answer_html:
(a) Definition, types and indications (5 marks)

Definition

  • Caesarean section (CS) is an operation in which the fetus is delivered through an incision in the abdominal wall (laparotomy) and the uterine wall (hysterotomy) after the age of viability.

Types

  • By uterine incision
    • Lower segment caesarean section (LSCS) – a transverse incision in the lower uterine segment; done in almost all cases because it bleeds less, heals well and has a low risk of rupture in later pregnancies.
    • Classical caesarean section – a vertical incision in the upper segment; now rare – used for a very preterm baby with a poorly formed lower segment, transverse lie with the back down, large lower-segment fibroid, or post-mortem/peri-mortem delivery; the scar has a high risk of rupture.
    • Low vertical incision (rare).
  • By timing – elective (planned) before labour, or emergency during labour or for complications.
  • Categories of urgency – Category 1: immediate threat to the life of mother or fetus (delivery within about 30 minutes); Category 2: compromise not immediately life-threatening; Category 3: needs early delivery without compromise; Category 4: at a time suitable to the woman and team.

Indications

Group Examples
Absolute (vaginal delivery impossible or very unsafe) Major degree of CPD/contracted pelvis, central placenta praevia, obstructing pelvic tumour, advanced carcinoma of the cervix, previous classical scar or two or more previous caesareans (usually)
Maternal Failure to progress or failed induction, severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia not delivering quickly, abruption with live fetus not delivering soon, previous caesarean with unfavourable conditions, cardiac or other disease needing controlled delivery, active genital herpes, HIV with high viral load
Fetal Fetal distress not deliverable vaginally, cord prolapse with a live fetus, malpresentations (breech in selected cases, transverse lie, brow, mentoposterior face), monoamniotic or conjoined twins, severe growth restriction with abnormal Doppler, big baby with diabetes

(b) Pre-operative preparation and the nurse's role in the theatre (4 marks)

1. Pre-operative preparation

  • Informed written consent after explaining the reason, benefits and risks; emotional support to the woman and her family.
  • Investigations – haemoglobin, blood group and cross-matched blood (at least one or two units), urine, HIV/HBsAg/syphilis status, coagulation profile where needed.
  • Fasting for elective CS (about 6 hours for food and 2 hours for clear fluids); aspiration prophylaxis – an H₂ blocker or proton-pump inhibitor and an antiemetic, with sodium citrate before an emergency general anaesthetic.
  • Skin preparation – bath, clipping (not shaving) of hair just before surgery if needed; remove jewellery, nail polish, dentures; theatre gown and cap.
  • Indwelling urinary catheter to keep the bladder empty.
  • IV line; prophylactic antibiotic (such as cefazolin 2 g IV) within 60 minutes before the skin incision; thromboprophylaxis as per risk.
  • Check and record the fetal heart just before shifting; inform the paediatrician.
  • Transfer in the left lateral tilt to avoid aortocaval compression.

2. Role of the nurse in the operation theatre

  • Circulating nurse – checks identity, consent and site (WHO surgical safety checklist), positions the woman with a wedge under the right hip, assists the anaesthetist (usually spinal anaesthesia), connects suction and diathermy, records the times, receives specimens, and maintains the swab, needle and instrument count.
  • Scrub nurse – prepares the sterile trolley and instruments, hands instruments, maintains asepsis, and keeps accurate counts before closure.
  • Baby nurse/midwife – warm resuscitation corner ready; receives the baby, dries and keeps warm, performs resuscitation if needed, identifies the baby (name band with the mother), records APGAR and weight, and places the baby skin-to-skin with the mother as early as possible.
  • After delivery of the baby – oxytocin (slow IV and infusion) or carbetocin as ordered; monitor blood loss.

(c) Post-operative care, complications and the Indian situation (6 marks)

1. Immediate post-operative care (recovery room)

  • Monitor pulse, BP, respiration, SpO₂ every 15 minutes for the first hour, then half-hourly till stable; level of consciousness and return of sensation after spinal anaesthesia.
  • Check the uterine tone and lochia every 15 minutes (PPH can be hidden), the wound dressing for soaking, and the urine output (at least 30 ml/hour) through the catheter.
  • Keep the oxytocin infusion running as ordered; IV fluids; effective pain relief (regular paracetamol and NSAIDs, opioids as prescribed).
  • Initiate breastfeeding within the first hour with skin-to-skin contact – help her into a comfortable position (side-lying or rugby hold).

2. Care in the ward (first days)

  • Early oral fluids and diet (within a few hours if she is well, as per the unit's enhanced recovery policy).
  • Early ambulation within 12–24 hours; deep breathing, coughing with wound support, leg exercises; stockings or heparin when at risk – to prevent thromboembolism and chest infection.
  • Catheter removal after about 12–24 hours; check that she passes urine.
  • Wound care – dressing removed after 24–48 hours; keep clean and dry; look for redness, discharge or gaping; remove sutures/staples on about day 5–7 if non-absorbable.
  • Perineal hygiene, breast care, emotional support (some women feel disappointed after an unplanned caesarean).
  • Discharge advice – wound care, iron and calcium, diet with fibre, no heavy lifting for about 6 weeks, danger signs (fever, wound discharge, heavy bleeding, calf pain, breathlessness), contraception (PPIUCD, condoms, Antara) and a gap of at least 18–24 months before the next pregnancy; tell every future care provider about the caesarean.

3. Complications

Time Complications
During surgery Haemorrhage, extension of the uterine incision, injury to bladder, ureter or bowel, anaesthetic complications (hypotension, high spinal, aspiration with general anaesthesia), injury to the baby
Early post-operative PPH, infection (wound, endometritis, urinary tract), paralytic ileus, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, wound haematoma or dehiscence, post-spinal headache, chest infection
Late and future pregnancy Adhesions, incisional hernia, chronic pain, scar dehiscence or rupture in the next labour, placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum, caesarean scar ectopic pregnancy, more repeat caesareans

4. Caesarean section rates in India

  • NFHS-6 (2023–24) – 27.2% of births were by caesarean section, up from 21.5% in NFHS-5; 54.1% in private facilities compared with 16.9% in public facilities.
  • WHO states that, at population level, caesarean rates above about 10–15% are not linked with further falls in maternal and newborn deaths; the aim is to ensure caesarean for every woman who needs it and to avoid unnecessary ones.
  • WHO recommends the Robson ten-group classification to audit and compare caesarean rates within hospitals.
  • Nursing contribution to reducing unnecessary caesareans – good antenatal education, birth companions, upright positions, good labour monitoring with the Labour Care Guide, and support for vaginal birth after caesarean where suitable.

Nursing importance

  • Most women in Indian hospitals will see a caesarean in their family; careful pre-operative preparation, theatre safety, early skin-to-skin and breastfeeding, and vigilant post-operative care by the nurse make the operation safe.

Conclusion Caesarean section is a life-saving operation when indicated. The lower segment operation, sound preparation, safe theatre practice and good post-operative care keep complications low, while sensible use is needed to curb rising unnecessary caesarean rates.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)

question: (a) What is operative (instrumental) vaginal delivery? List the types of obstetric forceps and vacuum extractors and the indications. (4 marks) (b) Explain the prerequisites and the steps of a forceps and a vacuum delivery. (6 marks) (c) Describe the complications and the nursing care of mother and baby. (5 marks)

diagram.caption: Obstetric forceps and vacuum extractor
labels: Labelled drawing of a pair of obstetric forceps (blade with fenestration
handle) with small sketches of Wrigley's
Kielland's and Piper forceps; vacuum cups (metal Malmström
Kiwi OmniCup); fetal head showing the flexion point on the sagittal suture about 3 cm in front of the posterior fontanelle where the cup is applied

answer_html:
(a) Definition, types and indications (4 marks)

Definition

  • Operative (instrumental) vaginal delivery is the delivery of the fetus vaginally with the help of obstetric forceps or a vacuum extractor, applied to the fetal head in the second stage of labour.
  • Used correctly, it shortens a difficult second stage and can avoid a caesarean section at full dilatation, which is technically difficult and risky.

Types of obstetric forceps

Forceps Use
Wrigley's Short, light forceps for outlet delivery and for delivering the head at caesarean section
Simpson's / Neville-Barnes (with axis-traction) Long forceps for low (and mid-cavity) delivery with the occiput anterior
Kielland's Rotational forceps (minimal pelvic curve, sliding lock) for transverse or posterior positions – only by experts
Piper For the after-coming head of a breech

By station: outlet (scalp visible at the introitus, head on the pelvic floor), low (leading point at +2 cm or lower) and mid-cavity (head engaged but above +2); high forceps are never used.

Types of vacuum extractor (ventouse)

  • Metal cup (Malmström) – good grip, more scalp marks.
  • Soft silicone or plastic cups – gentler, more likely to detach.
  • Hand-held disposable devices (such as the Kiwi OmniCup) – easy to use, with an in-built pump.

Indications

  • Maternal – prolonged second stage, maternal exhaustion, and conditions in which bearing down must be avoided or cut short – heart disease, severe pre-eclampsia, some neurological or eye conditions.
  • Fetal – fetal distress in the second stage with the head low enough.
  • Specific – after-coming head of breech (Piper forceps), cord prolapse at full dilatation with the head low, delivery of the second twin when suitable.

(b) Prerequisites and steps (6 marks)

1. Prerequisites (all must be present)

  • Cervix fully dilated and membranes ruptured.
  • Head engaged – not more than one-fifth palpable abdominally; station at or below 0 (preferably +2).
  • Exact position of the head known (by examination, and ultrasound if in doubt).
  • No cephalopelvic disproportion; pelvis adequate.
  • Bladder empty (catheterise).
  • Adequate uterine contractions and maternal cooperation.
  • Adequate analgesia – pudendal block and perineal infiltration, or epidural.
  • Informed consent, a skilled operator, and readiness to change to caesarean section (a trial in theatre for doubtful mid-cavity cases).
  • Neonatal resuscitation team and equipment ready.
  • For vacuum – gestation of 34 weeks or more, vertex presentation (not face or breech).

2. Steps of forceps delivery

  • Lithotomy position, aseptic cleaning and draping, catheterisation, analgesia.
  • Confirm position; hold the assembled forceps in front of the perineum as they will lie on the head ("ghost application").
  • Insert the left blade first (held in the left hand, into the left side of the mother's pelvis), guided by the fingers of the right hand; then the right blade; lock the handles easily (difficulty locking means wrong application).
  • Check application – the sagittal suture midway between the blades, the posterior fontanelle about a finger's breadth above the plane of the shanks, fenestrations hardly admitting a fingertip.
  • Traction only with a contraction and maternal effort, along the axis of the birth canal – first downwards and backwards, then forwards, then upwards as the head crowns (Pajot's manoeuvre keeps traction in the correct axis).
  • Episiotomy as the head distends the perineum, when needed.
  • Remove the blades as the head crowns (in reverse order) and deliver the head by extension; deliver the shoulders and body normally.

3. Steps of vacuum delivery

  • Same preparation. Choose the cup; apply it on the flexion point – on the sagittal suture about 3 cm in front of the posterior fontanelle.
  • Run a finger around the cup to make sure no vaginal or cervical tissue is trapped.
  • Raise the vacuum gradually to about 0.6–0.8 kg/cm² (about 450–600 mm Hg).
  • Pull with each contraction, perpendicular to the cup and along the curve of the pelvis; the head flexes and rotates as it descends.
  • Abandon the vacuum if there is no descent after three pulls, or if the cup detaches ("pops off") two or three times – then deliver by caesarean section; do not switch blindly to forceps.
  • Release the vacuum once the head is delivered.

(c) Complications and nursing care (5 marks)

1. Complications

Mother Baby
Perineal, vaginal and cervical tears, including third- and fourth-degree tears (more with forceps) Bruising and marks of the face (forceps) or chignon (vacuum)
PPH and vulval or vaginal haematoma Cephalhaematoma (especially vacuum)
Bladder and urethral injury, urinary retention Subgaleal haemorrhage – a dangerous bleed under the scalp (vacuum)
Infection; pain; later pelvic floor problems and anal incontinence Facial nerve palsy, skull fracture and intracranial haemorrhage (forceps)
Psychological distress Scalp lacerations, retinal haemorrhages, neonatal jaundice, shoulder dystocia injuries

2. Nursing care before and during the procedure

  • Explain the reason and procedure to the woman and her companion and obtain consent; maintain privacy.
  • Prepare the trolley – forceps or vacuum set, episiotomy and suture set, local anaesthetic, catheter, sterile drapes, oxytocin; check the vacuum pump.
  • Position her, catheterise, and monitor the fetal heart before and between pulls.
  • Encourage her to push with contractions; keep the baby corner warm and the resuscitation set ready; inform the paediatrician.
  • Record the indication, station and position, number of pulls and time taken.

3. Care of the mother afterwards

  • Inspect for tears and haematoma; assist in repair; give oxytocin; watch for PPH, pulse and BP.
  • Pain relief, ice pack and perineal care; check that she passes urine within 6 hours.
  • Help with early breastfeeding; give her a chance to talk about the birth.

4. Care of the baby

  • Examine for marks, bruises, cephalhaematoma, facial palsy and limb movements.
  • Watch closely for subgaleal haemorrhage – a boggy scalp swelling that crosses suture lines, increasing head size, pallor, fast heart rate – and report it at once.
  • Monitor for jaundice; reassure parents that the chignon and marks fade within days.

5. Forceps compared with vacuum

Point Forceps Vacuum
Analgesia Pudendal block or epidural needed Less analgesia needed
Maternal tears More (including anal sphincter tears) Fewer
Fetal injury Facial marks, facial palsy, rarely skull fracture Chignon, cephalhaematoma, subgaleal haemorrhage, retinal haemorrhage
Rotation Possible with Kielland's in skilled hands Allows autorotation of the head
Failure rate Lower Higher (cup detachment)
Restrictions Not for a high head Not before 34 weeks, not for face or breech

The choice depends on the operator's skill, the position and station of the head and the urgency.

Nursing importance

  • A well-performed instrumental delivery is often safer than a caesarean at full dilatation; the nurse ensures that every prerequisite is met, keeps a close watch on the fetal heart and detects early injuries to mother and baby.

Conclusion Forceps and vacuum are valuable tools when the prerequisites are met and a skilled operator follows strict rules; careful preparation and post-delivery nursing reduce injuries to mother and baby.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: Explain occipito-posterior position – its diagnosis, possible outcomes of labour and management.
answer_html:
Introduction In occipito-posterior (OP) position the vertex presents with the occiput directed towards the sacroiliac joint (right OP is commoner than left). It is found in about 10–15% of women at the onset of labour and is the commonest malposition. Because the head is often deflexed, larger diameters present and labour tends to be long and painful.

1. Causes

  • Android or anthropoid pelvis, flat sacrum.
  • Deflexion of the head, anterior placenta, pendulous abdomen.
  • Weak or incoordinate contractions.

2. Diagnosis

  • Abdominal – a flattened, saucer-shaped area below the umbilicus; limbs felt on both sides of the midline in front; the back is felt far out in the flank; fetal heart heard in the flank or near the midline; the head may be high.
  • Vaginal – the posterior fontanelle lies near a posterior sacroiliac joint; the anterior fontanelle is easily felt anteriorly (head deflexed); early rupture of membranes is common.
  • Ultrasound confirms the position when examination is unclear.

3. Clinical course and possible outcomes

  • Long anterior rotation (about 90% of cases) – with good flexion and contractions the occiput rotates 3/8 of a circle (135°) to the front and delivery is normal (occipito-anterior).
  • Short posterior rotation → persistent OP – the occiput turns into the hollow of the sacrum and the baby is born "face to pubis", with more perineal trauma.
  • Incomplete anterior rotation → deep transverse arrest – the head is arrested with the sagittal suture transverse at the level of the ischial spines.
  • Non-rotation with a high, deflexed head – may need caesarean section.
  • Effects – prolonged labour, severe backache, early urge to push, maternal exhaustion, operative delivery, PPH, perineal tears, fetal hypoxia.

4. Management

  • First stage – patience while progress continues; hydration, bladder care, good pain relief (epidural), encouraging positions that are comfortable (hands-and-knees, side-lying, upright); avoid early pushing before full dilatation; monitor the fetal heart.
  • Second stage – allow time if the head is descending and rotating; manual rotation, vacuum extraction (which allows the head to rotate) or rotational forceps by an expert; face-to-pubis delivery with an episiotomy if needed.
  • Caesarean section for a high head, deep transverse arrest that cannot be corrected safely, CPD or fetal distress.

5. Nursing care

  • Sacral counter-pressure and massage for backache, warm packs, encouragement and companionship.
  • Record progress on the Labour Care Guide; report prolonged labour.
  • Prepare for instrumental delivery; watch for PPH and perineal tears after delivery.

Conclusion Most OP positions rotate and deliver normally with patience, good support and pain relief; persistent OP and deep transverse arrest need skilled assisted delivery or caesarean section.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: Explain face and brow presentations – diagnosis and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Face and brow presentations are deflexion attitudes of a cephalic presentation. In face presentation the head is fully extended and the face presents (denominator mentum); in brow presentation the head is partially extended, midway between flexion and full extension.

A. Face presentation (about 1 in 500 births)

1. Causes

  • Fetal – anencephaly, thyroid or neck tumours, cord coiled round the neck, prematurity.
  • Maternal – flat pelvis, multiparity with a lax uterus, polyhydramnios; many arise in labour from a deflexed OP position.

2. Diagnosis

  • Abdominal – a prominent head on the same side as the back, with a deep groove between head and back; fetal heart heard on the side of the limbs (through the chest).
  • Vaginal – the mouth with hard gums, the nose, malar eminences and orbital ridges; the baby may suck the examining finger (in breech, the anus and ischial tuberosities lie in a straight line and meconium is seen).
  • Ultrasound confirms and excludes anomalies.

3. Mechanism and management

  • Mentoanterior positions (and most mentoposteriors that rotate forward) deliver vaginally by flexion, the presenting diameter being submentobregmatic (9.5 cm).
  • Persistent mentoposterior cannot deliver vaginally because the extended neck cannot extend further – caesarean section.
  • Management – exclude CPD and anomalies; continuous fetal monitoring; allow labour in mentoanterior with good progress; episiotomy at delivery; vacuum is contraindicated; low forceps only in mentoanterior by an expert; caesarean section for persistent mentoposterior, CPD, fetal distress or poor progress.
  • Gentle vaginal examinations – avoid injuring the eyes.

B. Brow presentation (about 1 in 1,000–1,500 births)

  • The presenting diameter is mentovertical (13.5–14 cm) – the largest diameter, so a normal-sized baby cannot pass through a normal pelvis; neglected cases end in obstructed labour.
  • Diagnosis – on vaginal examination the anterior fontanelle, frontal suture, orbital ridges and root of the nose are felt; the head is high.
  • Management – early in labour the brow may convert to a face or vertex, so a short period of observation is allowed with good contractions and no distress; persistent brow at term needs caesarean section; forceps and vacuum are never used.

4. Nursing care

  • Monitor the fetal heart and progress closely; prepare for caesarean section.
  • After birth – the baby's face is swollen and bruised; check the airway and feeding, and reassure the parents that the swelling subsides in a few days.

Conclusion Mentoanterior face usually delivers vaginally, but persistent mentoposterior face and persistent brow are indications for caesarean section; early recognition prevents obstructed labour.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: Explain transverse lie (shoulder presentation) – causes, diagnosis and management.
tags: internal podalic version for second twin
answer_html:
Introduction In transverse lie the long axis of the fetus lies across the long axis of the uterus; in labour the shoulder usually presents. An oblique lie is in between and often becomes longitudinal or transverse in labour. It occurs in about 1 in 300 deliveries at term. A transverse lie cannot deliver vaginally at term.

1. Causes

  • Multiparity with a lax uterus and abdominal wall (commonest).
  • Placenta praevia, pelvic tumours, contracted pelvis – the head cannot enter the pelvis.
  • Polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy (especially the second twin), prematurity.
  • Uterine anomalies (arcuate or subseptate uterus), fibroids, fetal anomalies.

2. Diagnosis

  • Inspection – the uterus looks broad and its height is less than the period of gestation.
  • Palpation – no fetal pole at the fundus or the pelvic brim ("empty lower pole"); the head is felt in one flank and the breech in the other; fetal heart heard near the umbilicus.
  • Vaginal examination in labour – the presenting part is high; the shoulder (acromion), ribs, scapula or axilla may be felt; a prolapsed hand or arm or the cord may be found.
  • Ultrasound confirms and identifies the cause (placenta praevia, anomalies).

3. Management

  • Antenatal – look for the cause; external cephalic version at about 37 weeks if there is no contraindication; admit at 37–38 weeks because of the risk of cord prolapse with rupture of membranes; plan delivery.
  • Early labour with intact membranes – ECV can be attempted, followed by controlled rupture of membranes once the head is fixed (stabilising induction), in selected cases.
  • Otherwise – caesarean section (a lower-segment or, if the back is down and the lower segment poorly formed, a vertical uterine incision).
  • Second twin in transverse lie – ECV or internal podalic version with breech extraction by a skilled operator.

4. Neglected shoulder presentation

  • Membranes have ruptured long ago, the shoulder is impacted in the pelvis, an arm is prolapsed and swollen, the uterus is moulded around the fetus with a Bandl's ring, and the fetus is often dead.
  • Never pull on the prolapsed arm; never attempt internal version (it will rupture the uterus).
  • Resuscitate, give antibiotics, and deliver by caesarean section (a destructive operation only by an expert when safer).
  • Complications – cord prolapse, obstructed labour, rupture of the uterus, sepsis, fetal death.

5. Nursing role

  • Identify an unstable or transverse lie at antenatal visits and refer; advise early admission and immediate hospital visit if membranes rupture.
  • In labour, check for cord prolapse whenever membranes rupture; prepare for caesarean section.

Conclusion Transverse lie must be detected before labour; ECV, planned admission and caesarean section prevent cord prolapse, neglected shoulder presentation and uterine rupture.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: Explain cord presentation and cord prolapse – causes, diagnosis and immediate management.
tags: operative vaginal delivery at full dilatation
answer_html:
Introduction

  • Cord presentation – the umbilical cord lies below the presenting part with the membranes intact.
  • Cord prolapse – the cord descends below or beside the presenting part after the membranes have ruptured and may be felt in the vagina or seen outside the vulva. (Occult prolapse – the cord lies beside the presenting part and is not felt.)
  • It occurs in about 1–6 per 1,000 births and is an obstetric emergency: compression of the cord and spasm of its vessels (from cold and handling) cut off oxygen to the fetus.

1. Causes and risk factors – anything that prevents the presenting part from filling the lower uterus:

  • Malpresentations – breech (especially footling), transverse lie, compound presentation.
  • High presenting part – CPD, placenta praevia, unengaged head at artificial rupture of membranes.
  • Prematurity, low birth weight, polyhydramnios, multiparity, second twin, long cord.

2. Diagnosis

  • Sudden fetal bradycardia or variable decelerations, especially soon after rupture of membranes.
  • Cord felt on vaginal examination (pulsating if the fetus is alive) or seen at the vulva.
  • Cord presentation – pulsating cord felt through intact membranes; ultrasound/colour Doppler.

3. Immediate management (fetus alive)

  • Call for help (obstetrician, anaesthetist, paediatrician) and note the time; stop any oxytocin infusion.
  • Do not handle the cord unnecessarily; do not try to push it back. If it is outside the vagina, cover it with a warm, wet sterile pad or gently replace it into the vagina.
  • Relieve compression on the cord:
    • Manual elevation – a gloved hand in the vagina pushes the presenting part up off the cord, and keeps it there until delivery.
    • Position – knee-chest position or exaggerated Sims (left lateral) position with a pillow under the left hip, or head-down (Trendelenburg) tilt.
    • Bladder filling – 500–750 ml of normal saline through a Foley catheter, then clamp it (very useful during transfer); empty it before the uterus is opened.
    • Tocolysis – terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously to reduce contractions, if ordered.
  • Expedite delivery:
    • Category 1 caesarean section if the cervix is not fully dilated.
    • Operative vaginal delivery (forceps or vacuum) or breech extraction if the cervix is fully dilated and delivery can be quick.
  • Neonatal resuscitation team ready; send cord blood gases if available.
  • If the fetus is dead – vaginal delivery, unless there is another indication.

4. Cord presentation – avoid rupture of membranes; deliver by caesarean section.

5. Nursing role

  • Check the fetal heart immediately after any rupture of membranes; a vaginal examination is done at once in high-risk women.
  • Avoid amniotomy with a high presenting part; keep women with high-risk factors in hospital near term.
  • During transfer from a peripheral centre – keep her in the knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position with the bladder filled.
  • Document times and actions; support and explain to the mother.

Conclusion Cord prolapse needs instant recognition, relief of cord compression by elevation of the presenting part, positioning and bladder filling, and the quickest safe delivery.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: Explain shoulder dystocia – risk factors, management (HELPERR) and complications.
answer_html:
Introduction Shoulder dystocia is a delivery in which, after the head is born, the shoulders fail to deliver with gentle downward traction and additional manoeuvres are needed – usually because the anterior shoulder is impacted behind the pubic symphysis. It occurs in about 0.2–1% of vaginal births. The head may be pulled back tightly against the perineum ("turtle sign"). It is an emergency – the baby can be damaged by hypoxia within minutes.

1. Risk factors

  • Big baby (macrosomia), maternal diabetes, obesity, post-term pregnancy.
  • Previous shoulder dystocia.
  • Prolonged second stage, instrumental mid-cavity delivery, oxytocin augmentation.
  • Most cases occur without any warning, so every birth attendant must be ready.

2. Management – the HELPERR mnemonic

  • H – Call for Help – senior obstetrician, paediatrician, anaesthetist, extra midwives; note the time of delivery of the head; tell the mother to stop pushing.
  • E – Evaluate for Episiotomy – to make room for internal manoeuvres (it does not by itself free the shoulder).
  • L – Legs: McRoberts manoeuvre – two assistants sharply flex the mother's thighs onto her abdomen; this flattens the sacral promontory and rotates the pubis upwards, and frees many shoulders.
  • P – Suprapubic Pressure – an assistant presses just above the pubis, from the side of the fetal back, with the heel of the hand (like CPR), continuously or in a rocking motion, to push the anterior shoulder under the pubis. Never apply fundal pressure – it impacts the shoulder further and may rupture the uterus.
  • E – Enter manoeuvres (internal rotation) – Rubin II (push the back of the anterior shoulder towards the baby's chest), Woods' screw (rotate the posterior shoulder forward), reverse Woods.
  • R – Remove the posterior arm – sweep it across the chest and deliver it, reducing the shoulder width.
  • R – Roll the patient onto all-fours (Gaskin manoeuvre) and retry traction.
  • Last resort – deliberate fracture of the clavicle, Zavanelli manoeuvre (head replaced and caesarean section) or symphysiotomy, by experts only.
  • Avoid excessive traction, twisting or bending the neck.

3. Complications

  • Fetal – brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy), fracture of the clavicle or humerus, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, death.
  • Maternal – PPH, third- or fourth-degree perineal tears, vaginal and cervical tears, uterine rupture (with fundal pressure), psychological trauma.

4. Nursing role

  • Anticipate in high-risk women – inform senior staff, empty the bladder, position her at the edge of the bed.
  • Perform McRoberts and suprapubic pressure as directed; keep time and document the time of head delivery, each manoeuvre, which shoulder was anterior, and the time of body delivery.
  • Neonatal resuscitation; examine the baby for arm movement and fractures.
  • Prevent PPH; repair tears; debrief the mother and family; regular skills drills for the team.

Conclusion Shoulder dystocia is unpredictable. A calm, practised team using HELPERR – especially McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, never fundal pressure – delivers most babies safely within minutes.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: Explain rupture of the uterus – causes, clinical features and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Rupture of the uterus is a tear in the uterine wall during pregnancy or labour. In a complete rupture the tear involves the whole wall including the peritoneum, and the fetus may pass into the abdominal cavity; in an incomplete rupture the peritoneum is intact. A scar dehiscence is a silent separation of an old scar with intact membranes. It is a catastrophe that kills mothers and babies, and in India it is still mostly caused by neglected obstructed labour.

1. Causes

  • Scar rupture – previous caesarean section (classical scar far more than lower segment), myomectomy, hysterotomy; trial of labour after caesarean.
  • Spontaneous rupture of an unscarred uterus – obstructed labour (CPD, neglected shoulder, brow, hydrocephalus), grand multiparity, injudicious oxytocin or misoprostol.
  • Traumatic – internal podalic version, difficult forceps, fundal pressure, manual removal of an adherent placenta, road accidents.
  • Placenta percreta and uterine anomalies.

2. Clinical features

  • Impending rupture (obstructed labour) – restlessness, rising pulse, Bandl's ring rising towards the umbilicus, a tender, thinned lower segment, haematuria.
  • Abnormal fetal heart pattern – the commonest and earliest sign of scar rupture.
  • Actual rupture
    • Sudden severe pain at the height of a contraction, followed by cessation of contractions and a feeling of relief.
    • Shock – pallor, rapid pulse, low BP – out of proportion to visible vaginal bleeding (much bleeding is internal).
    • Fetal parts felt easily under the abdominal wall, the uterus felt separately as a contracted mass; fetal heart absent.
    • On vaginal examination the presenting part recedes (loss of station); haematuria if the bladder is torn.
  • Silent scar dehiscence may be found only at caesarean section.

3. Management

  • Call for help; resuscitate – two large-bore IV lines, crystalloids, oxygen, blood cross-matched and transfused.
  • Immediate laparotomy – deliver the baby and placenta; then
    • Repair of the tear when it is clean, recent and the woman wants more children (with advice that the next pregnancy carries a high risk and needs elective caesarean before labour), or
    • Hysterectomy (subtotal or total) when the tear is extensive, ragged, infected or the woman is unstable.
  • Check the bladder and ureters and repair injuries; tubal ligation may be offered if the uterus is repaired and the family is complete.
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics, ICU care, correction of anaemia and coagulopathy.

4. Prevention

  • Proper antenatal risk assessment and institutional delivery for women with a scar or high parity.
  • Labour monitoring with the Labour Care Guide; timely caesarean for obstructed labour.
  • Careful use of oxytocin in multiparae and scarred uterus; no misoprostol in women with a previous caesarean in the third trimester.
  • No fundal pressure; internal version only for the second twin.

5. Nursing role

  • Watch for warning signs in labour – scar tenderness, abnormal fetal heart, haematuria, rising pulse – and report at once.
  • Rapid preparation for laparotomy; post-operative monitoring; emotional support, especially after hysterectomy or loss of the baby.

Conclusion Uterine rupture is largely preventable by good labour monitoring, cautious oxytocin use and timely caesarean section; when it occurs, immediate resuscitation and laparotomy are life-saving.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: Explain acute inversion of the uterus – causes, degrees, clinical features and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Acute inversion of the uterus is a rare but dangerous complication of the third stage in which the uterus turns inside out, the fundus descending through the cervix. It occurs in roughly 1 in 2,000–20,000 deliveries and causes profound shock – often out of proportion to the blood loss – and severe haemorrhage.

1. Causes

  • Mismanaged third stage – pulling on the cord before the uterus has contracted, or fundal pressure (Credé's method) on a relaxed uterus – the commonest cause.
  • Fundal implantation of the placenta, adherent placenta, short cord.
  • Uterine atony, a fundal fibroid, and very rarely spontaneous inversion.

2. Degrees

  • First degree – the fundus is inverted but stays within the uterine cavity.
  • Second degree – the fundus passes through the cervix into the vagina.
  • Third degree – the fundus reaches or protrudes beyond the vulva (complete).
  • Fourth degree (total) – the vagina is also inverted.

3. Clinical features

  • Sudden severe lower abdominal pain and shock (pallor, sweating, rapid weak pulse, low BP) – partly neurogenic from traction on the peritoneum and ovaries.
  • Haemorrhage, especially once the placenta separates.
  • Fundus not felt abdominally, or a cup-shaped depression felt.
  • A firm, rounded, purplish mass in the vagina or outside the vulva, often with the placenta still attached.

4. Management

  • Call for help; stop oxytocin; start two IV lines, give fluids and blood; oxygen.
  • Immediate manual replacement – the sooner the better, before a cervical ring forms:
    • Do not remove the placenta first if it is still attached (it increases bleeding).
    • Johnson's manoeuvre – the whole hand grasps the fundus and pushes it upwards through the cervix towards the umbilicus, the part that came out last going back first; the hand is kept in the uterus till it contracts.
    • Tocolysis (terbutaline or magnesium sulphate) or general anaesthesia may be needed to relax the cervical ring.
  • Hydrostatic method (O'Sullivan) – warm saline is run into the posterior fornix while the vulva is sealed with the operator's hand, so the pressure pushes the fundus back.
  • Surgery at laparotomy if these fail – Huntington's (traction on the round ligaments) or Haultain's (incision of the cervical ring) operation.
  • After replacement – oxytocin infusion to keep the uterus contracted, remove the placenta (manually if needed), bimanual compression, broad-spectrum antibiotics, careful watch for recurrence and PPH.

5. Prevention and nursing role

  • Correct active management of the third stage – controlled cord traction only with a contracted uterus and with counter-traction (guarding the uterus) above the pubis; no fundal pressure or pulling on the cord of a relaxed uterus.
  • Recognise early, treat shock, assist replacement, monitor vital signs and uterine tone, and support the frightened mother.

Conclusion Acute inversion is largely preventable by correct third-stage management. When it occurs, treatment of shock and immediate manual replacement without first removing the placenta save the woman's life.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: Explain amniotic fluid embolism – clinical features and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) is a rare (about 2–8 per 1,00,000 births) but often fatal obstetric emergency in which amniotic fluid, fetal cells or debris enter the maternal circulation and trigger an abnormal immune (anaphylaxis-like) reaction – hence the alternative name "anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy". It causes sudden cardiorespiratory collapse and severe bleeding.

1. Time of occurrence and risk factors

  • During labour, at caesarean section, or within about 30 minutes after delivery; occasionally after abortion or amniocentesis.
  • Associated with induction of labour, operative delivery and caesarean section, placenta praevia or abruption, multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, cervical tears, uterine rupture and advanced maternal age; it cannot be predicted or prevented.

2. Clinical features (a classic triad of hypoxia, hypotension and coagulopathy)

  • Sudden breathlessness, cyanosis and hypoxia; restlessness, a feeling of impending doom, chills.
  • Sudden hypotension and cardiovascular collapse, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest.
  • Seizures and loss of consciousness.
  • DIC with severe bleeding from the uterus, wounds and puncture sites (in those who survive the first phase).
  • Fetal distress (if undelivered).
  • Diagnosis is clinical – by exclusion of other causes (pulmonary embolism, eclampsia, haemorrhagic shock, anaphylaxis, anaesthetic complications, myocardial infarction).

3. Management – supportive, rapid and by a team

  • Call for help – obstetric, anaesthetic, ICU and neonatal teams; activate massive haemorrhage protocol.
  • Airway and breathing – high-flow oxygen; early intubation and ventilation.
  • Circulation – two large-bore IV lines, fluids, vasopressors and inotropes; left uterine displacement.
  • Cardiac arrest – start high-quality CPR immediately with manual left uterine displacement; if there is no return of circulation, perimortem caesarean section within about 4–5 minutes of arrest improves the chance of survival for the mother (and baby).
  • Coagulopathy – early blood, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate and platelets; tranexamic acid; uterotonics and other measures for PPH; hysterectomy if bleeding is uncontrollable.
  • Transfer to ICU for ventilation and organ support.

4. Nursing role

  • Recognise sudden breathlessness, falling SpO₂ and collapse; shout for help and begin CPR.
  • Position with left lateral tilt; provide oxygen and suction; prepare the resuscitation trolley, defibrillator and blood products.
  • Keep accurate time records; support the family; care for the newborn.
  • Take part in emergency drills so the team works fast.

Conclusion AFE is unpredictable and deadly. Survival depends on immediate recognition, high-quality resuscitation, early perimortem caesarean when needed and aggressive treatment of the coagulopathy in a well-coordinated team.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: Explain fetal distress (intrapartum fetal compromise) – causes, signs and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Fetal distress (intrapartum fetal compromise) means that the fetus is not receiving enough oxygen (hypoxia), which may lead to acidosis, brain damage or death if not corrected. The term "non-reassuring fetal status" is often used, because the signs only suggest, and do not prove, hypoxia.

1. Causes

  • Uteroplacental insufficiency – pre-eclampsia, post-term pregnancy, growth restriction, diabetes, anaemia.
  • Excessive contractions (tachysystole) from oxytocin or prostaglandins.
  • Cord compression – cord prolapse, oligohydramnios, tight cord around the neck, true knot.
  • Abruptio placentae, uterine rupture.
  • Maternal hypotension – supine position, epidural, haemorrhage; maternal fever, ketosis and hypoxia.
  • Prolonged and obstructed labour.

2. Signs

  • Fetal heart rate abnormalities (by intermittent auscultation – every 15–30 minutes in the active first stage and every 5 minutes in the second stage – or by CTG):
    • Baseline bradycardia (<110/minute) or tachycardia (>160/minute).
    • Reduced variability (less than 5 beats/minute for a long period).
    • Late decelerations (after the peak of contractions), complicated variable decelerations, a prolonged deceleration (more than 3 minutes), or a sinusoidal pattern.
  • Thick meconium-stained liquor, especially with heart-rate changes.
  • Reduced fetal movements; fetal scalp blood pH below 7.20 where tested.

3. Management – intrauterine resuscitation, then decide on delivery

  • Stop or reduce oxytocin; remove a prostaglandin pessary.
  • Turn the mother to her left side (or change position).
  • IV fluid bolus if she is hypotensive (for example after an epidural); correct dehydration and ketosis.
  • Tocolysis (terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously) for tachysystole, as ordered.
  • Vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse and to assess progress (rapid descent may explain the changes).
  • Treat maternal fever (paracetamol) and look for infection.
  • Stop active pushing for a short while in the second stage.
  • Inform the doctor; begin continuous CTG where available.
  • If the abnormality persists – expedite delivery: operative vaginal delivery if the cervix is fully dilated and the head is low; otherwise caesarean section (category 1 or 2 depending on severity).
  • Neonatal resuscitation team at delivery; cord blood gases if available.

4. Nursing role

  • Correct technique and timing of fetal heart auscultation, counted for a full minute after a contraction, and recorded on the Labour Care Guide.
  • Prompt intrauterine resuscitation measures and reporting.
  • Careful titration of oxytocin; avoiding the supine position.
  • Explaining to the mother what is happening and why urgent delivery may be needed.

Conclusion Regular, correct fetal heart monitoring, early recognition of abnormal patterns, prompt intrauterine resuscitation and timely delivery prevent most hypoxic injury to the baby.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: Explain induction of labour – indications, contraindications, methods and nursing care.
answer_html:
Introduction Induction of labour (IOL) is the artificial initiation of uterine contractions before their spontaneous onset, with the aim of achieving a vaginal birth, when continuing the pregnancy carries more risk to mother or baby than delivery. Augmentation means stimulating contractions after labour has begun.

1. Indications

  • Post-term pregnancy – WHO recommends offering induction at 41 completed weeks.
  • Hypertensive disorders (pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension), diabetes.
  • PROM at term, chorioamnionitis.
  • Fetal growth restriction, oligohydramnios, Rh isoimmunisation.
  • Intrauterine fetal death, lethal fetal anomaly.
  • Medical conditions (renal disease, cholestasis), and selected social reasons.

2. Contraindications

  • Placenta praevia, vasa praevia, transverse lie or other malpresentation unsuitable for vaginal birth.
  • Cephalopelvic disproportion, pelvic tumour obstructing labour.
  • Previous classical caesarean or other upper-segment scar; relative – two or more previous caesareans.
  • Active genital herpes, cord presentation, severe fetal compromise needing immediate delivery.

3. Pre-induction assessment

  • Confirm the indication and gestational age; check presentation, engagement, fetal well-being (CTG) and the pelvis.
  • Assess the cervix by the Bishop score – a score of 8 or more is favourable; a low score (6 or less) needs cervical ripening first.
  • Informed consent; explain the process and expected time.

4. Methods

  • Membrane sweeping at term (in outpatients) – reduces the need for formal induction.
  • Mechanical ripening – a Foley balloon catheter passed through the cervix and inflated (30–60 ml); safe in women with a previous caesarean.
  • Pharmacological ripening
    • Misoprostol – 25 µg orally every 2 hours or 25 µg vaginally every 6 hours (WHO regimens) in a live term pregnancy; not used in women with a previous caesarean scar in the third trimester.
    • Dinoprostone (PGE₂) gel 0.5 mg intracervically or a vaginal insert.
  • Amniotomy (artificial rupture of membranes) once the cervix is favourable, usually followed by
  • Oxytocin infusion – started at a low dose and increased every 30 minutes until there are 3–4 good contractions in 10 minutes.

5. Complications

  • Failed induction and increased caesarean section.
  • Tachysystole/hyperstimulation with fetal distress; rupture of the uterus (especially in multiparae and scarred uterus).
  • Cord prolapse after amniotomy with a high head; infection after long induction.
  • Water intoxication with prolonged high-dose oxytocin in large volumes of fluid; PPH from an exhausted uterus.

6. Nursing care

  • Prepare and explain; record baseline vital signs, Bishop score and CTG.
  • After each misoprostol dose or during oxytocin – monitor contractions (frequency, duration, strength) and fetal heart every 15–30 minutes; record the drip rate.
  • Stop oxytocin and inform the doctor for more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, a contraction lasting over 2 minutes, or an abnormal fetal heart.
  • Check for cord prolapse after amniotomy; maintain intake–output; encourage mobility, fluids and emptying the bladder.
  • Provide emotional support – induction can be long and tiring.

Conclusion Induction of labour is valuable when its indication is clear; correct selection, cervical ripening with low-dose misoprostol or a balloon, careful oxytocin titration and close monitoring make it safe.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: Explain retained placenta and the procedure of manual removal of the placenta, with nursing care.
answer_html:
Introduction Retained placenta means that the placenta has not been delivered within 30 minutes after the birth of the baby despite active management of the third stage. It can cause severe PPH, infection and shock, and is an important cause of maternal death when women deliver at home or in poorly equipped places.

1. Causes

  • Placenta separated but not expelled – uterine atony, a full bladder, mismanagement, or a constriction ring that traps it (sometimes after ergometrine).
  • Placenta not separated – weak contractions or morbidly adherent placenta (accreta spectrum).
  • Placenta in a uterine horn or with abnormal shape.

2. Initial management

  • If there is no bleeding – empty the bladder, give a second dose of oxytocin 10 IU, and repeat controlled cord traction with a contracted uterus; encourage breastfeeding.
  • Do not pull hard on the cord or press on the fundus (risk of inversion); avoid ergometrine, which can trap the placenta.
  • If the placenta is still not delivered or bleeding starts – manual removal at once.
  • Start an IV line, take blood for grouping and cross-matching, treat shock.

3. Procedure of manual removal of placenta (MRP)

  • Explain and obtain consent; analgesia or anaesthesia (spinal, general, or IV analgesia with sedation); prophylactic antibiotic (such as ampicillin or cefazolin, single dose).
  • Lithotomy position; strict asepsis – sterile gown and elbow-length gloves; catheterise the bladder.
  • Hold the cord taut with one hand and introduce the other hand, shaped like a cone, into the vagina and through the cervix, following the cord to the placenta.
  • The outside hand steadies the fundus through the abdomen (counter-pressure) to prevent perforation.
  • Find the edge of the placenta and separate it with the ulnar (little-finger) border of the hand using a gentle side-to-side slicing movement, until the whole placenta is free.
  • Withdraw the hand with the placenta; explore the cavity to make sure nothing is left.
  • Give oxytocin infusion and massage the uterus; examine the placenta and membranes for completeness; inspect for tears.
  • If no cleavage plane is found (placenta accreta), stop – do not tear pieces away – and prepare for laparotomy/hysterectomy.

4. Complications – haemorrhage, infection (endometritis), uterine inversion or perforation, retained fragments, anaesthetic complications.

5. Nursing care

  • Prepare the MRP tray (long gloves, antiseptic, catheter, oxytocin, antibiotics), IV line and blood.
  • Monitor pulse, BP, bleeding and uterine tone every 15 minutes for at least 2 hours after the procedure.
  • Continue oxytocin and antibiotics as ordered; record intake–output; check temperature for infection.
  • Correct anaemia; reassure and explain; encourage breastfeeding.

Conclusion Retained placenta needs a second oxytocin dose and careful cord traction, and – if bleeding or delay continues – prompt manual removal under asepsis and analgesia, followed by close monitoring for PPH and infection.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: Explain the pharmacological methods of pain relief in labour, with the nursing care of a woman receiving epidural analgesia.
answer_html:
Introduction Labour pain is one of the most intense pains a woman experiences. Along with non-drug comfort measures, pharmacological methods can be offered according to the woman's wishes, the stage of labour and the facilities available. WHO (2018) recommends epidural analgesia and parenteral opioids as options for healthy women who request pain relief.

1. Inhalational analgesia

  • Nitrous oxide and oxygen (50:50, Entonox) breathed through a mask or mouthpiece, starting with the beginning of each contraction.
  • Quick onset and offset, self-administered, does not affect the baby much; may cause nausea and light-headedness.

2. Systemic opioids

  • Pethidine 50–100 mg IM (with an antiemetic), fentanyl or other opioids as prescribed.
  • Side effects – drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, respiratory depression in the mother; neonatal respiratory depression if given within about 2–4 hours of birth (keep naloxone ready for the baby), and reduced early breastfeeding.

3. Regional analgesia

  • Epidural analgesia – local anaesthetic (often with an opioid) injected through a catheter into the epidural space (L2–L4); the most effective method; can be topped up or run as an infusion and extended for caesarean section.
  • Combined spinal–epidural – quicker onset.
  • Pudendal block – for the second stage and instrumental delivery; perineal infiltration for episiotomy and repair; paracervical block (rarely now).

4. Epidural – indications and contraindications

  • Indications – maternal request; prolonged or painful labour, incoordinate uterine action, OP position; pre-eclampsia (helps BP control); heart or respiratory disease; anticipated operative delivery; twins and breech.
  • Contraindications – maternal refusal, coagulopathy or anticoagulants, low platelets, infection at the injection site or sepsis, uncorrected hypovolaemia, raised intracranial pressure, allergy to local anaesthetics, lack of trained staff.

5. Nursing care of a woman receiving epidural analgesia

  • Before – explain the procedure, obtain consent, secure an IV line, record baseline BP, pulse and fetal heart; empty the bladder; help her into a sitting or lateral curled position and keep her still.
  • After the test dose and each top-up – BP and pulse every 5 minutes for 15–20 minutes, then every 15–30 minutes; continuous or frequent fetal heart monitoring.
  • Hypotension – turn her to the left side, run IV fluids faster, give oxygen and inform the anaesthetist (a vasopressor may be needed).
  • Assess the block – level of sensory block and motor power of the legs; prevent falls; help her change position every 1–2 hours.
  • Bladder care – sensation may be lost; encourage voiding or catheterise to prevent retention.
  • Second stage – coach pushing with contractions, as the urge may be reduced; allow a longer second stage if progress is good.
  • Watch for complications – shivering, itching, fever, nausea, high block (breathlessness, numb hands), local anaesthetic toxicity (tingling round the mouth, ringing in the ears, convulsions), and later post-dural puncture headache.
  • Remove the catheter with the tip intact after delivery; check the site and the return of sensation and movement.

Conclusion Entonox, opioids and especially epidural analgesia give effective labour pain relief; careful selection and close nursing observation, particularly of BP, block level, bladder and fetal heart, keep epidural analgesia safe.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: What is Bandl's ring?
answer_html:
• Bandl's ring is a pathological retraction ring seen in obstructed labour – an exaggeration of the normal (physiological) retraction ring between the upper and lower uterine segments.
  • With continued strong contractions the upper segment becomes thick and short, while the lower segment becomes very thin and over-stretched; the junction is seen and felt as an oblique groove across the abdomen that gradually rises towards the umbilicus.
  • It is a sign of impending rupture of the uterus.
  • Unlike a constriction ring, it moves upward and is felt abdominally.
  • Management – stop oxytocin, resuscitate and deliver urgently by caesarean section.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: What is precipitate labour? Mention its complications.
answer_html:
• Precipitate labour is labour in which the combined first and second stages last less than 3 hours – the baby is born very rapidly after the onset of contractions.
  • Causes – multiparity with a lax birth canal, a small baby, very strong contractions, overdose of oxytocin or prostaglandins.
  • Maternal complications – cervical, vaginal and perineal tears, PPH, uterine inversion, amniotic fluid embolism, infection from an unattended or unclean birth.
  • Fetal complications – hypoxia from strong contractions, intracranial haemorrhage from rapid compression and decompression of the head, injury from falling, cord avulsion, hypothermia and infection.
  • Care – anticipate from previous history, admit early near term, stop oxytocin, control the delivery of the head, examine for tears and prevent PPH.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: What is vasa praevia?
answer_html:
• In vasa praevia, fetal blood vessels run through the membranes, unprotected by cord or placenta, across or near the internal os, ahead of the presenting part.
  • It occurs with a velamentous cord insertion or a succenturiate or bilobed placenta, and more often after IVF.
  • When the membranes rupture, the vessels may tear, causing painless bleeding of fetal blood; because the fetal blood volume is small, fetal distress (often a sinusoidal pattern) and death follow within minutes, while the mother is unaffected.
  • Diagnosis – antenatal transvaginal ultrasound with colour Doppler.
  • Management – admission and planned caesarean section at about 34–36 weeks before labour; emergency caesarean if bleeding occurs; the newborn may need a blood transfusion.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: What is VBAC? State the conditions for a trial of labour after caesarean section.
answer_html:
• VBAC (vaginal birth after caesarean) is a vaginal birth in a woman who has had a previous caesarean section; the attempt is called a trial of labour after caesarean (TOLAC). About 60–80% of well-selected women succeed; the risk of scar rupture is about 0.5% after one lower-segment caesarean.
  • Conditions
    • One previous lower-segment transverse caesarean, for a non-recurring indication (for example fetal distress or breech).
    • No other uterine scar or previous rupture; adequate gap since the caesarean (usually 18 months or more).
    • Singleton, cephalic presentation, no CPD or other indication for caesarean; preferably spontaneous labour.
    • Delivery in a hospital with facilities for immediate caesarean section and blood; continuous fetal monitoring; no misoprostol; oxytocin only with great caution.
  • Watch for signs of scar rupture – abnormal fetal heart, scar pain, vaginal bleeding, haematuria, loss of station, maternal tachycardia.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: What is internal podalic version?
answer_html:
• Internal podalic version (IPV) is a manoeuvre in which the operator introduces a hand into the uterus, grasps one or both fetal feet and brings them down through the cervix, turning the fetus into a breech (podalic) presentation, followed by breech extraction.
  • Indication today – almost only for the second twin in transverse lie when ECV fails.
  • Prerequisites – cervix fully dilated, membranes intact or just ruptured, enough liquor, a relaxed uterus (anaesthesia), no disproportion, and a skilled operator.
  • Contraindications – a singleton with transverse lie (caesarean is safer) and a neglected shoulder presentation, where it can rupture the uterus.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: What is the Robson ten-group classification?
answer_html:
• The Robson ten-group classification sorts every woman who gives birth into ten mutually exclusive groups using six simple features – parity, previous caesarean, onset of labour, number of fetuses, gestational age, and fetal lie and presentation. WHO (2015) recommends it as the global standard for monitoring and comparing caesarean section rates.
  • Groups – (1) nullipara, single cephalic, ≥37 weeks, spontaneous labour; (2) nullipara, single cephalic, ≥37 weeks, induced or caesarean before labour; (3) multipara without previous caesarean, single cephalic, ≥37 weeks, spontaneous labour; (4) the same, induced or caesarean before labour; (5) previous caesarean, single cephalic, ≥37 weeks; (6) all nulliparous breeches; (7) all multiparous breeches; (8) all multiple pregnancies; (9) all transverse or oblique lies; (10) all single cephalic below 37 weeks.
  • It shows which groups contribute most (usually groups 1, 2 and 5) so that audits and interventions can target them.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Recognition and Management of Abnormal Labour
question: What is uterine tachysystole (hyperstimulation)? How is it managed?
answer_html:
• Tachysystole is more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over 30 minutes; when it is accompanied by fetal heart rate changes it was traditionally called hyperstimulation. A single contraction lasting more than 2 minutes (hypertonus) is also dangerous.
  • It is usually caused by oxytocin, misoprostol or other prostaglandins, and can lead to fetal hypoxia and rupture of the uterus.
  • Management
    • Stop or reduce the oxytocin infusion; remove a prostaglandin pessary.
    • Turn the woman to her left side; give IV fluids; inform the doctor.
    • Tocolysis – terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously if it persists or the fetal heart is abnormal.
    • Continuous fetal heart monitoring; expedite delivery if fetal distress persists.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Management of Women with Abnormal Postnatal Conditions
question: (a) Define puerperal pyrexia and puerperal sepsis, and list their causes and risk factors. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features of the different types of puerperal infection and the investigations. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management, nursing care and prevention of puerperal sepsis. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Routes of spread of puerperal genital infection
labels: ovaries and pelvis – local infection of the perineum
cervix and placental site (endometritis) → spread by lymphatics to the parametrium (pelvic cellulitis); by direct extension through the tubes (salpingitis
pelvic abscess in the pouch of Douglas); by veins (pelvic thrombophlebitis
septic emboli); and by the bloodstream (septicaemia

answer_html:
(a) Definitions, causes and risk factors (4 marks)

Definitions

  • Puerperal pyrexia – a rise of temperature to 38°C (100.4°F) or more, maintained for 24 hours or recurring, within the first 10 days after delivery (excluding the first 24 hours, when a slight rise may be physiological).
  • Puerperal sepsis (WHO) – infection of the genital tract occurring at any time between the onset of rupture of membranes or labour and the 42nd day after delivery, with fever and one or more of: pelvic pain, abnormal (purulent) vaginal discharge, foul-smelling lochia and delayed involution of the uterus.
  • Maternal sepsis (WHO, 2016) – a life-threatening condition with organ dysfunction resulting from infection during pregnancy, childbirth, after abortion or after delivery. Sepsis is one of the leading direct causes of maternal death.

Causes of fever in the puerperium (remember all sites – not only the uterus)

Site Conditions
Genital tract Infected perineal or vaginal tears and episiotomy, endometritis, parametritis, salpingitis, pelvic peritonitis, pelvic abscess
Urinary tract Cystitis, acute pyelonephritis (common after catheterisation)
Breasts Engorgement (mild fever), mastitis, breast abscess
Wound Caesarean section wound infection
Veins Superficial thrombophlebitis, deep vein thrombosis, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
Respiratory Atelectasis, pneumonia (after general anaesthesia)
Intercurrent Malaria, typhoid, dengue, viral infections; drug or transfusion reactions

Organisms – often mixed: group A β-haemolytic streptococcus (rapid, severe sepsis), E. coli and other gram-negative bacilli, Staphylococcus aureus, anaerobes (Bacteroides, anaerobic streptococci, Clostridium), Chlamydia, gonococcus.

Risk factors

  • Maternal – anaemia, malnutrition, diabetes, obesity, HIV, genital infections in pregnancy.
  • Labour-related – prolonged labour, prolonged rupture of membranes, repeated vaginal examinations, chorioamnionitis, unclean or unattended delivery, perineal tears, operative delivery and caesarean section, manual removal of placenta, retained products, PPH and blood transfusion.

(b) Clinical features of the types of puerperal infection and investigations (5 marks)

1. Localised infections

  • Infection of perineal wounds and tears – pain, redness, swelling, discharge or gaping of the episiotomy; low-grade fever.
  • Endometritis (infection of the placental site) – onset usually 2–5 days after delivery; fever with chills, rapid pulse, lower abdominal pain, uterus tender, soft and subinvoluted, lochia foul-smelling, profuse and often purulent (with group A streptococci the lochia may be scanty and odourless).

2. Spreading infections

  • Parametritis (pelvic cellulitis) – spread by lymphatics; high fever persisting after the 7th–10th day, deep pelvic pain, a tender, firm mass on one or both sides of the uterus pushing it to the opposite side.
  • Salpingitis and pelvic peritonitis – bilateral lower abdominal pain and tenderness, guarding; a pelvic abscess in the pouch of Douglas causes swinging fever, rectal pressure and diarrhoea.
  • Generalised peritonitis – abdominal distension, vomiting, rigidity, absent bowel sounds.
  • Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis – swinging fever not responding to antibiotics.
  • Septicaemia and septic shock – high or low temperature, rapid pulse, fast breathing, falling BP, cold extremities, confusion, reduced urine output, jaundice, bleeding (DIC); death may follow within hours with group A streptococcus.

3. Investigations

  • High vaginal or endocervical swab and blood cultures (before antibiotics, but antibiotics must not be delayed); urine culture; wound swab; breast milk culture when indicated.
  • Complete blood count (raised white cells), CRP, serum lactate (above 2 mmol/L suggests poor perfusion), renal and liver function, coagulation profile, blood sugar.
  • Ultrasound for retained products and pelvic collections; chest X-ray when breathing is affected; malaria test where endemic.
  • Monitoring with an obstetric early warning score chart.

(c) Management, nursing care and prevention (6 marks)

1. Immediate management – treat sepsis as an emergency ("golden hour")

  • Assess airway, breathing and circulation; give oxygen if SpO₂ is low.
  • Within one hour – take cultures, start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, give IV fluids (crystalloid boluses for hypotension), measure lactate and haemoglobin, and monitor urine output with a catheter (the "sepsis six" approach).
  • Antibiotics – for example ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole (or clindamycin + gentamicin), changed according to culture; continued until she has been fever-free for about 48 hours; anti-staphylococcal cover for wound or breast infection.
  • Shift to ICU for septic shock – vasopressors, ventilation, organ support.

2. Treat the source

  • Evacuation of retained products of conception under antibiotic cover.
  • Drainage of a pelvic abscess (colpotomy or ultrasound-guided) or wound abscess; removal of infected sutures; resuturing later.
  • Laparotomy for peritonitis, uterine necrosis or failure to respond; hysterectomy may be needed.
  • Anticoagulation for septic pelvic thrombophlebitis.

3. Nursing care

  • Monitoring – temperature, pulse, respiration, BP, SpO₂ and consciousness 4-hourly or more often, plotted on the early warning score chart; intake–output; colour and smell of lochia; fundal height and tenderness; wound condition.
  • Prevent cross-infection – isolate or barrier-nurse women with group A streptococcal infection; strict hand hygiene; separate linen and safe disposal of pads.
  • Perineal care – wash from front to back with clean water after each void and stool; change pads often; sitz bath for wound infection.
  • Comfort – tepid sponging and antipyretics for fever; Fowler's (semi-sitting) position, which helps lochia drain and localises pelvic infection; adequate pain relief.
  • Fluids and nutrition – 2–3 litres of fluid a day, a high-protein, high-calorie diet, correction of anaemia.
  • Breastfeeding – usually continued (the antibiotics used are safe); help her express if she is too ill; care of the baby by a relative under supervision.
  • Prevent thrombosis – early mobility as her condition allows, leg exercises, hydration.
  • Emotional support – reassure the mother and family; explain all procedures.
