  • Discharge advice – complete the antibiotic course, hygiene, danger signs, iron and diet, follow-up and contraception.

4. Prevention

  • Antenatal – correct anaemia and malnutrition; treat genital and urinary infections; promote institutional delivery.
  • During labour – the "six cleans" of clean birth: clean hands, clean perineum, clean delivery surface, clean blade for cutting the cord, clean cord tie and clean towel/cloth; minimum necessary vaginal examinations, done with sterile gloves; avoid prolonged labour; no routine episiotomy.
  • Prophylactic antibiotics for caesarean section (before skin incision), manual removal of placenta and third- or fourth-degree tears.
  • Postnatal – perineal hygiene, early ambulation, frequent breastfeeding, early detection of fever and foul lochia by the nurse, ASHA and ANM during home visits.

5. Complications of puerperal sepsis

  • Immediate – septic shock, DIC, acute kidney injury, ARDS, liver dysfunction and maternal death.
  • Local – pelvic abscess, generalised peritonitis, wound dehiscence, secondary PPH.
  • Vascular – septic pelvic thrombophlebitis, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
  • Long-term – chronic pelvic pain, tubal blockage and infertility, ectopic pregnancy, intrauterine adhesions (Asherman's syndrome), and the emotional impact of a severe illness after birth.

Nursing importance

  • Sepsis can kill a young mother within a day; the nurse who records temperature and pulse regularly, notices foul-smelling lochia or a confused, breathless woman, and starts the sepsis response within the hour saves lives.
  • Clean birth practices and aseptic technique, which the nurse controls, prevent most puerperal infection.

Conclusion Puerperal sepsis is a preventable cause of maternal death. Clean birth practices, early detection through regular monitoring, the one-hour sepsis bundle, source control and good nursing care give an excellent outcome.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Management of Women with Abnormal Postnatal Conditions
question: Explain secondary postpartum haemorrhage – causes and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Secondary (late) postpartum haemorrhage is excessive bleeding from the genital tract occurring more than 24 hours after delivery and up to 12 weeks after birth, most often between the 7th and 14th day. It usually occurs after the woman has gone home, so health workers and families must know its danger signs.

1. Causes

  • Retained bits of placenta, membranes or clots – the commonest cause.
  • Infection (endometritis) and subinvolution of the placental site.
  • Separation of a slough from an infected wound or tear in the cervix or vagina.
  • Breakdown (dehiscence) of a caesarean section scar – may cause sudden, heavy bleeding.
  • Rare – uterine artery pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous malformation, choriocarcinoma, submucous fibroid or polyp, coagulation disorders (for example von Willebrand disease), anticoagulant therapy.

2. Clinical features

  • Fresh red bleeding or passage of clots, sometimes sudden and heavy, after the lochia had become lighter.
  • Fever, foul lochia and uterine tenderness when infection is present.
  • Uterus larger and softer than expected; the os may be open with tissue felt.
  • Pallor, rapid pulse, falling BP and shock with heavy bleeding.

3. Management

  • Resuscitate – IV line, fluids, blood for haemoglobin, grouping and cross-matching; transfusion when needed; at a peripheral facility, stabilise and refer.
  • Uterotonics – oxytocin infusion, ergometrine or misoprostol to contract the uterus.
  • Antibiotics – broad-spectrum (ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole) because infection is usually present.
  • Ultrasound to look for retained products.
  • Evacuation of retained products by gentle suction under antibiotic cover by an experienced doctor – the soft, infected uterus is easily perforated.
  • Send tissue for histopathology and check β-hCG if bleeding persists (to exclude choriocarcinoma).
  • Caesarean scar dehiscence – laparotomy with repair or hysterectomy; uterine artery embolisation for vascular malformations where available.
  • Correct anaemia with iron or IV iron.

4. Nursing care

  • Teach every mother at discharge that heavy fresh bleeding, clots, foul-smelling lochia or fever after delivery are danger signs needing immediate care.
  • In hospital – pad count and weight, vital signs, fundal height and tone, temperature; record intake–output.
  • Prepare for evacuation or surgery; give drugs on time; perineal hygiene.
  • Support breastfeeding; emotional support; follow-up for anaemia.

Conclusion Secondary PPH is usually due to retained products and infection; prompt resuscitation, uterotonics, antibiotics and careful evacuation stop the bleeding, while education at discharge brings women early for care.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Management of Women with Abnormal Postnatal Conditions
question: Explain subinvolution of the uterus – causes, clinical features and management.
answer_html:
Introduction After delivery the uterus returns to its non-pregnant size by involution. The fundus, at about the level of the umbilicus soon after birth, falls by about 1 cm (a finger's breadth) a day and is usually not palpable abdominally by the 10th–14th day. Subinvolution is the condition in which involution is slower than normal or stops.

1. Causes

  • Predisposing factors – grand multiparity, over-distension (twins, polyhydramnios, big baby), caesarean section, prolonged labour, general anaesthesia, not breastfeeding, poor general health and anaemia.
  • Aggravating (main) factors – retained products of conception, infection (endometritis), uterine fibroids, a retroverted uterus or uterine prolapse, a persistently full bladder or rectum.

2. Clinical features

  • Fundal height greater than expected for the postnatal day; the uterus feels bulky, soft and boggy.
  • Lochia excessive or prolonged; the red stage (lochia rubra) persists beyond the first week; irregular bleeding.
  • Secondary PPH in some women.
  • Fever, foul lochia and uterine tenderness when infection is present; backache and a feeling of heaviness.

3. Investigations – ultrasound for retained products or fibroids; blood count and CRP; high vaginal swab when infection is suspected.

4. Management

  • Treat the cause – antibiotics for infection; evacuation of retained products under antibiotic cover; correct a retroverted uterus (knee-chest position or pessary rarely); treat anaemia.
  • Uterotonics – methylergometrine or other drugs as prescribed to improve tone (avoided in hypertension).
  • Encourage breastfeeding – sucking releases oxytocin, which contracts the uterus.
  • Regular emptying of bladder and bowels; adequate fluids and fibre.
  • Early ambulation and postnatal exercises; prone lying for short periods may help drainage of lochia.

5. Nursing role

  • Daily measurement of fundal height (after emptying the bladder) and recording on the postnatal chart; assessment of lochia (colour, amount, smell).
  • Teach the mother about normal lochia changes and danger signs; support exclusive breastfeeding.
  • Follow up at home visits (ASHA/ANM HBNC visits) and refer when the uterus remains large or bleeding continues.

6. Normal involution for comparison

Time after delivery Fundal height / uterine weight
Soon after birth At or just below the umbilicus; about 1,000 g
End of first week Midway between umbilicus and symphysis; about 500 g
10–14 days Behind the symphysis – not palpable abdominally; about 300 g
6 weeks Almost non-pregnant size; about 60–100 g

Conclusion Subinvolution is a sign that something – usually retained products or infection – is wrong. Daily fundal assessment by the nurse allows early treatment and prevents secondary PPH.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Management of Women with Abnormal Postnatal Conditions
question: Explain the urinary complications of the puerperium and their nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Pregnancy and labour affect the bladder and urethra – the bladder may be bruised and oedematous after delivery, sensation is reduced, and the bladder fills rapidly because of postnatal diuresis. Urinary complications are common in the first days after delivery and are easily missed.

1. Retention of urine

  • Definition – inability to pass urine within 6 hours of vaginal delivery (or of removal of a catheter after caesarean section), or incomplete emptying with a large residual volume.
  • Causes – bladder atony and reduced sensation, oedema and bruising of the bladder neck and urethra, perineal pain and fear of passing urine, epidural analgesia, prolonged labour and instrumental delivery, vulval or paravaginal haematoma, unfamiliar surroundings and lack of privacy.
  • Features – no urge or inability to void, suprapubic discomfort, a palpable bladder, the uterus pushed up and to one side, frequent dribbling of small amounts (overflow). An over-distended bladder prevents uterine contraction and causes PPH.
  • Management
    • Privacy, an upright position on a commode or toilet, running water, pouring warm water over the vulva, analgesia for perineal pain, encouragement and early ambulation.
    • If she still cannot void by 6 hours – in-and-out catheterisation with strict asepsis and measurement of the volume; an indwelling catheter for 24–48 hours when the volume is large or retention recurs.
    • Treat the cause (haematoma, pain).

2. Urinary incontinence

  • Stress incontinence – leakage on coughing, laughing or lifting, from weakened pelvic floor after vaginal delivery; managed with pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises taught before discharge, and specialist review if it persists after 3–6 months.
  • Overflow incontinence – due to unrecognised retention; managed by catheterisation.
  • Continuous (true) incontinence – constant dribbling day and night suggests an obstetric fistula; needs urgent referral.

3. Urinary tract infection

  • Common after catheterisation, prolonged labour and retention.
  • Cystitis – frequency, burning micturition, suprapubic pain; acute pyelonephritis – fever with chills, loin pain and tenderness, vomiting.
  • Management – urine culture, antibiotics safe in breastfeeding, 2–3 litres of fluid a day, frequent emptying, perineal hygiene.

4. Nursing role

  • Record the time and volume of the first void after delivery; palpate for a full bladder during fourth-stage and postnatal checks.
  • Use catheters only when needed, with aseptic technique and closed drainage; remove them early.
  • Teach pelvic floor exercises and perineal hygiene (front to back), and ask about leakage at follow-up visits.

Conclusion Careful attention to the first void, early relief of retention, aseptic catheter care and pelvic floor exercises prevent most urinary complications after childbirth.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Management of Women with Abnormal Postnatal Conditions
question: Explain venous thromboembolism in the puerperium – risk factors, clinical features, prevention and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Venous thromboembolism (VTE) – deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and its complication pulmonary embolism (PE) – is a leading direct cause of maternal death in many countries. The risk is highest in the first six weeks after delivery, especially after caesarean section, because all three parts of Virchow's triad are present: hypercoagulable blood, venous stasis and injury to vessels at delivery.

1. Risk factors

  • Delivery – caesarean section (especially emergency), mid-cavity or rotational instrumental delivery, prolonged labour, PPH of more than 1 litre or transfusion, preterm birth, stillbirth.
  • Maternal – age above 35, obesity (BMI 30 or more), parity of three or more, smoking, gross varicose veins, previous VTE or thrombophilia, heart or lung disease, sickle cell disease.
  • Transient – immobility, dehydration, infection, pre-eclampsia, long-distance travel.

2. Clinical features

  • DVT – usually in the left leg: pain and tenderness in the calf or thigh, swelling (difference in calf circumference of more than 2 cm), warmth, low-grade fever; extensive iliofemoral thrombosis causes a swollen, pale, painful leg (phlegmasia alba dolens).
  • PE – sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, tachycardia, low SpO₂, anxiety; a large embolus causes collapse and sudden death.
  • Investigations – compression duplex ultrasound for DVT; CT pulmonary angiography or V/Q scan, ECG, chest X-ray, blood gases and echocardiography for PE. (D-dimer is not useful after delivery.)

3. Prevention

  • Risk assessment of every woman at booking, on admission, after delivery and before discharge.
  • Early mobilisation after vaginal birth and caesarean section; adequate hydration; leg exercises.
  • Graduated compression stockings for women at risk.
  • Thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin (for example enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily, adjusted for weight) for 10 days to 6 weeks depending on risk, as prescribed.

4. Management

  • Therapeutic anticoagulation – LMWH (enoxaparin about 1 mg/kg twice daily) started as soon as VTE is suspected; continued for the rest of the puerperium and for at least 6 weeks after delivery and 3 months in total; warfarin may be used after delivery – both LMWH and warfarin are safe during breastfeeding.
  • DVT – leg elevation, compression stockings once pain settles, analgesia, early mobilisation once anticoagulated.
  • PE – oxygen, IV access, heparin, ICU care; thrombolysis or embolectomy for massive PE with collapse.
  • Contraception – avoid oestrogen-containing pills; progestogen-only methods or IUCD are suitable.

5. Nursing care

  • Encourage early ambulation, leg exercises and fluids; fit stockings correctly.
  • Examine the legs daily for swelling, redness or tenderness; never massage a painful calf.
  • Give heparin injections into the abdominal wall with correct technique and teach self-injection; watch for bleeding (wound, lochia, gums) and bruising.
  • Teach her to report breathlessness, chest pain or leg swelling at once; support breastfeeding.

Conclusion Puerperal VTE is preventable – risk assessment, early mobilisation, hydration and timely heparin prophylaxis, with prompt diagnosis and anticoagulation when it occurs, save mothers' lives.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Management of Women with Abnormal Postnatal Conditions
question: Explain vulval and paravaginal haematoma – causes, clinical features and management.
answer_html:
Introduction A puerperal haematoma is a collection of blood in the tissues of the vulva, vagina or broad ligament, from injury to blood vessels during delivery, usually without a visible tear of the overlying skin or mucosa. Because the bleeding is concealed, a large haematoma can cause shock with little external bleeding.

1. Types

  • Vulval (infralevator) – below the levator ani, in the labia and perineum; the commonest.
  • Vaginal or paravaginal – in the vaginal wall or alongside it, also below the levator.
  • Supralevator (broad ligament or retroperitoneal) – above the levator ani; dangerous, with large concealed bleeding.

2. Causes

  • Instrumental delivery (forceps or vacuum), episiotomy with a vessel not secured, deep tears.
  • Prolonged second stage, a big baby, primigravida.
  • Vulval varicosities, pre-eclampsia, coagulation disorders.

3. Clinical features

  • Usually within a few hours of delivery.
  • Severe perineal, vaginal or rectal pain – out of proportion to the findings; a feeling of pressure or need to pass stool.
  • A tense, tender, bluish-purple swelling of the labium or vaginal wall (felt on vaginal or rectal examination in paravaginal haematoma).
  • Retention of urine.
  • Signs of shock – pallor, rapid pulse, low BP – with only slight external bleeding.
  • Supralevator haematoma – a mass above the inguinal ligament, the uterus pushed to one side, falling haemoglobin; ultrasound or CT helps.

4. Management

  • Small, non-expanding haematoma (less than about 3–5 cm) – ice packs, analgesics, observation of size, vital signs and haemoglobin.
  • Large or expanding haematoma – under anaesthesia: incision, evacuation of clots, ligation of bleeding vessels, closure with or without a drain, and vaginal packing for 12–24 hours.
  • Indwelling catheter (retention and packing); broad-spectrum antibiotics; blood transfusion and correction of coagulopathy.
  • Supralevator haematoma – laparotomy or arterial embolisation.

5. Nursing role

  • Inspect the perineum during fourth-stage checks and take any complaint of severe pain seriously – do not dismiss it as "normal stitch pain".
  • Monitor pulse, BP, the size of the swelling and the bladder; apply ice packs; report expansion.
  • Prepare for theatre; care for the catheter and pack (record the time of insertion and removal); perineal hygiene and comfort.

Conclusion Puerperal haematoma should be suspected when a woman has severe perineal pain or shock out of proportion to visible blood loss; early evacuation of large haematomas and good nursing observation prevent serious blood loss and infection.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Management of Women with Abnormal Postnatal Conditions
question: Explain obstetric fistula (vesico-vaginal and recto-vaginal fistula) – causes, clinical features, management and prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction An obstetric fistula is an abnormal opening between the vagina and the bladder (vesico-vaginal fistula, VVF) or the rectum (recto-vaginal fistula, RVF), caused by childbirth. It leads to continuous leakage of urine or faeces and devastating social and emotional suffering, yet it is almost entirely preventable with timely obstetric care.

1. Causes

  • Ischaemic (pressure-necrosis) fistula – in prolonged obstructed labour the fetal head presses the vaginal wall and bladder base (or rectum) against the pelvic bones; the tissue dies and sloughs out 3–10 days after delivery, leaving a hole. This is the commonest type in low-resource settings.
  • Traumatic (surgical) fistula – injury during caesarean section, caesarean hysterectomy, difficult forceps, destructive operations or symphysiotomy; leakage starts within the first 24–48 hours.
  • Rarely – radiation, cancer of the cervix, unskilled abortion.

2. Clinical features

  • VVF – continuous dribbling of urine through the vagina, day and night, with no normal voiding (or reduced voiding with a small fistula).
  • RVF – passage of flatus and faeces through the vagina.
  • Excoriation and dermatitis of the vulva and thighs, a constant smell, recurrent infections.
  • Associated injuries of obstructed labour – foot drop, vaginal scarring, amenorrhoea, infertility.
  • Social consequences – stigma, desertion by the husband, isolation, depression and poverty.

3. Diagnosis

  • Speculum examination – the opening may be seen.
  • Dye test – methylene blue instilled into the bladder stains a swab in the vagina (three-swab test distinguishes VVF from a ureterovaginal fistula, where clear urine wets the upper swab).
  • Cystoscopy, and intravenous or CT urography to detect ureteric involvement; examination under anaesthesia.

4. Management

  • Early continuous bladder drainage – an indwelling catheter for 2–4 weeks or longer can heal a small, fresh fistula.
  • Surgical repair – for ischaemic fistulas usually done about 3 months after delivery, when the slough has separated and inflammation has settled (surgical-injury fistulas may be repaired early); most are repaired through the vagina with careful layered closure; complex cases need an abdominal approach, or urinary diversion.
  • After repair – catheter drainage for 10–14 days, high fluid intake (3–4 litres/day) to keep urine dilute and the catheter free, antibiotics as prescribed, avoidance of constipation; no intercourse for about 3 months.
  • Rehabilitation – physiotherapy (foot drop), counselling, family support, livelihood support.
  • Future pregnancy – elective caesarean section to protect the repair.

5. Prevention

  • Prevent prolonged and obstructed labour – birth preparedness, institutional delivery, use of the Labour Care Guide, timely referral and caesarean section.
  • Continuous bladder drainage for 10–14 days after any prolonged obstructed labour.
  • Delay marriage and first pregnancy; family planning.
  • Careful surgical technique during caesarean section and hysterectomy.

6. Nursing care

  • Skin care – frequent washing, barrier creams, absorbent pads; prevent infection and odour.
  • Encourage fluids and nutrition; correct anaemia.
  • Care of the catheter after repair – keep it patent, never let it block or kink; strict intake–output; report any leakage.
  • Compassionate, non-judgemental support; help the woman and her family understand that the condition can be cured.

Conclusion Obstetric fistula is a preventable consequence of neglected labour. Timely delivery, bladder drainage after obstructed labour, skilled surgical repair and compassionate rehabilitation restore the woman's health and dignity.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Management of Women with Abnormal Postnatal Conditions
question: What is Sheehan's syndrome?
tags: loss of axillary and pubic hair
answer_html:
• Sheehan's syndrome is ischaemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary gland following severe postpartum haemorrhage with shock (the pituitary is enlarged in pregnancy and very sensitive to low blood flow).
  • Features – failure of lactation (often the first sign), amenorrhoea after delivery, loss of axillary and pubic hair, breast atrophy, symptoms of hypothyroidism (tiredness, cold intolerance) and adrenal insufficiency (weakness, low BP, hypoglycaemia); it may appear months or years later.
  • Treatment – lifelong hormone replacement – corticosteroids first, then thyroxine, and oestrogen–progestogen; ovulation induction if pregnancy is desired.
  • Prevention – prompt treatment of PPH and shock.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Management of Women with Abnormal Postnatal Conditions
question: What is phlegmasia alba dolens?
answer_html:
• Phlegmasia alba dolens ("white leg" or "milk leg") is iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis in the puerperium, usually appearing in the second week after delivery and more often in the left leg.
  • The whole leg is swollen, tense, pale (white) and very painful, owing to venous obstruction, oedema and arterial spasm; low-grade fever and tenderness along the femoral vein are present.
  • It carries a risk of pulmonary embolism; a more severe form with a blue, cold leg is phlegmasia cerulea dolens.
  • Management – confirm with duplex ultrasound; anticoagulation with LMWH (then warfarin if chosen), leg elevation, analgesia, compression stockings once pain settles, early mobilisation after anticoagulation, and watch for PE.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Management of Women with Abnormal Postnatal Conditions
question: What is lochiometra?
answer_html:
• Lochiometra is the retention of lochia inside the uterus because its drainage through the cervix is obstructed.
  • Causes – a clot or piece of membrane blocking the os, acute anteflexion or retroversion of the uterus, cervical stenosis or oedema, tight vaginal packing, prolonged bed rest in the supine position.
  • Features – scanty or absent lochia with a uterus that is enlarged, soft and tender; low-grade fever and lower abdominal discomfort; it may become infected (pyometra).
  • Management – early ambulation and prone or upright positioning, gentle dilatation of the os or removal of the clot to drain the lochia, uterotonics and antibiotics when infection is present.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Management of Women with Abnormal Postnatal Conditions
question: What is an obstetric early warning score (MEOWS) chart?
answer_html:
• A Modified Early Obstetric Warning Score (MEOWS) chart is a colour-coded observation chart adapted for pregnant and postnatal women (whose normal values differ) to detect deterioration early.
  • Parameters recorded – respiratory rate, SpO₂, temperature, pulse, systolic and diastolic BP, level of consciousness (AVPU), pain, lochia/bleeding and urine output.
  • Each value falls in a normal (white), yellow (moderately abnormal) or red (severely abnormal) zone; a trigger – for example one red or two yellow scores – requires urgent review by a doctor.
  • It helps nurses recognise sepsis, PPH, pre-eclampsia and thromboembolism early, improves communication and documentation, and reduces delays in treatment.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of the High-risk Newborn
question: (a) Define a high-risk newborn and list the conditions that make a newborn high-risk. (4 marks) (b) Explain the identification and screening of high-risk newborns at birth, with the criteria for admission to an SNCU. (5 marks) (c) Describe the referral and safe transport of a sick newborn, with the role of the nurse. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Identification, stabilisation and referral of a high-risk newborn
labels: Flowchart – birth at the delivery point → newborn assessment (weight
danger signs) → well baby: routine care with mother
HBNC visits; high-risk baby: stabilise at the NBCC/NBSU → check TOPS (Temperature – warm
Sugar – feed or IV 10% dextrose) → inform and refer to SNCU with a trained escort
mother and referral slip (JSSK free transport
102) → feedback from SNCU and follow-up after discharge

answer_html:
(a) Definition and conditions (4 marks)

Definition

  • A high-risk newborn is a newborn, regardless of gestational age or birth weight, who has a greater than average chance of illness or death because of conditions or circumstances before, during or after birth that interfere with the normal adjustment to life outside the uterus.
  • About 1 in 10 Indian newborns needs special care; prematurity, birth asphyxia and infection cause most neonatal deaths (India's NMR was 18 per 1,000 live births in SRS 2024).

Conditions that make a newborn high-risk

Basis Conditions
Birth weight Low birth weight (<2,500 g), very low (<1,500 g), extremely low (<1,000 g); macrosomia (>4,000 g)
Gestational age Preterm (<37 weeks), post-term (≥42 weeks)
Intrauterine growth Small for gestational age / growth-restricted, large for gestational age
Maternal factors Diabetes, hypertension and pre-eclampsia, anaemia, infections (HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis, TB, chorioamnionitis), Rh or ABO incompatibility, teenage or elderly mother, drug or alcohol use, previous neonatal death or stillbirth
Intrapartum factors Prolonged or obstructed labour, rupture of membranes >18 hours, maternal fever, meconium-stained liquor, fetal distress, malpresentation, instrumental delivery or emergency caesarean, multiple birth
Neonatal conditions Birth asphyxia, respiratory distress, congenital malformations, birth injuries, jaundice, sepsis, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, convulsions, feeding difficulty

(b) Identification, screening and criteria for SNCU admission (5 marks)

1. Identification at birth

  • Before birth – review the mother's antenatal and labour record for the risk factors above and inform the paediatric team for high-risk deliveries.
  • At birth – assess breathing, heart rate, colour and tone (APGAR), weigh the baby, estimate gestational age, check temperature, look for visible birth defects and injuries.
  • In the first hours and days – watch for danger signs: poor feeding or not sucking, lethargy, fast breathing (60 or more per minute), chest indrawing or grunting, temperature below 35.5°C or above 37.5°C, convulsions, jaundice in the first 24 hours or on palms and soles, umbilical redness or pus, bleeding, abdominal distension, cyanosis.

2. Newborn screening

  • Birth defects – every baby is examined at the delivery point and during home visits under the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), which covers defects at birth among its "4 Ds"; babies are referred to District Early Intervention Centres (DEIC).
  • Hearing screening (otoacoustic emissions), pulse oximetry for critical congenital heart disease, TSH screening for congenital hypothyroidism where available, ROP screening for preterm babies.
  • Follow-up through home-based newborn care (HBNC) visits by the ASHA, who identifies and refers sick and small babies.

3. Levels of newborn care (briefly)

  • Newborn care corner (NBCC) at every delivery point – resuscitation and essential newborn care.
  • Newborn stabilisation unit (NBSU) at CHCs/FRUs – stabilisation of sick babies and care of small babies before referral.
  • Special newborn care unit (SNCU) at district hospitals and NICU at medical colleges.

4. Criteria for admission to an SNCU (as in the national facility-based newborn care guidelines)

  • Birth weight below 1,800 g or gestation below 34 weeks.
  • Perinatal asphyxia needing resuscitation; respiratory distress, apnoea or central cyanosis.
  • Neonatal sepsis, refusal to feed, lethargy; hypothermia or hyperthermia; hypoglycaemia.
  • Jaundice needing phototherapy or exchange transfusion; convulsions; bleeding; shock.
  • Major congenital malformations, abdominal distension or persistent vomiting, and any baby the doctor judges sick.

(c) Referral and safe transport of a sick newborn and the nurse's role (6 marks)

1. When possible – in-utero transfer

  • The mother's uterus is the best transport incubator: high-risk women (preterm labour, severe pre-eclampsia) should be referred before delivery to a facility with an SNCU.

2. Pre-transport stabilisation – maintain "TOPS"

  • T – Temperature – dry, wrap in warm clothes with cap and socks; kangaroo (skin-to-skin) transport with the mother or a relative is the simplest and best method; a transport incubator if available; check temperature before leaving.
  • O – Oxygenation – position the neck slightly extended, clear the airway, give oxygen by nasal prongs or hood if the baby has respiratory distress; bag-and-mask ventilation for apnoea.
  • P – Perfusion – check capillary refill time (normal <3 seconds), pulse and colour; a bolus of normal saline (10 ml/kg) as ordered for shock.
  • S – Sugar – prevent hypoglycaemia: breastfeed or give expressed breast milk by paladai or tube if the baby can tolerate it; otherwise IV 10% dextrose as ordered; check blood glucose.
  • Treat specific conditions before leaving – first dose of antibiotics for suspected sepsis, anticonvulsant for seizures, cover exposed gut or myelomeningocele with sterile moist gauze, insert an orogastric tube for abdominal distension or tracheo-oesophageal fistula.

3. Arranging the referral

  • Explain to the parents why referral is needed and obtain consent; encourage the mother to accompany the baby (for KMC and breastfeeding).
  • Inform the receiving SNCU by phone about the baby's condition and expected arrival.
  • Transport – free transport for sick newborns and infants under the Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram (JSSK) through 102/108 ambulances, with drop-back after discharge.
  • Referral slip – name, date and time of birth, birth weight, gestation, APGAR, maternal history, reason for referral, treatment given (drugs with time and dose), vital signs at departure; send the mother's records and, if possible, a sample of her blood (for cross-matching or jaundice).
  • A trained health worker accompanies the baby with a transport kit (bag and mask, suction, oxygen, thermometer, glucometer, IV fluids, syringes).

4. During transport

  • Keep the baby warm and in skin-to-skin contact; check breathing, colour, temperature and feeding every 15–30 minutes; avoid sudden jerks; continue oxygen; record observations.

5. Role of the nurse

  • Recognise risk early – before birth from the mother's history, and at birth by careful assessment and weighing.
  • Stabilise – warmth, airway, feeding and glucose, infection prevention.
  • Communicate – with the family (counselling, reassurance), with the receiving unit and through accurate referral notes.
  • Support the mother – teach her to express breast milk and to provide KMC; arrange her stay near the SNCU.
  • Follow-up after discharge – link with ASHA HBNC/HBYC visits, immunisation, growth monitoring and the RBSK/DEIC for developmental follow-up.

6. Counselling the family of a high-risk newborn

  • Explain the baby's condition, the reason for special care and what will happen next in simple, honest words; repeat information, since anxious parents remember little.
  • Encourage the mother to touch, hold (KMC) and feed her baby as soon as possible, and to stay in the mothers' room near the SNCU.
  • Teach hand washing, expression and storage of breast milk, and the danger signs to watch for after discharge.
  • Address fears, guilt and costs – inform them that care in public SNCUs and transport are free under JSSK.

Nursing importance

  • Most sick newborns die not because treatment is unavailable but because they reach it cold, hypoglycaemic and hypoxic. The nurse who identifies risk early and maintains TOPS during referral gives the baby a real chance of survival.

Conclusion Early identification of high-risk newborns, admission to the right level of care using clear criteria, and safe, stabilised transport with warmth, oxygen, perfusion and sugar maintained are key nursing contributions to reducing neonatal deaths.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of the High-risk Newborn
question: Explain birth injuries of the newborn other than those of the scalp – brachial plexus injuries, fractures and facial nerve palsy.
answer_html:
Introduction Birth injuries are injuries to the newborn caused by mechanical forces during labour and delivery. They are more likely with a big baby, shoulder dystocia, breech delivery, instrumental delivery, prolonged labour, CPD and prematurity. (Injuries of the scalp – caput, cephalhaematoma and subgaleal haemorrhage – are considered separately.)

1. Brachial plexus injuries

  • Cause – stretching of the nerve roots of the neck during shoulder dystocia, traction on the head, or delivery of the arms in breech.
  • Erb's palsy (C5–C6, upper plexus) – the commonest; the affected arm lies adducted and internally rotated, with the elbow extended, forearm pronated and wrist flexed (the "waiter's tip" position); Moro reflex absent on that side, but the grasp reflex is present.
  • Klumpke's palsy (C8–T1, lower plexus) – paralysis of the hand muscles (claw hand), absent grasp; Horner's syndrome (small pupil, drooping eyelid) if T1 is involved.
  • Total plexus palsy – the whole arm is flaccid.
  • Management – gentle handling; keep the arm in a comfortable position (pinned across the upper abdomen for the first week to reduce pain); gentle passive range-of-motion exercises after about 7–10 days, taught to the mother; physiotherapy; most babies recover within 3–6 months; nerve surgery is considered when there is no recovery of elbow flexion by 3–6 months.
  • Phrenic nerve palsy (C3–C5) may accompany Erb's palsy and cause breathing difficulty.

2. Fractures

  • Fracture of the clavicle – the commonest birth fracture (shoulder dystocia, big baby); swelling, crepitus, reduced movement of the arm, asymmetric Moro reflex; a lump of callus appears in 7–10 days. Management – gentle handling, pinning the sleeve to the vest to limit movement, analgesia; it heals well.
  • Fracture of the humerus or femur – after difficult breech delivery or caesarean extraction; swelling, deformity, pain on movement. Management – immobilisation (arm strapped to the chest; splint or traction for the femur) for 2–3 weeks; heals quickly.

3. Facial nerve palsy

  • Pressure on the nerve by a forceps blade or the mother's sacral promontory.
  • On crying, the mouth is drawn to the normal side; on the affected side the eye does not close, the forehead is smooth and the nasolabial fold is flat.
  • Management – most recover within a few weeks; eye care (artificial tears, cover the eye to protect the cornea); help with feeding (it may be difficult to seal the lips on the breast).

4. Other injuries

  • Sternomastoid "tumour" (congenital muscular torticollis) – a firm lump in the sternomastoid muscle at 2–3 weeks; the head tilts to the affected side; treated by gentle stretching exercises and positioning.
  • Intra-abdominal injuries (liver, spleen, adrenal haemorrhage) after breech delivery – pallor, shock, abdominal distension; spinal cord injury with a hyperextended head in breech.

5. Nursing care

  • Examine every baby carefully after a difficult delivery – symmetry of movements, Moro and grasp reflexes, swelling, crepitus, facial symmetry.
  • Handle gently, relieve pain, position correctly, and support breastfeeding in a comfortable position.
  • Teach parents the exercises and handling, and explain the expected recovery honestly; arrange follow-up and physiotherapy.
  • Document the findings accurately (they may have medico-legal importance).

Conclusion Most birth injuries heal well with gentle handling, correct positioning, exercises and parent education; good obstetric care – especially skilled management of shoulder dystocia and breech – prevents them.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of the High-risk Newborn
question: Explain the problems and nursing management of an infant of a diabetic mother.
answer_html:
Introduction An infant of a diabetic mother (IDM) is a baby born to a mother with pregestational or gestational diabetes. Maternal high blood sugar crosses the placenta, the fetal pancreas responds with excess insulin (fetal hyperinsulinism), and this causes overgrowth before birth and a sudden fall of blood sugar after birth (Pedersen hypothesis). Good control of maternal diabetes greatly reduces these problems.

1. Problems of the IDM

  • Macrosomia (birth weight above 4 kg) with a large, plump, plethoric "cushingoid" look – risking shoulder dystocia and birth injuries (Erb's palsy, fractured clavicle, asphyxia).
  • Hypoglycaemia – the most common problem, usually within the first 1–6 hours; may be silent or cause jitteriness, poor feeding, apnoea, convulsions.
  • Hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia – jitteriness, convulsions.
  • Respiratory distress – delayed lung maturity (insulin interferes with surfactant), transient tachypnoea, especially after caesarean section.
  • Polycythaemia and hyperviscosity – plethora, poor feeding, risk of thrombosis (renal vein thrombosis) and jaundice.
  • Congenital anomalies (with poor control at conception) – heart defects including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (thick septum), neural tube defects, caudal regression syndrome, small left colon syndrome.
  • Growth restriction when the mother has vascular disease; later childhood obesity and diabetes.

2. Nursing management

  • Anticipate – inform the paediatrician; be ready for resuscitation and shoulder dystocia.
  • Warmth and skin-to-skin contact; initiate breastfeeding within 30 minutes of birth and feed every 2–3 hours.
  • Blood glucose monitoring – check at about 1, 2 and 3 hours, then before feeds every 3–4 hours for the first 24–48 hours (or as per unit policy).
  • Hypoglycaemia (below 45 mg/dl) – extra breastfeed or expressed milk; if low or symptomatic, IV 10% dextrose (2 ml/kg bolus followed by infusion) as ordered; recheck after 30–60 minutes.
  • Check serum calcium in jittery babies; give calcium gluconate as prescribed.
  • Watch breathing (oxygen or CPAP for distress), colour and haematocrit (partial exchange for symptomatic polycythaemia), and jaundice (phototherapy).
  • Examine for anomalies and birth injuries; echocardiography if there is a murmur or distress.
  • Teach the mother about frequent breastfeeding, signs of low sugar and jaundice, and her own postnatal glucose test.

Conclusion The IDM is at risk mainly of hypoglycaemia, respiratory distress, polycythaemia, jaundice, birth injury and malformations; early feeding, regular glucose checks and careful observation prevent most complications.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of the High-risk Newborn
question: Explain meconium aspiration syndrome – causes, clinical features, management and prevention.
tags: positive pressure ventilation in first minute
answer_html:
Introduction Meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS) is respiratory distress in a newborn born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid, caused by the presence of meconium in the lungs, which cannot be explained otherwise. Meconium-stained liquor is found in about 10–15% of births (more in post-term pregnancies), and a small proportion of these babies develop MAS.

1. Causes and mechanism

  • Fetal hypoxia (post-term pregnancy, growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, cord compression, prolonged labour) causes passage of meconium and gasping in the uterus or at birth.
  • Meconium in the airways causes mechanical obstruction – complete (collapse) or partial (ball-valve effect with air trapping and pneumothorax) – plus chemical pneumonitis, inactivation of surfactant and often persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN).

2. Clinical features

  • Meconium staining of the skin, nails and cord; a post-term, growth-restricted look.
  • Respiratory distress soon after birth – tachypnoea, grunting, chest retractions, cyanosis; a barrel-shaped chest.
  • Chest X-ray – patchy opacities with hyperinflation; pneumothorax may be seen.

3. Management

  • At birth (current neonatal resuscitation guidelines)
    • Suction of the mouth and nose before delivery of the shoulders is not recommended.
    • Vigorous baby (good breathing and tone, heart rate >100) – routine care with the mother; clear secretions if needed.
    • Non-vigorous baby – routine tracheal intubation and suction are no longer recommended; begin the initial steps and start positive pressure ventilation within the first minute (the "golden minute"); suction the trachea only if the airway is obstructed.
  • In the SNCU/NICU – oxygen to keep SpO₂ in the target range, CPAP or mechanical ventilation, surfactant in severe cases, antibiotics when infection cannot be excluded, treatment of PPHN, drainage of pneumothorax.
  • Supportive nursing – minimal handling (handling increases hypoxia), thermoregulation, blood glucose monitoring, IV fluids at first, then gradual feeds; monitoring of SpO₂, respiratory rate and signs of pneumothorax (sudden deterioration).

4. Prevention

  • Induction of labour at 41 weeks to avoid post-term pregnancy.
  • Careful fetal monitoring in labour, recognising thick meconium with heart-rate changes, and timely delivery for fetal distress.
  • A trained person skilled in resuscitation present at every birth with meconium-stained liquor.

Conclusion MAS is a preventable result of fetal hypoxia. Good intrapartum monitoring, effective ventilation of non-vigorous babies within the golden minute and skilled respiratory care give good outcomes.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of the High-risk Newborn
question: Explain sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) – risk factors, safe-sleep counselling and support to the bereaved family.
answer_html:
Introduction Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) is the sudden, unexpected death of an apparently healthy infant under one year of age, usually during sleep, which remains unexplained after a thorough investigation (autopsy, examination of the death scene and review of the history). It is most common at 2–4 months, and most deaths occur before 6 months. The cause is thought to be a vulnerable baby, at a critical stage of development, meeting an outside stress such as an unsafe sleep position.

1. Risk factors

  • Prone (tummy) or side sleeping position – the most important modifiable factor.
  • Soft bedding – pillows, quilts, soft mattresses, soft toys; bed-sharing, especially on a sofa or with parents who smoke, drink or are very tired.
  • Overheating – heavy wrapping, covering the head.
  • Maternal smoking in pregnancy and passive smoking after birth.
  • Prematurity and low birth weight, male sex, young mother, not being breastfed, recent minor illness.

2. Safe-sleep counselling (what the nurse teaches)

  • Put the baby on the back for every sleep – night and day ("back to sleep").
  • A firm, flat sleep surface with a fitted sheet; no pillows (including mustard-seed pillows used to shape the head), bolsters, soft toys or loose blankets in the sleep area.
  • Room-sharing without bed-sharing – the baby sleeps close to the mother in a separate cot or crib, ideally for at least the first 6 months; never on a sofa.
  • Avoid overheating – light clothing, do not cover the head or face.
  • Smoke-free home; no smoking during pregnancy.
  • Exclusive breastfeeding, which protects against SIDS.
  • A pacifier at sleep time may be offered after breastfeeding is well established (not forced).
  • Complete immunisation on schedule.
  • Supervised tummy time when the baby is awake, for development and to prevent a flat head.

3. Support to the bereaved family

  • Provide a private place; allow parents to see and hold the baby; use the baby's name.
  • Avoid any blame; explain gently that SIDS is not caused by anything they intentionally did.
  • Explain the need for an autopsy and the formalities in simple language.
  • Offer grief counselling, involve family and religious supports, watch for depression in the parents.
  • Follow-up visits; support and closer monitoring for the next baby.

Conclusion SIDS cannot always be prevented, but safe-sleep practices – back to sleep, a firm surface, no soft bedding, room-sharing without bed-sharing, a smoke-free home and breastfeeding – greatly reduce the risk; bereaved families need compassionate, blame-free support.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)

question: Explain the calculation of fluid and feeding requirements of a newborn, with an example.
tags: choice of feeding method by gestation
answer_html:
Introduction Newborns, especially small and sick ones, need carefully calculated fluids and feeds. Immediately after birth the body contains extra water, which is lost in the first days (a weight loss of up to about 10% in term babies), and the kidneys are immature – so fluid is started low and increased day by day.

1. Daily fluid requirement (commonly used schedule – facility-based newborn care guidelines)

Day of life Birth weight 1,500 g or more (ml/kg/day) Birth weight below 1,500 g (ml/kg/day)
Day 1 60 80
Day 2 75 95
Day 3 90 110
Day 4 105 125
Day 5 120 140
Day 6 135 150
Day 7 onwards 150 160
  • The amount is increased by about 15 ml/kg each day, up to 150–160 ml/kg/day by the end of the first week (feeds may later increase to about 180 ml/kg/day for good growth).
  • IV fluid – 10% dextrose for the first two days; sodium and potassium are added from about the third day once urine output is established.

2. Calculating the feed per sitting

  • Daily volume = ml/kg/day for that day × body weight (kg).
  • Volume per feed = daily volume ÷ number of feeds (12 feeds if 2-hourly, 8 feeds if 3-hourly).
  • Example 1 – a baby of 1.6 kg on day 3 needs 90 × 1.6 = 144 ml/day; given 2-hourly (12 feeds) = 12 ml per feed.
  • Example 2 – a baby of 1.2 kg on day 4 needs 125 × 1.2 = 150 ml/day; given 2-hourly = 12.5 ml per feed.
  • When part of the requirement is given IV, the oral feed volume is subtracted from the total.

3. Adjustments

  • Increase fluids (by about 10–20 ml/kg/day) for very small babies under a radiant warmer or phototherapy.
  • Restrict fluids in birth asphyxia, renal failure, heart failure or excessive weight gain.

4. Choosing the feeding method (by maturity)

  • Babies able to suck well (usually 34 weeks or more) – direct breastfeeding.
  • Babies who cannot breastfeed but can swallow – expressed breast milk by paladai, cup or spoon.
  • Smaller or sicker babies – orogastric tube feeds, with IV fluids at first for the very small or sick; trophic feeds are started early.

5. Monitoring and nursing responsibilities

  • Weigh daily on the same scale; weight loss beyond 10% (term) or failure to regain birth weight by 10–14 days needs review.
  • Urine output (about 1–3 ml/kg/hour; six or more wet nappies a day after the first few days); signs of dehydration or overload (oedema, puffiness).
  • Use an infusion pump or micro-drip set, check the IV site hourly, and record intake–output accurately.
  • Check blood glucose and serum sodium as ordered; observe for feed intolerance (vomiting, abdominal distension, large aspirates).
  • Support the mother to express milk every 2–3 hours so that her own milk is used.

Conclusion Day-wise, weight-based calculation of fluids and feeds, adjusted to the baby's condition and supported by careful monitoring of weight and urine output, keeps the newborn well hydrated and growing.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of the High-risk Newborn
question: What is transient tachypnoea of the newborn?
answer_html:
• Transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN, "wet lung") is mild respiratory distress caused by delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid.
  • More common after elective caesarean section without labour, in infants of diabetic mothers, after precipitate delivery and in late-preterm babies.
  • Features – rapid breathing (above 60/minute) starting soon after birth, mild grunting or retractions, good air entry; chest X-ray shows fluid in the fissures and streaky lung markings.
  • It is self-limiting, settling within 24–72 hours.
  • Management – oxygen or CPAP if needed, tube feeds when breathing is very fast, warmth; exclude sepsis and RDS. Prevention – avoid elective caesarean before 39 weeks.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of the High-risk Newborn
question: What is hydrops fetalis?
tags: fluid in two or more fetal compartments
answer_html:
• Hydrops fetalis is the abnormal accumulation of fluid in two or more fetal compartments – skin oedema, ascites, pleural effusion or pericardial effusion – often with polyhydramnios and a thick placenta.
  • Immune hydrops – due to Rh (or other red-cell) isoimmunisation causing severe fetal anaemia; now uncommon because of anti-D prophylaxis.
  • Non-immune hydrops (most cases today) – heart defects and arrhythmias, chromosomal anomalies, α-thalassaemia major, infections (parvovirus B19, CMV, syphilis), twin-to-twin transfusion, fetal anaemia and lymphatic disorders.
  • Management – find the cause; intrauterine transfusion for anaemia; delivery in a tertiary centre; at birth, resuscitation with drainage of effusions and ventilation. The outlook is often poor.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of the High-risk Newborn
question: What is pulse oximetry screening for critical congenital heart disease?
answer_html:
• It is a simple, painless test to detect critical congenital heart disease (CCHD) – heart defects needing surgery or catheter treatment in the first weeks of life – before the baby becomes sick.
  • Done at 24–48 hours of age (or before discharge): oxygen saturation is measured in the right hand (pre-ductal) and either foot (post-ductal).
  • Pass – 95% or more in the hand or foot with a difference of 3% or less.
  • Fail – below 90% in either limb → immediate evaluation and echocardiography.
  • Values of 90–94% or a difference of more than 3% → the test is repeated after about an hour; a persistent abnormality is treated as a fail.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of the High-risk Newborn
question: What is universal newborn hearing screening?
answer_html:
• Universal newborn hearing screening means testing the hearing of every newborn, because congenital hearing loss (about 1–6 per 1,000 births) is otherwise detected late, harming speech, language and learning.
  • Tests – otoacoustic emissions (OAE) before discharge or within the first month; babies who fail, and high-risk babies (NICU stay of more than 5 days, exchange transfusion for jaundice, meningitis, TORCH infection, craniofacial anomalies, family history), have an automated auditory brainstem response (ABR/BERA) test.
  • The "1–3-6" goal – screen by 1 month, diagnose by 3 months and begin intervention (hearing aids, cochlear implant, therapy) by 6 months.
  • Congenital deafness is among the birth defects covered under RBSK.

question: (a) Define infertility and explain the causes of female infertility. (4 marks) (b) Explain the investigation of an infertile couple, with special reference to the woman. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management of female infertility, including assisted reproductive techniques, and the role of the nurse. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Steps of in-vitro fertilisation (IVF)
labels: Flow diagram – controlled ovarian stimulation with injections and ultrasound monitoring of follicles → trigger injection → transvaginal ultrasound-guided oocyte retrieval → fertilisation in the laboratory (conventional IVF or ICSI with a single sperm injected into each egg) → embryo culture for 3–5 days → transfer of one or two embryos into the uterus through a catheter (spare embryos frozen) → luteal phase support with progesterone → pregnancy test about two weeks later

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes of female infertility (4 marks)

Definition

  • Infertility is the failure of a couple to conceive after 12 months or more of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse (WHO); evaluation is started after 6 months if the woman is 35 years or older.
  • Primary infertility – the woman has never conceived; secondary infertility – she has conceived before (whatever the outcome) but cannot conceive now.
  • WHO (2023) estimates that about 1 in 6 people worldwide experiences infertility in their lifetime.
  • Causes are shared – roughly female factors in about 40%, male factors in 30–40%, both partners in about 20%, and unexplained in 10–15% – so both partners are always evaluated together.

Causes of female infertility

Factor Causes
Ovulatory (about one-third) PCOS (the commonest), hypothalamic amenorrhoea (stress, weight loss, excessive exercise), hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disorders, premature ovarian insufficiency, obesity
Tubal and peritoneal PID and STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhoea), genital tuberculosis (important in India), post-abortal or puerperal sepsis, previous pelvic surgery, endometriosis, adhesions, previous sterilisation
Uterine Fibroids (especially submucous), endometrial polyps, intrauterine adhesions (Asherman's syndrome), congenital anomalies (septate uterus), tubercular endometritis
Cervical and vaginal Cervical stenosis after surgery, vaginal septum, vaginismus and other sexual problems
General Age above 35 (declining egg number and quality), smoking, alcohol, obesity or under-weight, diabetes, chronic illness, stress, drugs

(b) Investigation of the infertile couple (5 marks)

1. Initial assessment of both partners

  • History – duration of infertility, frequency and timing of intercourse, sexual difficulties, previous pregnancies, contraception, STIs, surgery, TB, medical illness, drugs, occupation and habits.
  • Examination – BMI, signs of hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne), galactorrhoea, thyroid; pelvic examination for tenderness, masses or fixed uterus.
  • Semen analysis of the husband early in the work-up (simple and non-invasive).

2. Tests of ovulation

  • Menstrual history – regular cycles of 21–35 days usually mean ovulation.
  • Basal body temperature chart – a rise of about 0.3–0.5°C after ovulation (simple but less reliable).
  • Mid-luteal serum progesterone (about day 21 of a 28-day cycle) – a raised level confirms ovulation.
  • Follicular monitoring by transvaginal ultrasound – growth and rupture of the dominant follicle.
  • Urinary LH kits detect the LH surge.

3. Ovarian reserve and hormones

  • Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) and antral follicle count on ultrasound; day-2/3 FSH and oestradiol.
  • TSH, prolactin, and testosterone in women with irregular cycles or hirsutism.

4. Tubal patency and the uterine cavity

  • Hysterosalpingography (HSG) – contrast X-ray of the uterus and tubes, done in the follicular phase after menstruation.
  • Sonosalpingography (HyCoSy) – ultrasound with contrast or saline.
  • Diagnostic laparoscopy with chromotubation (dye test) – the gold standard; also shows endometriosis and adhesions.
  • Hysteroscopy for polyps, septum, adhesions; saline infusion sonography.
  • Endometrial biopsy (premenstrual) for genital tuberculosis (histology, culture, GeneXpert) in suspected cases.

(c) Management of female infertility, ART and the nurse's role (6 marks)

1. General measures

  • Counselling of the couple together – explain the reproductive process and the fertile window (about days 10–17 of a 28-day cycle); intercourse every 2–3 days.
  • Healthy weight (a 5–10% weight loss in obese women often restores ovulation), stopping smoking and alcohol, folic acid 400 µg daily, treatment of diabetes and thyroid disease.
  • Treatment of infections and anti-tubercular treatment for genital TB.

2. Specific treatment by cause

  • Ovulatory dysfunction – ovulation induction with letrozole or clomiphene (and gonadotrophins when needed), with ultrasound monitoring; dopamine agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine) for hyperprolactinaemia; thyroxine for hypothyroidism; laparoscopic ovarian drilling in selected PCOS.
  • Tubal factor – laparoscopic adhesiolysis, salpingostomy, tubal recanalisation (after sterilisation); IVF when tubes are badly damaged; removal of hydrosalpinx before IVF.
  • Uterine factor – hysteroscopic removal of polyps, septum or adhesions; myomectomy for distorting fibroids.
  • Endometriosis – laparoscopic surgery and/or IVF.

3. Assisted reproductive techniques (ART)

  • Intrauterine insemination (IUI) – washed, concentrated sperm (husband's or donor's) placed into the uterus around ovulation; for mild male factor, cervical factor, sexual problems and unexplained infertility.
  • In-vitro fertilisation (IVF) – ovarian stimulation, oocyte retrieval, fertilisation in the laboratory, embryo culture and embryo transfer into the uterus; for tubal disease, endometriosis, failed IUI, unexplained infertility.
  • Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) – a single sperm injected into each egg, for severe male factor or previous fertilisation failure.
  • Donor eggs, donor sperm or donor embryos; cryopreservation of embryos, eggs and sperm (also for fertility preservation before cancer treatment).
  • Surrogacy – permitted in India only in its altruistic form.
  • Regulation – the ART (Regulation) Act 2021 and the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act 2021 require registered clinics and banks and lay down eligibility, consent and record-keeping.
  • Complications of ART – ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) (abdominal distension, pain, vomiting, breathlessness, reduced urine), multiple pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, procedure-related bleeding and infection, emotional and financial stress.

4. Role of the nurse

  • Counselling and emotional support – infertility causes grief, anxiety, marital stress and social stigma, and in India the woman is often unfairly blamed; involve both partners and correct the myth that infertility is "the woman's fault".
  • Education – fertile period, tests and their timing, lifestyle change, medication schedules; teach self-injection of gonadotrophins and correct storage.
  • Coordination – scheduling investigations on the correct cycle days, preparing women for HSG, laparoscopy and egg retrieval; maintaining confidentiality and records.
  • Monitoring – recognising OHSS (weight gain, abdominal girth, urine output) and ectopic pregnancy; early ultrasound after ART pregnancy.
  • Information about alternatives – adoption through CARA and childfree living, without pressure.

5. Genital tuberculosis – an important cause in India

  • Usually secondary to TB elsewhere (lungs, lymph nodes); it affects the tubes (almost always) and the endometrium, causing tubal block, hydrosalpinx and intrauterine adhesions.
  • Often silent – infertility, scanty or absent periods, chronic pelvic pain.
  • Diagnosed by premenstrual endometrial biopsy (histology, culture, GeneXpert), HSG and laparoscopy findings (beaded tubes, tubercles).
  • Treated with the full course of anti-tubercular drugs under the national TB programme; pregnancy outcome is often poor once the endometrium is damaged, so IVF (or surrogacy) may be needed.

6. Prevention of infertility

  • Prevention and early treatment of STIs and PID; condom use; safe abortion and clean delivery to prevent pelvic infection.
  • Early diagnosis and treatment of tuberculosis.
  • Healthy weight, no smoking or alcohol, management of PCOS, diabetes and thyroid disease.
  • Awareness that fertility declines after 35 years, and early evaluation when conception is delayed.

7. Practical fertility-awareness advice for couples

  • Around ovulation the cervical mucus becomes clear, slippery and stretchy – a sign of the fertile days; urinary LH kits can confirm the surge.
  • Regular intercourse every 2–3 days through the cycle is better than "timed" intercourse, which adds stress.
  • Avoid oil-based lubricants, which can harm sperm; there is no need to lie down for long after intercourse.

Nursing importance

  • Nurses are often the first professionals an infertile couple trusts; sensitive, non-judgemental counselling and clear guidance through complex tests and treatments make a large difference to the couple's well-being and success.

Conclusion Infertility is a problem of the couple. Systematic joint evaluation, correction of the cause, ovulation induction and ART when needed, together with sensitive nursing support, help many couples achieve parenthood.

question: (a) Define uterine fibroid (leiomyoma) and classify fibroids. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and complications of fibroids, including in pregnancy. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management of fibroids and the nursing care of a woman undergoing abdominal hysterectomy. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Types of uterine fibroids according to location
labels: Coronal section of the uterus showing a submucous fibroid bulging into the cavity
a pedunculated submucous fibroid (fibroid polyp) hanging through the cervix
an intramural fibroid within the wall
a subserous fibroid under the peritoneum
a pedunculated subserous fibroid on a stalk
a cervical fibroid and a broad-ligament fibroid

answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks)

Definition

  • A uterine fibroid (leiomyoma, myoma) is a benign tumour arising from the smooth muscle of the uterus, with variable fibrous tissue. It is the commonest tumour of the female pelvis, present in about 20–40% of women of reproductive age.
  • It is oestrogen- and progesterone-dependent – it grows in reproductive years and in pregnancy and shrinks after menopause.
  • Risk factors – nulliparity, early menarche, obesity, family history, African ancestry; parity and long use of combined pills lower the risk.

Classification by location

Type Site Main effect
Submucous (about 5–10%) Under the endometrium, projecting into the cavity; may become pedunculated (fibroid polyp) Heavy bleeding, infertility, miscarriage – even when small
Intramural (interstitial) (commonest) Within the muscle wall Heavy bleeding, enlarged uterus
Subserous Under the peritoneum; may be pedunculated Pressure symptoms, torsion; little bleeding
Cervical In the cervix Urinary retention, obstructed labour, difficult surgery
Broad ligament Between the layers of the broad ligament Ureteric displacement
  • The FIGO system (types 0–8) describes the exact position relative to the cavity and serosa, used to plan surgery.

(b) Clinical features and complications (5 marks)

1. Clinical features

  • About half are symptom-free, found on examination or ultrasound.
  • Heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) – the commonest symptom, leading to anaemia.
  • Pressure symptoms – frequency of urine, retention (cervical or anterior fibroids), constipation, backache, leg oedema.
  • Lump in the abdomen, heaviness.
  • Pain – dysmenorrhoea; acute pain with degeneration or torsion.
  • Infertility and recurrent miscarriage (submucous fibroids distorting the cavity).
  • Examination – a firm, irregular, enlarged uterus that moves with the cervix; a fibroid polyp may be seen at the os.

2. Complications

  • Degenerations – hyaline (commonest), cystic, fatty, calcareous; red (carneous) degeneration, typically in mid-pregnancy, with acute pain, fever and tenderness; sarcomatous change is very rare (less than 0.5%).
  • Torsion of a pedunculated subserous fibroid; infection and ulceration of a fibroid polyp; chronic inversion of the uterus by a submucous polyp.
  • Anaemia and its effects.

3. Fibroids in pregnancy

  • Miscarriage, preterm labour, red degeneration, malpresentation, placental abruption.
  • Obstructed labour with a cervical or lower-segment fibroid.
  • PPH and subinvolution; difficult caesarean section.
  • Most fibroids are left alone in pregnancy; red degeneration is treated with rest and analgesics; myomectomy is not done at caesarean section except for a pedunculated fibroid.

4. Investigations – ultrasound (transabdominal and transvaginal), saline infusion sonography or hysteroscopy for submucous fibroids, MRI for complex cases; haemoglobin; endometrial sampling in older women with abnormal bleeding.

(c) Management and nursing care of abdominal hysterectomy (7 marks)

1. Management of fibroids

  • Observation – small, symptom-free fibroids, and women near menopause; review every 6–12 months.
  • Medical treatment (for bleeding and before surgery) – tranexamic acid and NSAIDs during periods, LNG-IUS when the cavity is not distorted, combined pills or progestins; GnRH analogues for 3–6 months before surgery to shrink the fibroid and correct anaemia; iron or blood transfusion.
  • Surgical treatment
    • Myomectomy – removal of fibroids with preservation of the uterus, for women who want children (abdominal, laparoscopic, or hysteroscopic myomectomy for submucous fibroids). Fibroids can recur.
    • Hysterectomy – the definitive treatment when the family is complete; abdominal, vaginal or laparoscopic; ovaries are usually conserved in younger women.
    • Uterine artery embolisation and focused ultrasound ablation in selected women.

2. Nursing care of a woman undergoing abdominal hysterectomy

Pre-operative care

  • Counselling – explain the operation, its effects (no periods, no pregnancy, menopause if ovaries are removed) and address fears about femininity, sexuality and weight gain; involve the husband; informed written consent.
  • Investigations – haemoglobin (correct anaemia), blood group and cross-match, blood sugar, renal function, ECG, chest X-ray as needed; Pap/VIA and endometrial assessment where indicated.
  • Physical preparation – teaching of deep breathing, coughing and leg exercises; bowel preparation as per policy; nil by mouth for 6–8 hours; skin preparation (clipping); removal of jewellery; urinary catheter; prophylactic antibiotic before incision; thromboprophylaxis for high-risk women.

Post-operative care

  • Vital signs every 15 minutes initially, then hourly; watch for haemorrhage – from the wound and the vagina (vault) – and signs of shock.
  • Pain relief – regular analgesics; position of comfort.
  • IV fluids until bowel sounds return; then oral fluids and a gradual return to a normal diet; watch for paralytic ileus.
  • Catheter care and removal after about 24 hours; check that she passes urine well (risk of bladder or ureteric injury, retention).
  • Early ambulation (day 1), deep breathing and leg exercises to prevent chest infection and DVT; compression stockings.
  • Wound care – aseptic dressing, watch for infection; perineal hygiene for vaginal discharge.
  • Emotional support – some women feel loss or low mood after hysterectomy.

Discharge advice

  • Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous work for about 6 weeks; walk daily.
  • No intercourse for about 6 weeks; resume when vaginal discharge stops and she feels ready.
  • High-fibre diet, plenty of fluids, avoid constipation and straining.
  • Report fever, foul discharge, vaginal bleeding, wound redness, burning micturition or calf pain.
  • If the ovaries were removed – symptoms of surgical menopause, calcium and vitamin D, and hormone therapy as advised.
  • Follow-up visit after about 6 weeks.

3. Choosing the treatment

  • The choice depends on the woman's age, her wish for children, the size, number and site of the fibroids, the severity of symptoms and anaemia, and how near she is to menopause.
Point Myomectomy Hysterectomy
Fertility Preserved Lost
Periods Continue Stop
Recurrence Fibroids may recur (in up to a quarter of women) No recurrence
Blood loss and risk May be more bleeding, adhesions; caesarean may be advised in later pregnancy Definitive, single operation
Suitable for Young women wanting pregnancy Women with completed family, multiple large fibroids

4. Psychological and social care

  • Many women fear that the "lump" is cancer – reassure them that fibroids are benign and that sarcoma is very rare.
  • Address concerns about sexuality, weight gain and "weakness" after hysterectomy, which are common myths; involve the husband in counselling.
  • Encourage women with long-standing heavy bleeding not to delay treatment because of fear of surgery.

5. Red (carneous) degeneration in pregnancy – care

  • Typically at 12–22 weeks: acute localised pain and tenderness over the fibroid, low-grade fever, vomiting, raised white cell count.
  • Exclude appendicitis, abruption, pyelonephritis and torsion.
  • Treated conservatively – bed rest, analgesics as prescribed, ice packs, fluids and reassurance; it settles in about 1–2 weeks. Surgery is avoided in pregnancy.

Nursing importance

  • Fibroids are among the commonest reasons for gynaecological admission; the nurse corrects anaemia, prepares the woman physically and emotionally, and prevents post-operative haemorrhage, infection and thrombosis.

Conclusion Fibroids are common, benign tumours; treatment depends on symptoms, size, site and the wish for children – from observation and medical therapy to myomectomy or hysterectomy – supported by thorough nursing care before and after surgery.
