question: (a) Define abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) and explain the terms used to describe it. (4 marks) (b) Explain the PALM-COEIN classification of the causes of AUB. (5 marks) (c) Describe the investigation, management and nursing care of a woman with heavy menstrual bleeding. (6 marks)
tags: old terms menorrhagia polymenorrhoea metrorrhagia oligomenorrhoea
answer_html:
(a) Definition and terms (4 marks)

Definition

  • Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) is bleeding from the uterine body that is abnormal in frequency, regularity, duration or volume, in a woman who is not pregnant (FIGO, revised 2018). It is one of the commonest gynaecological complaints.
  • Acute AUB – an episode of heavy bleeding needing immediate treatment; chronic AUB – abnormal bleeding present for most of the previous 6 months.

Normal menstruation (FIGO 2018) for comparison

Parameter Normal
Frequency (cycle length) 24–38 days
Duration of flow Up to 8 days
Regularity Variation between the shortest and longest cycle of about 7–9 days or less
Volume Not felt by the woman to be heavy

Terms used

Current term Meaning Older term often used in exams
Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) Excessive menstrual blood loss that interferes with the woman's physical, social, emotional or material quality of life (traditionally >80 ml per cycle) Menorrhagia
Frequent menstrual bleeding Cycles shorter than 24 days Polymenorrhoea
Infrequent menstrual bleeding Cycles longer than 38 days Oligomenorrhoea
Prolonged menstrual bleeding Flow lasting more than 8 days –
Intermenstrual bleeding Bleeding between clearly defined periods Metrorrhagia
Irregular bleeding Cycle-to-cycle variation more than 7–9 days Menometrorrhagia (heavy and irregular)
Postcoital bleeding Bleeding after intercourse –

FIGO recommends dropping the older terms, but they are still widely used.

(b) PALM-COEIN classification (5 marks)

FIGO's PALM-COEIN system groups the causes of AUB in non-pregnant women of reproductive age into structural (PALM) causes, seen on imaging or histology, and non-structural (COEIN) causes.

A. Structural causes – PALM

  • P – Polyp (AUB-P) – endometrial or cervical polyps; intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding; diagnosed by ultrasound or hysteroscopy.
  • A – Adenomyosis (AUB-A) – endometrial glands within the myometrium; heavy, painful periods with a uniformly enlarged, tender ("globular") uterus; more common in multiparous women in their late 30s and 40s.
  • L – Leiomyoma (AUB-L) – fibroids, subdivided into submucous (most likely to cause bleeding) and other fibroids.
  • M – Malignancy and hyperplasia (AUB-M) – endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer, cervical cancer; must be excluded especially in women over 45, obese women, women with PCOS or on tamoxifen.

B. Non-structural causes – COEIN

  • C – Coagulopathy (AUB-C) – von Willebrand disease (commonest), low platelets, leukaemia, anticoagulants; suspected when heavy bleeding has been present since menarche.
  • O – Ovulatory dysfunction (AUB-O) – anovulatory cycles at the extremes of reproductive life (puberty and perimenopause), PCOS, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, obesity, stress; bleeding is irregular, unpredictable and sometimes heavy (previously called dysfunctional uterine bleeding).
  • E – Endometrial (AUB-E) – a primary disorder of the endometrium's local haemostasis (for example altered prostaglandins) with regular but heavy periods, or endometritis.
  • I – Iatrogenic (AUB-I) – bleeding due to hormonal contraceptives, IUCDs, HRT, anticoagulants, antidepressants and other drugs.
  • N – Not yet classified (AUB-N) – rare causes such as arteriovenous malformations and caesarean scar niche (isthmocele).

A woman may have more than one cause (for example AUB-L and AUB-O).

(c) Investigation, management and nursing care of heavy menstrual bleeding (6 marks)

1. Assessment and investigations

  • History – pattern, duration and amount of bleeding (number of pads, clots, flooding, night soiling); a pictorial blood loss assessment chart (PBAC) – a score above 100 suggests HMB; pain, pressure symptoms, contraception, drugs, symptoms of anaemia, thyroid or bleeding disorders.
  • Examination – pallor, BMI, thyroid, abdominal and pelvic examination; speculum examination of the cervix.
  • Investigations
    • Urine pregnancy test (always first).
    • Complete blood count (anaemia), ferritin; TSH; coagulation tests (and von Willebrand screen) when suggested by history.
    • Transvaginal ultrasound – fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, endometrial thickness; saline infusion sonography.
    • Endometrial sampling (Pipelle biopsy or hysteroscopy-directed biopsy) in women aged 45 or more, and in younger women with risk factors, persistent intermenstrual bleeding or failed treatment.
    • Hysteroscopy for suspected intracavitary lesions; Pap smear/VIA as per screening schedule.

2. Management

  • Acute heavy bleeding – resuscitate (IV fluids, blood transfusion); hormonal treatment (high-dose combined pills or progestins as prescribed), tranexamic acid; intrauterine balloon tamponade or curettage if bleeding does not stop.
  • Medical treatment of chronic HMB
    • LNG-IUS (levonorgestrel intrauterine system) – the most effective medical treatment; also contraceptive.
    • Tranexamic acid (for example 1 g three times a day during heavy days) and NSAIDs (mefenamic acid) – taken only during menses; also reduce pain.
    • Combined oral contraceptives, cyclical oral progestins (norethisterone), injectable DMPA.
    • GnRH analogues for short-term use before surgery.
    • Treat the cause – thyroxine, treatment of PCOS, haematology referral for coagulopathy; iron (oral or IV) for anaemia.
  • Surgical treatment – hysteroscopic removal of polyps or submucous fibroids; endometrial ablation for women with completed families; myomectomy; hysterectomy when other treatments fail or are unsuitable, or for malignancy.

3. Nursing care

  • Teach the woman to keep a menstrual calendar and PBAC chart; record pad counts in hospital.
  • Monitor vital signs and haemoglobin; give iron, transfusion and drugs as ordered; observe for side effects.
  • Diet rich in iron, protein and vitamin C; rest during heavy days.
  • Explain procedures (ultrasound, biopsy, hysteroscopy, LNG-IUS insertion) and prepare her physically and emotionally.
  • Health education – HMB is not "normal" and needs evaluation; postmenopausal or intermenstrual bleeding must be reported at once; importance of follow-up.
  • Address the effect on work, school and social life; reassure about the effectiveness of treatment.

4. AUB at different ages – common causes and approach

  • Adolescence – mostly anovulatory cycles of an immature axis; but heavy bleeding since menarche may be due to a bleeding disorder (von Willebrand disease) or low platelets; also pregnancy complications and PCOS. Treated with tranexamic acid, iron and hormones; transfusion for severe anaemia; curettage is rarely needed.
  • Reproductive years – pregnancy-related bleeding (always exclude), fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, PCOS, thyroid disease, IUCD and hormonal contraceptives.
  • Perimenopause (40 years onwards) – anovulatory cycles, fibroids and adenomyosis, but also endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, so endometrial sampling is essential, especially from 45 years or with risk factors (obesity, diabetes, PCOS, tamoxifen).
  • After menopause – any bleeding is postmenopausal bleeding and needs urgent evaluation.

5. Counselling about LNG-IUS and endometrial ablation

  • LNG-IUS – a small T-shaped device releasing levonorgestrel into the uterus; it reduces menstrual blood loss by over 80–90%, also gives contraception for several years, and may cause irregular spotting in the first 3–6 months, after which periods become light or stop (harmless).
  • Endometrial ablation – destruction of the endometrium by heat or other energy; suitable only for women whose family is complete, because pregnancy afterwards is dangerous, so reliable contraception is still needed.

Nursing importance

  • Many Indian women suffer years of heavy bleeding and anaemia silently; the nurse who asks about periods, recognises HMB and refers for evaluation prevents severe anaemia and detects early cancer.

Conclusion AUB is described using standard FIGO terms and classified by PALM-COEIN into structural and non-structural causes; systematic investigation, medical treatment (LNG-IUS, tranexamic acid, hormones), surgery when needed and supportive nursing care relieve most women.

question: (a) Define genital (pelvic organ) prolapse; list its types and degrees and explain its causes. (5 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnosis of uterovaginal prolapse. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management, the nursing care of a woman undergoing vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair, and prevention. (6 marks)
tags: vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair

diagram.caption: Types and degrees of genital prolapse
labels: Sagittal sections of the female pelvis – normal; cystocele (bladder bulging into the anterior vaginal wall); rectocele (rectum bulging into the posterior wall); enterocele (pouch of Douglas with bowel into the upper posterior wall); first-degree uterine prolapse (cervix descends but stays within the vagina); second-degree (cervix outside the introitus
body inside); third-degree/procidentia (whole uterus outside with the vagina everted

answer_html:
(a) Definition, types, degrees and causes (5 marks)

Definition

  • Genital (pelvic organ) prolapse is the descent of one or more pelvic organs – the uterus, the vaginal walls, the bladder, the rectum or small bowel – from their normal position into or through the vagina, due to weakness of the pelvic supports (levator ani muscles, endopelvic fascia, cardinal and uterosacral ligaments).
  • It is common in multiparous women, especially rural women who do heavy work, and in older women after menopause.

Types

Compartment Type
Anterior vaginal wall Urethrocele (urethra), cystocele (bladder)
Posterior vaginal wall Rectocele (rectum), enterocele (pouch of Douglas with small bowel – upper posterior wall)
Uterus Uterine (uterovaginal) prolapse – the commonest combination with cystocele and rectocele
After hysterectomy Vault prolapse

Degrees of uterine prolapse (commonly used clinical grading)

  • First degree – the cervix descends below its normal level but remains within the vagina.
  • Second degree – the cervix protrudes outside the introitus, the body of the uterus remains inside.
  • Third degree (procidentia) – the whole uterus lies outside the introitus, with the vagina turned inside out.
  • The POP-Q (Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification) system is used in specialist practice for precise measurement and staging (0–IV).

Causes

  • Childbirth injury (the main cause) – multiparity, prolonged second stage, bearing down before full dilatation, big babies, difficult instrumental delivery, fundal pressure, poorly repaired tears, and early return to heavy work after delivery.
  • Menopause – oestrogen deficiency weakens the supporting tissues.
  • Raised intra-abdominal pressure – chronic cough (COPD, TB), chronic constipation, heavy lifting, obesity, ascites, pelvic tumours.
  • Congenital weakness of supports – prolapse in young nulliparous women, spina bifida, connective tissue disorders.
  • Ageing and previous pelvic surgery (vault prolapse after hysterectomy).

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis (4 marks)

1. Symptoms

  • Feeling of "something coming down" (mass per vaginum), worse on standing, walking or straining and relieved by lying down.
  • Dragging pain in the lower abdomen and backache.
  • Urinary symptoms (cystocele) – frequency, urgency, a feeling of incomplete emptying, having to push the bulge back to pass urine, stress incontinence, recurrent urinary infections, rarely retention.
  • Bowel symptoms (rectocele) – difficulty in emptying the bowel, needing to press on the posterior vaginal wall to pass stool.
  • Vaginal discharge or bleeding from a decubitus ulcer on the exposed cervix; difficulty in intercourse.

2. Examination

  • In the dorsal position and in the left lateral (Sims') position with a Sims' speculum, while the woman strains (Valsalva) or coughs.
  • Note the degree of descent, presence of cystocele, rectocele and enterocele, the state of the perineum, elongation of the cervix (measured with a uterine sound), decubitus ulcer (biopsy if suspicious), and stress incontinence on coughing.
  • General examination – chronic cough, constipation, obesity, abdominal masses.

3. Investigations – urine examination and culture, residual urine, ultrasound (kidneys for hydronephrosis in procidentia, pelvic masses), Pap smear/VIA, fitness for anaesthesia; urodynamic studies when incontinence is complex.

(c) Management, nursing care of vaginal hysterectomy and prevention (6 marks)

1. Conservative management (mild prolapse, young women planning pregnancy, pregnancy, elderly women unfit for surgery)

  • Pelvic floor muscle training (Kegel exercises) – the first-line treatment for mild prolapse and stress incontinence.
  • Treat chronic cough and constipation, reduce weight, avoid heavy lifting.
  • Vaginal pessary (ring or shelf pessary) to support the organs; changed and cleaned every 3–6 months, with vaginal oestrogen cream to prevent ulceration.

2. Surgical management (chosen according to age, wish for children, degree and fitness)

  • Anterior colporrhaphy (cystocele) and posterior colpoperineorrhaphy (rectocele and deficient perineum).
  • Manchester (Fothergill's) operation – amputation of an elongated cervix, plication of the cardinal ligaments and anterior and posterior repair; conserves the uterus in younger women.
  • Vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair – the commonest operation for uterovaginal prolapse in women who have completed their family.
  • Sling operations (such as the Shirodkar and Purandare operations, developed in India) and abdominal or laparoscopic sacrohysteropexy/sacrocolpopexy – for young women and for vault prolapse.
  • Colpocleisis (Le Fort's operation) – closure of the vagina for very old women who are not sexually active and unfit for major surgery.

3. Nursing care of a woman undergoing vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair

Pre-operative

  • Treat a decubitus ulcer first – reduce the prolapse, daily vaginal packing with glycerine (and acriflavine) or oestrogen cream until it heals.
  • Treat urinary infection, cough and constipation; correct anaemia; control diabetes and hypertension.
  • Explanation, consent and emotional support; teach breathing exercises and pelvic floor exercises.
  • Bowel preparation, nil by mouth, perineal and vaginal preparation as per policy, prophylactic antibiotics.

Post-operative

  • Monitor vital signs and look for bleeding – vaginal bleeding, soaked pads and signs of shock.
  • Vaginal pack is usually removed after about 24 hours; indwelling catheter for 24–72 hours; after removal, check that she voids well and measure residual urine if needed.
  • Perineal care – keep the area clean and dry; change pads; sitz baths later.
  • Pain relief, early ambulation, leg exercises, deep breathing.
  • Avoid straining – stool softeners, high-fibre diet, plenty of fluids; support for coughing.
  • Watch for urinary retention, urinary infection, haematoma and wound infection.

Discharge advice

  • No heavy lifting or strenuous work for about 3 months; avoid prolonged standing at first.
  • No intercourse for about 6 weeks.
  • Continue pelvic floor exercises; prevent constipation and treat cough.
  • Report fever, foul discharge, bleeding or difficulty in passing urine; attend follow-up.

4. Prevention

  • Good conduct of labour – no bearing down before full dilatation, avoiding prolonged second stage and fundal pressure, timely and skilled instrumental delivery, proper repair of tears and episiotomy.
  • Postnatal pelvic floor exercises, adequate rest and avoidance of heavy work during the puerperium.
  • Small family norm and birth spacing.
  • Treatment of chronic cough and constipation; healthy weight.

5. Teaching pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises

  • Identify the muscles – the muscles squeezed to hold back wind or to stop the flow of urine (stopping urine midstream is used only once to identify them, not as a routine exercise).
  • Exercise – tighten and lift the pelvic floor, hold for 5–10 seconds, then relax for 10 seconds; repeat 10 times, three times a day, in lying, sitting and standing positions; add a few quick contractions.
  • "The knack" – contract the pelvic floor just before coughing, sneezing or lifting.
  • Breathe normally; do not tighten the abdomen, thighs or buttocks.
  • Benefits appear after 8–12 weeks of regular practice; continue for life, and start again soon after every delivery.

Nursing importance

  • Prolapse is preventable to a large extent by good midwifery practice; nurses teach pelvic floor exercises, give pre- and post-operative care, and counsel women who often hide the problem out of shame for years.

Conclusion Genital prolapse results mainly from childbirth injury and weakened supports. Conservative measures and pessaries help mild cases, while surgery – from Manchester repair to vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair – corrects advanced prolapse; good midwifery care prevents it.

question: (a) Explain the risk factors and clinical features of carcinoma of the cervix. (4 marks) (b) Describe the FIGO staging and the diagnosis of carcinoma cervix. (5 marks) (c) Explain the management and nursing care of a woman with carcinoma cervix, and its prevention including HPV vaccination in India. (6 marks)
tags: second commonest cancer in Indian women
stage IA IB IIA IIB IIIA IIIB IIIC IVA IVB

diagram.caption: FIGO 2018 staging of carcinoma of the cervix
labels: Series of coronal diagrams of the uterus
parametria and pelvic walls – Stage I confined to the cervix (IA microscopic
IB visible); Stage II beyond the uterus to the upper two-thirds of the vagina (IIA) or parametrium (IIB) but not to the pelvic wall; Stage III lower third of the vagina (IIIA)
pelvic or para-aortic lymph nodes (IIIC); Stage IV bladder or rectal mucosa (IVA) or distant spread (IVB)

answer_html:
(a) Risk factors and clinical features (4 marks)

Introduction

  • Carcinoma of the cervix is the second commonest cancer among Indian women, with roughly 1.2 lakh new cases and about 80,000 deaths every year – India accounts for about a quarter of the world's cervical cancer deaths.
  • Almost all cases are caused by persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), especially types 16 and 18. It develops slowly through pre-cancerous lesions (CIN) over 10–15 years, so it is preventable by vaccination and screening. About 80–90% are squamous cell carcinomas; the rest are adenocarcinomas.

Risk factors

  • Early age at first intercourse and early marriage; multiple sexual partners (of the woman or her husband).
  • High parity and early first pregnancy.
  • HIV infection and other immunosuppression; other STIs.
  • Smoking and tobacco use; long-term use of combined oral pills (slight increase).
  • Low socio-economic status, poor genital hygiene, lack of screening.

Clinical features

  • Early (pre-invasive and early invasive) – often no symptoms; detected only by screening.
  • Abnormal vaginal bleeding – postcoital bleeding (the classic early symptom), intermenstrual bleeding, postmenopausal bleeding.
  • Vaginal discharge – watery, blood-stained and later foul-smelling (from necrosis and infection).
  • Advanced disease – pelvic pain, backache, pain radiating down the legs (nerve involvement), leg oedema, urinary symptoms, haematuria, vesico-vaginal or recto-vaginal fistula, ureteric obstruction leading to uraemia (a common cause of death), weight loss, anaemia and cachexia.
  • On speculum examination – an ulcer or a cauliflower-like (exophytic) growth that bleeds on touch, or a hard, barrel-shaped cervix (endocervical growth); rectovaginal examination assesses spread to the parametria.

(b) FIGO staging and diagnosis (5 marks)

FIGO staging (2018)

Stage Extent
I Confined to the cervix
IA Microscopic invasive cancer; deepest invasion <5 mm (IA1 <3 mm; IA2 3 to <5 mm)
IB Invasion ≥5 mm; IB1 lesion <2 cm, IB2 2 to <4 cm, IB3 ≥4 cm
II Beyond the uterus, but not to the lower third of the vagina or the pelvic wall
IIA Upper two-thirds of the vagina, no parametrial spread (IIA1 <4 cm, IIA2 ≥4 cm)
IIB Parametrial involvement, not reaching the pelvic wall
III Lower third of vagina, pelvic wall, hydronephrosis/non-functioning kidney, or lymph nodes
IIIA Lower third of the vagina
IIIB Pelvic wall and/or hydronephrosis or non-functioning kidney
IIIC Pelvic (IIIC1) or para-aortic (IIIC2) lymph node metastasis
IV Bladder or rectum, or distant spread
IVA Mucosa of bladder or rectum
IVB Distant organs (lungs, liver, bones, distant nodes)

Diagnosis

  • Screening tests in asymptomatic women – VIA, Pap smear or HPV DNA test; positive results are followed by colposcopy.
  • Biopsy – colposcopy-directed or punch biopsy of a visible lesion; cone biopsy when needed – histopathology confirms the diagnosis.
  • Staging work-up – clinical examination (under anaesthesia if needed), MRI of the pelvis (tumour size, parametria), CT or PET-CT for nodes and distant spread, chest X-ray, cystoscopy and proctoscopy when bladder or rectal involvement is suspected, renal function and ultrasound for hydronephrosis, haemoglobin and HIV test.

(c) Management, nursing care and prevention (6 marks)

1. Treatment by stage

  • Pre-cancerous lesions (CIN) – thermal ablation, cryotherapy or LEEP/LLETZ (loop excision) – "screen and treat" in the same visit where possible.
  • Stage IA1 – cone biopsy (to preserve fertility) or simple hysterectomy.
  • Stage IA2, IB1–IB2 and IIA1 – radical hysterectomy (Wertheim's operation) with pelvic lymphadenectomy, or radiotherapy; fertility-sparing radical trachelectomy for selected young women.
  • Stage IB3, IIA2 to IVA – concurrent chemoradiation: external beam radiotherapy with weekly cisplatin, followed by brachytherapy.
  • Stage IVB and recurrence – palliative chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and palliative care (pain relief, management of bleeding, discharge, fistula and uraemia).

2. Nursing care

  • Psychological support – fear of cancer and death, guilt and stigma; involve the family; counselling at diagnosis and during treatment.
  • Before radical surgery – preparation as for major surgery; explain loss of fertility; bowel preparation; correct anaemia.
  • After radical hysterectomy – vital signs, bleeding, drains, prolonged bladder drainage (bladder dysfunction is common – catheter for 7–14 days with bladder training), thromboprophylaxis, wound care, lymphoedema watch.
  • During radiotherapy and chemotherapy – skin care of the treated area, high-protein diet and fluids, management of diarrhoea, nausea and cystitis, monitoring of blood counts and renal function; care during brachytherapy (bed rest with the applicator in place, catheter, radiation safety precautions).
  • Palliative care – regular analgesia (WHO ladder), management of foul discharge (vaginal douching with antiseptic solution, metronidazole), bleeding, fistula and odour; nutrition; dignity and end-of-life support.
  • Follow-up – regular examinations; vaginal dilators after radiotherapy to prevent stenosis; sexual counselling.

3. Prevention

  • Primary prevention – HPV vaccination
    • India launched a nationwide free HPV vaccination campaign on 28 February 2026 (from Ajmer, Rajasthan) using a single dose of the quadrivalent Gardasil-4 vaccine (HPV 6, 11, 16, 18) for girls aged 14 years at government health facilities – about 1.15 crore girls each year; more than 80 lakh girls had been vaccinated by September 2026.
    • Health education about delaying sexual debut, safe sex, condoms and avoiding tobacco.
  • Secondary prevention – screening and early treatment
    • Under the national NCD programme, women aged 30–65 years are screened by VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid) every 5 years at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs; HPV DNA testing and Pap smear where available.
    • "Screen and treat" of positive women with thermal ablation or cryotherapy.
  • WHO elimination targets (90-70-90 by 2030) – 90% of girls fully vaccinated by age 15, 70% of women screened with a high-performance test by 35 and again by 45, and 90% of women with pre-cancer or cancer treated.

4. Role of the nurse in VIA screening (secondary prevention)

  • Preparation – explain the test, obtain consent, ensure privacy, ask her to empty the bladder; position her in the dorsal position.
  • Procedure – insert a Cusco's speculum and identify the cervix and the squamocolumnar junction; apply 3–5% acetic acid with a cotton swab; wait for one minute and inspect under good light.
  • Result – VIA positive when a well-defined, dense acetowhite area appears near the squamocolumnar junction; a cauliflower growth or ulcer is suspicious of cancer.
  • Action – positive women are offered same-visit treatment (thermal ablation or cryotherapy) if eligible, or referred for colposcopy and biopsy; suspicious growths are referred urgently.
  • Recording and follow-up – entry in the NCD records/portal, tracing of positive women, and screening every 5 years for negative women aged 30–65.

Nursing importance

  • Nurses vaccinate girls, counsel parents, perform VIA screening, ensure follow-up of positive women and give skilled, compassionate care through surgery, radiotherapy and palliation – they are central to India's effort to eliminate cervical cancer.

Conclusion Cervical cancer is caused by HPV and is largely preventable. HPV vaccination of girls, regular VIA/HPV screening with treatment of pre-cancers, and stage-appropriate surgery or chemoradiation with good nursing and palliative care can greatly reduce suffering and deaths.

question: Explain pelvic inflammatory disease and the syndromic management of reproductive tract infections as per NACO guidelines.
answer_html:
Introduction Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is infection and inflammation of the upper female genital tract – the endometrium, fallopian tubes, ovaries and pelvic peritoneum (endometritis, salpingitis, tubo-ovarian abscess, pelvic peritonitis). It is usually caused by ascending infection from the cervix and vagina and is a major cause of infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain.

1. Causes and risk factors

  • Organisms – Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (sexually transmitted), Mycoplasma genitalium, anaerobes and other vaginal bacteria; genital tuberculosis is an important cause of chronic PID and infertility in India.
  • Risk factors – young age, multiple sexual partners or a partner with an STI, previous PID or STI, no barrier contraception, IUCD insertion (risk mainly in the first 3 weeks), unsafe abortion, childbirth with infection, uterine instrumentation (D&C, HSG).

2. Clinical features

  • Lower abdominal pain (usually bilateral), fever, purulent vaginal discharge, deep dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding, painful micturition.
  • Signs – lower abdominal tenderness, cervical motion (excitation) tenderness, adnexal tenderness, and sometimes a tender adnexal mass (tubo-ovarian abscess).
  • Chronic PID – recurrent pelvic pain, backache, heavy painful periods, infertility.
  • Investigations – urine pregnancy test (exclude ectopic pregnancy), blood count, CRP/ESR, cervical swabs (gonococcus, chlamydia), HIV and syphilis tests, ultrasound for abscess; laparoscopy when the diagnosis is uncertain.

3. Treatment

  • Outpatient – the yellow kit (below) for 14 days, analgesics, rest, abstinence from intercourse until both partners complete treatment; review after 72 hours.
  • Admit for high fever, vomiting, pregnancy, tubo-ovarian abscess, suspected surgical emergency or no response to oral treatment – IV antibiotics (for example ceftriaxone with doxycycline and metronidazole), IV fluids; drainage of an abscess; removal of an IUCD if there is no improvement in 48–72 hours.
  • Complications – tubal blockage and infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, recurrence, pelvic abscess, peritonitis, and perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome).

4. Syndromic case management (NACO)

  • Meaning – treating STIs/RTIs on the basis of syndromes (groups of symptoms and signs) using flowcharts and pre-packed colour-coded drug kits, so that a patient can be treated in the first visit without waiting for laboratory tests. The kits are provided free at designated STI/RTI clinics (Suraksha clinics) and health facilities.
  • Colour-coded kits (NACO National Technical Guidelines on STI/RTI, 2024)
Kit colour Syndrome Contents (2024)
Grey Urethral discharge, cervical discharge, painful scrotal swelling, presumptive treatment Azithromycin 1 g + cefixime 800 mg, single dose
Green Vaginal discharge (vaginitis) Secnidazole 2 g + fluconazole 150 mg, single dose
White Genital ulcer, non-herpetic Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM + azithromycin 1 g
Blue Genital ulcer, non-herpetic (penicillin allergy) Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 14 days + azithromycin 1 g
Red Genital ulcer, herpetic Acyclovir 400 mg three times daily × 7 days
Yellow Lower abdominal pain (PID) Cefixime 800 mg single dose + metronidazole 400 mg twice daily × 14 days + doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 14 days
Black Inguinal bubo; LGV proctitis Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 21 days
Brown (new) Anorectal discharge Cefixime 800 mg single dose + doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 14 days
  • The "4 Cs" with every treatment – Compliance (complete the course), Counselling (risk reduction), Condoms (promotion and supply) and Contact (partner) treatment; plus referral for HIV and syphilis testing.

5. Nursing role

  • Take a respectful, confidential history; examine with privacy and a chaperone.
  • Explain the treatment schedule, side effects (metronidazole – avoid alcohol) and the need for partner treatment.
  • Teach genital hygiene, safe sex and early reporting of symptoms; follow up for fertility concerns.

Conclusion PID is a serious, preventable complication of untreated lower genital infection. Early syndromic treatment with the yellow kit, partner treatment, condom use and follow-up protect a woman's future fertility.

question: Explain the common vaginal infections (vaginitis) – bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis and trichomoniasis – with their management.
answer_html:
Introduction The healthy vagina is protected by lactobacilli (Döderlein's bacilli), which keep the pH acidic (about 3.8–4.5). Physiological discharge (leucorrhoea) – clear or white, non-irritating and odourless – increases at puberty, around ovulation, in pregnancy and before menses. Vaginitis is inflammation of the vagina, usually due to infection, with abnormal discharge, itching, burning or odour.

1. Bacterial vaginosis (BV)

  • Cause – loss of lactobacilli and overgrowth of anaerobes and Gardnerella vaginalis (not strictly an STI).
  • Features – thin, grey-white, homogeneous discharge with a fishy odour, worse after intercourse or menses; little itching.
  • Diagnosis (Amsel's criteria – any 3 of 4) – the typical discharge, pH above 4.5, positive whiff test (fishy smell on adding 10% KOH), clue cells on microscopy.
  • Treatment – metronidazole 400–500 mg twice daily for 7 days (or a single 2 g dose), or clindamycin cream; avoid alcohol with metronidazole; partner treatment is not routine. In pregnancy BV is linked with preterm labour, so it is treated.

2. Vulvovaginal candidiasis (thrush)

  • Cause – Candida albicans; favoured by pregnancy, diabetes, antibiotics, steroids, combined pills, HIV and tight synthetic clothing.
  • Features – intense itching and burning, a thick, white, curdy ("cottage-cheese") discharge, red swollen vulva, painful intercourse and urination; pH normal.
  • Diagnosis – KOH mount shows budding yeast and hyphae; culture for recurrent cases.
  • Treatment – clotrimazole vaginal pessary (500 mg once or 100 mg for 6 nights) or oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose (not in pregnancy – use vaginal treatment); control blood sugar; recurrent cases need longer courses.

3. Trichomoniasis

  • Cause – the flagellate Trichomonas vaginalis; sexually transmitted.
  • Features – profuse, frothy, greenish-yellow, foul-smelling discharge, itching, burning micturition; the cervix may show punctate haemorrhages ("strawberry cervix"); pH above 5.
  • Diagnosis – wet mount showing motile trichomonads.
  • Treatment – metronidazole 2 g single dose or 400–500 mg twice daily for 7 days, with treatment of the sexual partner and abstinence until both are cured.

4. Other causes – atrophic vaginitis after menopause (thin, dry, bleeding-prone mucosa – local oestrogen cream), foreign bodies (forgotten tampon or pessary), cervicitis, allergic reactions to soaps and douches.

5. Syndromic treatment – where microscopy is not available, women with vaginal discharge are treated with the NACO green kit (secnidazole 2 g + fluconazole 150 mg), and the grey kit is added when cervicitis is suspected.

6. Nursing advice

  • Wash the genital area with plain water; wipe from front to back; avoid douching, scented soaps and sprays.
  • Wear loose cotton underwear; change sanitary pads 4–6 hourly; keep the area dry.
  • Complete the full course of treatment; partner treatment for trichomoniasis; condom use; control diabetes.
  • Report recurrent, blood-stained or foul discharge for further examination (including cervical screening).

Conclusion Bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis and trichomoniasis can be told apart by the type of discharge and simple bedside tests; correct treatment, partner management when needed and hygiene education prevent recurrence.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: Explain endometriosis – its sites, theories, clinical features and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Endometriosis is the presence of functioning endometrial tissue (glands and stroma) outside the uterine cavity. This tissue responds to cyclical hormones and bleeds during menstruation, causing inflammation, pain and adhesions. It affects about 10% of women of reproductive age and is oestrogen-dependent, so it regresses after menopause. (Adenomyosis – endometrium within the uterine muscle – is a related but separate condition.)

1. Common sites

  • Ovaries – blood-filled cysts called endometriomas ("chocolate cysts").
  • Pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligaments, pelvic peritoneum, rectovaginal septum.
  • Less often – bladder, bowel, umbilicus, caesarean or episiotomy scars, and rarely lungs.

2. Theories of origin

  • Retrograde menstruation (Sampson's implantation theory) – menstrual blood flows back through the tubes and endometrial cells implant on the peritoneum.
  • Coelomic metaplasia – peritoneal cells change into endometrium.
  • Lymphatic and vascular spread (Halban) – explains distant sites.
  • Direct (iatrogenic) implantation – in surgical scars.
  • Immune and genetic factors explain why only some women develop it.

3. Clinical features

  • Secondary, progressive dysmenorrhoea – the classic symptom.
  • Deep dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain, painful defaecation (dyschezia) during menses.
  • Infertility – in about a third to half of affected women.
  • Heavy or irregular periods; cyclical bleeding from bladder or bowel when involved.
  • Signs – a fixed, retroverted uterus, tender nodules in the pouch of Douglas or uterosacral ligaments, adnexal masses; examination may be normal in mild disease.

4. Diagnosis

  • Transvaginal ultrasound (endometrioma), MRI for deep disease.
  • Laparoscopy – the gold standard, showing "powder-burn" or red lesions and chocolate cysts, with biopsy and staging.
  • CA-125 may be raised but is not diagnostic.

5. Management (depends on age, symptoms, extent and wish for pregnancy)

  • Pain relief – NSAIDs (mefenamic acid, ibuprofen).
  • Hormonal suppression – combined oral pills (cyclical or continuous), progestins (dienogest, norethisterone), LNG-IUS, and GnRH analogues with "add-back" hormone therapy for short courses.
  • Surgery – laparoscopic excision or ablation of lesions and division of adhesions; ovarian cystectomy for endometriomas.
  • Infertility – surgery and/or IVF.
  • Severe disease with completed family – hysterectomy with removal of the ovaries and excision of deposits.

6. Nursing role

  • Listen and believe the woman's pain – diagnosis is often delayed for years because period pain is considered "normal".
  • Teach the use of analgesics and hormones, side effects, and the value of exercise, heat and healthy diet; counsel about fertility and sexual concerns; offer emotional support.

Conclusion Endometriosis is a common, chronic, oestrogen-dependent disease causing pain and infertility; early recognition, laparoscopic diagnosis and long-term medical or surgical treatment, with supportive nursing, improve quality of life.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: Explain polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) – diagnosis, long-term risks and management.
tags: commonest endocrine disorder of reproductive age
answer_html:
Introduction Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is the commonest hormonal (endocrine) disorder of women of reproductive age, affecting about 8–13% of women (and more in some Indian studies). It is a syndrome of ovulatory dysfunction, excess androgens and polycystic ovaries, closely linked with insulin resistance and obesity.

1. Diagnosis – Rotterdam criteria (any two of three), after excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia and congenital adrenal hyperplasia:

  • Oligo-ovulation or anovulation – irregular, infrequent or absent periods.
  • Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism – hirsutism, acne, scalp hair thinning; raised testosterone.
  • Polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound – 20 or more follicles per ovary and/or ovarian volume of 10 ml or more (not used in adolescents within 8 years of menarche).

2. Clinical features

  • Irregular or absent periods, heavy bleeding after long gaps.
  • Hirsutism, acne, male-pattern hair loss.
  • Obesity (especially central), acanthosis nigricans (dark velvety skin on the neck and axillae – a sign of insulin resistance).
  • Infertility due to anovulation; higher miscarriage and pregnancy complications (GDM, pre-eclampsia).
  • Anxiety, depression and poor body image.

3. Long-term risks

  • Type 2 diabetes, GDM, metabolic syndrome, dyslipidaemia, hypertension and cardiovascular disease.
  • Endometrial hyperplasia and cancer – from unopposed oestrogen when periods are infrequent.
  • Obstructive sleep apnoea, fatty liver, mood disorders.

4. Management

  • Lifestyle modification (first line) – healthy diet, regular exercise, and a weight loss of 5–10%, which alone can restore ovulation and improve symptoms.
  • Menstrual regulation and endometrial protection – combined oral contraceptive pills (also reduce hirsutism and acne) or cyclical progestins to cause regular withdrawal bleeds.
  • Metabolic treatment – metformin for insulin resistance, glucose intolerance or as advised; screening for diabetes and lipids.
  • Hirsutism – COCs, anti-androgens (spironolactone, with contraception), cosmetic measures (threading, waxing, laser).
  • Infertility – letrozole (first choice for ovulation induction) or clomiphene, gonadotrophins, laparoscopic ovarian drilling, and IVF when needed.
  • Psychological support and treatment of depression.

5. Nursing role

  • Health education on diet (low glycaemic index foods, millets, vegetables, avoiding sugary drinks and junk food), daily physical activity and weight monitoring.
  • Explain that PCOS is common and manageable; support adolescents and young women emotionally.
  • Encourage regular screening for blood sugar, BP and lipids, and prompt evaluation of very infrequent periods.

Conclusion PCOS is a common lifelong metabolic and reproductive disorder; lifestyle change is the foundation of treatment, supported by hormonal therapy, metformin and ovulation induction, with long-term screening for diabetes and endometrial disease.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: Explain dysmenorrhoea – types, causes and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Dysmenorrhoea means painful menstruation severe enough to interfere with daily activities. It is very common among adolescent girls and young women and a leading cause of school and work absence. It is classified as primary (no pelvic disease) and secondary (due to pelvic pathology).

1. Primary (spasmodic) dysmenorrhoea

  • Cause – excess prostaglandin F₂α produced by the endometrium of ovulatory cycles causes strong uterine contractions and ischaemia; anxiety lowers the pain threshold.
  • Features – begins 6–12 months after menarche (when cycles become ovulatory); cramping lower abdominal pain starting just before or with the flow and lasting 48–72 hours, radiating to the back and thighs; nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, fainting. Pelvic examination is normal.
  • It often improves with age and after childbirth.

2. Secondary (congestive) dysmenorrhoea

  • Causes – endometriosis, adenomyosis, PID, fibroids and polyps, IUCD, cervical stenosis, congenital anomalies with obstruction.
  • Features – starts years after menarche (often after 25), pain begins days before the period and may last throughout or after it, with dyspareunia, heavy bleeding or infertility; pelvic findings may be abnormal.
Point Primary Secondary
Onset Soon after menarche Later in life
Pathology None Present (endometriosis, PID, fibroids)
Timing of pain Starts with flow, lasts 1–3 days Begins before flow, lasts longer
Other symptoms Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea Dyspareunia, menorrhagia, infertility
Treatment NSAIDs, pills Treat the cause

3. Management

  • Reassurance and education about menstruation; adequate rest and sleep.
  • NSAIDs (prostaglandin inhibitors) – mefenamic acid or ibuprofen, started at the onset of pain or flow and taken regularly for 2–3 days, after food.
  • Combined oral contraceptive pills (they stop ovulation) for women who also need contraception or do not respond to NSAIDs.
  • Non-drug measures – heat (hot water bag on the lower abdomen), regular exercise and yoga, warm drinks, a balanced diet with less salt and caffeine before periods, relaxation, TENS.
  • Secondary dysmenorrhoea – investigate (ultrasound, laparoscopy) and treat the cause.
  • Refer if pain does not respond to NSAIDs and pills, is progressive, or is associated with heavy bleeding, dyspareunia or infertility.

4. Nursing role

  • Menstrual health education in schools and colleges; break myths and taboos; teach correct use of analgesics; provide a place to rest and sanitary facilities; identify girls with severe or worsening pain for referral.

Conclusion Primary dysmenorrhoea is due to prostaglandins and responds well to NSAIDs, pills and simple measures, whereas secondary dysmenorrhoea is a symptom of pelvic disease that must be found and treated.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: Explain the causes, investigations and management of primary and secondary amenorrhoea.
tags: 3 months regular or 6 months irregular cycles
answer_html:
Introduction Amenorrhoea is the absence of menstruation. It is physiological before puberty, during pregnancy (always exclude first) and lactation, and after menopause. Pathological amenorrhoea is a symptom of many disorders of the hypothalamus, pituitary, ovary, uterus or outflow tract.

  • Primary amenorrhoea – no menstruation by 15 years of age with normal secondary sexual characteristics, or by 13 years with no breast development (or within 3 years of breast development).
  • Secondary amenorrhoea – absence of menses for 3 months in a woman with previously regular cycles, or 6 months with irregular cycles.

1. Causes (compartment approach)

Level Causes
Hypothalamus Stress, rapid weight loss, eating disorders, excessive exercise, chronic illness, Kallmann syndrome (with loss of smell)
Pituitary Hyperprolactinaemia / prolactinoma, Sheehan's syndrome, other tumours
Ovary PCOS, Turner syndrome (45,X) and gonadal dysgenesis, premature ovarian insufficiency, damage by chemotherapy or radiation
Uterus MRKH syndrome (absent uterus and upper vagina), Asherman's syndrome (adhesions after curettage), endometrial tuberculosis
Outflow tract Imperforate hymen, transverse vaginal septum, cervical stenosis (cryptomenorrhoea – menses formed but not shed)
Others Thyroid disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY), drugs (antipsychotics, hormonal contraceptives)

2. Investigations

  • Urine pregnancy test – always first in secondary amenorrhoea.
  • History and examination – growth, BMI, secondary sexual characteristics (Tanner stage), hirsutism, galactorrhoea, signs of Turner syndrome, cyclical pain (cryptomenorrhoea), inspection of the hymen and vagina.
  • Hormones – TSH, prolactin, FSH, LH, oestradiol, testosterone.
  • Progesterone challenge test – a withdrawal bleed after progesterone shows that the uterus and outflow tract are normal and oestrogen is present; then the oestrogen–progesterone test if needed.
  • Pelvic ultrasound (uterus, ovaries, haematocolpos); karyotype (primary amenorrhoea, high FSH); MRI of the pituitary for raised prolactin; hysteroscopy for Asherman's; endometrial biopsy for TB.

3. Management – treat the cause

  • Hypothalamic – stress management, nutritional rehabilitation, moderating exercise; hormone replacement if oestrogen is low.
  • Hyperprolactinaemia – cabergoline or bromocriptine; stop causative drugs.
  • Hypothyroidism – thyroxine.
  • PCOS – lifestyle change, cyclical progestins or combined pills.
  • Ovarian failure / Turner syndrome – hormone replacement therapy for puberty, bone and heart health; fertility through donor eggs.
  • Outflow obstruction – hymenotomy (cruciate incision) for imperforate hymen; excision of a vaginal septum.
  • MRKH syndrome – vaginal dilators or vaginoplasty; counselling about surrogacy or adoption.
  • Asherman's – hysteroscopic adhesiolysis; TB – anti-tubercular treatment.

4. Nursing role

  • Sensitive, private counselling – girls and families are anxious about marriage and fertility; explain tests and diagnoses (such as MRKH or androgen insensitivity) gently and with specialist support.
  • Encourage healthy weight and diet, regular follow-up and adherence to hormone therapy.

Conclusion Amenorrhoea is a symptom, not a disease; after excluding pregnancy, a systematic compartment-wise evaluation identifies the cause, and treatment is directed at it with careful counselling.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: Explain the congenital anomalies of the female genital tract and their effects.
answer_html:
Introduction The uterus, cervix and upper two-thirds of the vagina develop from the fusion of the two Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts, followed by absorption of the dividing septum, while the lower vagina forms from the urogenital sinus. Failure of development, fusion or absorption produces congenital anomalies, found in a few per cent of women; they are often associated with urinary tract (kidney) anomalies.

1. Types

Group Anomaly Remarks
Failure of development Müllerian agenesis (MRKH syndrome) Absent uterus and upper vagina; normal ovaries and breasts; primary amenorrhoea
Unicornuate uterus Only one duct develops; may have a rudimentary horn
Failure of fusion Uterus didelphys Two uteri, two cervices, often a vaginal septum
Bicornuate uterus Heart-shaped uterus with a notch on the fundus
Failure of septal absorption Septate / subseptate uterus Commonest; worst reproductive outcome (recurrent miscarriage)
Arcuate uterus Slight fundal indentation; usually harmless
Vaginal and hymenal Transverse vaginal septum, longitudinal septum, imperforate hymen Obstruction to menstrual flow
Cervical Cervical agenesis or atresia Obstruction, pain

2. Effects

  • Gynaecological – primary amenorrhoea (agenesis); cryptomenorrhoea with cyclical lower abdominal pain, haematocolpos and haematometra (imperforate hymen – a bulging bluish membrane at the introitus, sometimes urinary retention); dyspareunia; dysmenorrhoea; endometriosis from retrograde flow.
  • Reproductive – infertility, recurrent first- and second-trimester miscarriage, preterm labour, malpresentation (breech, transverse lie), fetal growth restriction, retained placenta, PPH, obstructed labour (vaginal septum).
  • Associated renal anomalies – absent or abnormal kidney on the same side.

3. Diagnosis

  • Examination of the vulva, hymen and vagina; 3D ultrasound and MRI (best for classification); HSG; hysteroscopy and laparoscopy together for septate versus bicornuate uterus; renal ultrasound.

4. Management

  • Imperforate hymen – cruciate incision (hymenotomy) and drainage of retained blood.
  • Transverse vaginal septum – surgical excision.
  • Septate uterus – hysteroscopic resection of the septum in women with recurrent loss.
  • Bicornuate uterus – rarely needs metroplasty (Strassman); cervical cerclage may be advised in some.
  • MRKH syndrome – vaginal dilators (first choice) or vaginoplasty to create a functional vagina; fertility through surrogacy with her own eggs (IVF), or adoption; psychological support.
  • Pregnancy in an anomalous uterus – close surveillance for preterm labour, malpresentation and growth; delivery in hospital.

5. Nursing role

  • Recognise cyclical pain without menses in adolescent girls and refer; prepare for procedures; give compassionate counselling about sexuality and fertility; support the family.

Conclusion Müllerian anomalies range from harmless (arcuate) to those causing amenorrhoea, obstruction, infertility and pregnancy loss; accurate imaging and appropriate surgery, with sensitive counselling, give good results.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: Explain the gynaecological assessment of a woman, with the procedure of taking a Pap smear and the nurse's role.
answer_html:
Introduction A gynaecological assessment – history, general and systemic examination, and pelvic examination – is the basis of diagnosis of disorders of the female reproductive system. Because it involves intimate examination, it must be done with privacy, dignity, consent and a female chaperone. The Pap smear is a simple test, usually done during this examination, to detect precancerous changes of the cervix.

1. History

  • Presenting complaints – bleeding, discharge, pain, mass, urinary or bowel symptoms, infertility.
  • Menstrual history – age at menarche, cycle length, duration, amount, pain, last menstrual period, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, menopause.
  • Obstetric history – gravida, para, abortions, mode of delivery, complications.
  • Contraceptive, sexual and STI history; previous gynaecological surgery and screening tests.
  • Medical, drug, family and personal history.

2. Examination

  • General – build, BMI, pallor, BP, thyroid, lymph nodes, hirsutism.
  • Breast examination (and teaching of breast self-awareness).
  • Abdominal examination – masses, tenderness, scars, hernia.
  • Pelvic examination
    • Inspection of the external genitalia – lesions, discharge, prolapse on straining, stress incontinence.
    • Speculum examination – Cusco's bivalve speculum to view the cervix and vagina (Pap smear, VIA, swabs); Sims' speculum in the left lateral position for prolapse and fistula.
    • Bimanual examination – size, position, mobility and tenderness of the uterus; adnexal masses; cervical motion tenderness.
    • Rectovaginal examination when indicated (parametria, pouch of Douglas).
  • Positions – dorsal or lithotomy for most examinations; left lateral (Sims') for prolapse and VVF.

3. Procedure of Pap smear

  • Timing – mid-cycle is best; not during menstruation; avoid intercourse, douching and vaginal medicines for 48 hours before.
  • Equipment – Cusco's speculum, Ayre's spatula, endocervical brush (cytobrush), labelled glass slides, 95% ethyl alcohol fixative (or spray fixative), gloves, request form; or a liquid-based cytology vial.
  • Steps
    • Explain, obtain consent, ask her to empty the bladder, and position her in the dorsal position with draping.
    • Insert the speculum without lubricant (or with warm water only) – lubricants spoil the smear.
    • Place the longer arm of the Ayre's spatula in the external os and rotate it through 360° to scrape the squamocolumnar junction; then insert the cytobrush into the canal and rotate it gently.
    • Spread the material thinly on the slide and fix it immediately in 95% alcohol (within seconds) to prevent air-drying.
    • Label the slide, complete the form (age, LMP, findings) and send to the laboratory.
  • Reporting by the Bethesda system (normal, ASC-US, LSIL, HSIL, cancer); abnormal results are referred for colposcopy. (In India's national programme, VIA is the main screening test for women aged 30–65; HPV DNA testing is used where available.)

4. Nurse's role

  • Prepare the room, equipment and good light; ensure privacy and a female chaperone.
  • Explain each step; help her relax (deep breathing, knees apart, buttocks at the edge); warm the speculum.
  • Assist the doctor, label specimens correctly, fix smears promptly and dispatch them.
  • After the procedure – help her clean and dress; explain that slight spotting is possible; tell her when and how she will get the result; ensure follow-up of abnormal reports.
  • Educate women about regular screening and HPV vaccination for daughters.

Conclusion A careful, respectful gynaecological assessment and a correctly taken Pap smear are essential skills; the nurse's preparation, support and follow-up make the examination comfortable and the screening effective.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: What is precocious puberty?
answer_html:
• Precocious puberty is the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics (breast development, pubic hair) before 8 years of age in a girl, or menarche before about 10 years.
  • Central (true, gonadotrophin-dependent) – early activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary axis; in girls usually idiopathic, sometimes due to brain tumours, hydrocephalus or infection.
  • Peripheral (pseudo, gonadotrophin-independent) – oestrogen from ovarian tumours or cysts, adrenal disorders, McCune–Albright syndrome, or exogenous hormones.
  • Effects – early fusion of growth plates causing short adult height, and emotional and social problems.
  • Management – bone age, hormone tests (LH/FSH, GnRH stimulation), pelvic ultrasound, MRI brain; GnRH analogues for central type; treatment of the cause; counselling.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: What is a Bartholin's cyst and abscess? How are they managed?
answer_html:
• The Bartholin's glands lie on each side of the vaginal opening (at about 4 and 8 o'clock) and secrete lubricating mucus.
  • Bartholin's cyst – blockage of the duct leads to a painless, soft swelling of the posterior part of the labium majus.
  • Bartholin's abscess – infection of the cyst or gland (E. coli, staphylococci, gonococci, anaerobes) causing a very painful, red, tender, hot swelling, fever and difficulty in walking or sitting.
  • Management – small cysts: sitz baths and observation; abscess: analgesics, antibiotics and incision and drainage with a Word catheter or marsupialisation (preferred for recurrent cases, as it keeps the gland open); excision of recurrent cysts; biopsy in women above 40 to exclude cancer.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: What is colposcopy?
answer_html:
• Colposcopy is the examination of the cervix (and vagina and vulva) under magnification (about 6–40 times) with a bright light, using an instrument called a colposcope, to identify abnormal areas and take directed biopsies.
  • 3–5% acetic acid makes abnormal epithelium appear white (acetowhite); Lugol's iodine stains normal epithelium brown while abnormal areas remain unstained (Schiller's test); abnormal patterns include punctation, mosaicism and atypical vessels.
  • Indications – abnormal Pap smear, positive HPV test or VIA, suspicious-looking cervix, postcoital bleeding.
  • It also guides treatment of precancer (LEEP/LLETZ, thermal ablation).
  • Nursing – explain that it is painless, position her as for a speculum examination, and advise that mild spotting may follow a biopsy (avoid intercourse and tampons for a few days).

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: What is dilatation and curettage (D&C)? State the nursing care.
answer_html:
• D&C is a procedure in which the cervical canal is dilated with graduated (Hegar's) dilators and the lining of the uterus is scraped with a curette, usually under anaesthesia.
  • Uses – diagnostic (endometrial sampling in AUB or postmenopausal bleeding, endometrial TB in infertility) and therapeutic (removal of polyps; retained products – now mostly by suction/MVA). Today, Pipelle sampling and hysteroscopy-directed biopsy are often preferred.
  • Complications – perforation of the uterus, bleeding, infection, cervical injury, intrauterine adhesions (Asherman's syndrome).
  • Nursing care – consent, nil by mouth, empty bladder, perineal preparation; after the procedure, monitor vital signs and bleeding, give analgesics; send tissue in 10% formalin for histology (in normal saline when TB culture/GeneXpert is needed), labelled correctly; advise that spotting may occur for a few days, avoid intercourse and tampons for 1–2 weeks, and report heavy bleeding, fever or foul discharge.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: What is hysterosalpingography (HSG)?
answer_html:
• HSG is an X-ray examination of the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes after injecting a water-soluble radio-opaque contrast through the cervix under fluoroscopy.
  • Uses – mainly to test tubal patency in infertility (free spill of dye into the peritoneal cavity means open tubes); also shows uterine anomalies, polyps, adhesions and hydrosalpinx, and confirms tubal block after sterilisation.
  • Timing – in the follicular phase, after menstruation stops and before ovulation (about days 7–10), to avoid irradiating an early pregnancy.
  • Contraindications – pregnancy, active pelvic infection, recent curettage, heavy bleeding, iodine allergy.
  • Nursing care – explain the procedure, give an analgesic about an hour before and a prophylactic antibiotic when advised; watch afterwards for pain, vasovagal fainting, fever or foul discharge; mild cramps and spotting are common.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: What is postmenopausal bleeding? List its causes.
answer_html:
• Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) is any vaginal bleeding that occurs 12 months or more after the last menstrual period. It is always abnormal and must be investigated, because about 5–10% of women with PMB have endometrial cancer.
  • Causes
    • Atrophic vaginitis or atrophic endometrium (the commonest).
    • Endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma; carcinoma of the cervix; rarely vulval, vaginal or tubal cancer.
    • Endometrial or cervical polyps; hormone replacement therapy; oestrogen-secreting ovarian tumours (granulosa cell tumour).
    • Decubitus ulcer of a prolapse, pessary, trauma, anticoagulants, bleeding disorders; bleeding from a urethral caruncle or the rectum may be mistaken for it.
  • Evaluation – speculum examination, transvaginal ultrasound (an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less is reassuring), endometrial biopsy and hysteroscopy; cervical screening.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing II (including Safe Delivery App module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Women with Gynaecological Disorders and Infertility
question: What is torsion of an ovarian cyst? How is it managed?
tags: sudden severe unilateral lower abdominal pain
answer_html:
• Torsion is the twisting of the pedicle of an ovarian cyst (often with the tube), first blocking the veins and then the arteries, leading to congestion, haemorrhagic infarction and gangrene of the ovary.
  • It is common with moderate-sized (5–10 cm), mobile, benign cysts – especially dermoid cysts – and in pregnancy and the puerperium.
  • Features – sudden, severe, colicky pain in one iliac fossa, nausea and vomiting, low-grade fever, a tender adnexal mass; ultrasound with Doppler (reduced flow, "whirlpool sign").
  • Management – an emergency: laparoscopy or laparotomy, untwisting (detorsion) and removal of the cyst (cystectomy), conserving the ovary whenever possible even if it looks dusky; salpingo-oophorectomy only if it is clearly gangrenous.
